The proprietors of the Manchester Clothing Depitt have great pleasure in again submitting their very extensive prepara- tions for the approaching autumn and winter.

The reputation of the Manchester Clothing DepOt for men's. youths', and boys' fashionable and well-made clothing is known all over Lancashire and Cheshi:e, and is proved by the great and ever-increasing demand for their goods for many miles around their Depots. _ .

It is a well-known fact that no house can beat them for ready-made men's and boys' clothing and tailoring, either for quality, style, or perfect-fitting garments, as tl.ey pur,hase all their cloths for cash only from the best manufacturers, they employ the m•st skilled labour, use the best trimmings, and have all their goods made up under their own supervision at their extensive works in Manchester. ..
Those who have not patronised them should do so, as the proprietors feel confident that it would prove ths superiority and cheapness of their goods to those of any other house.

The Manchester Clothing Depot have a very extensive de- partment for juvenile clothing, in wh'cli will be found a very large and choice assortment of the newest designs In juven.ils. attire to suit all clas:es.

The Measure Order Department is a very important feature in this establishment. Extewive ranges of the newest fabecs. for the season are being shown, and as only skillful cutters are employed a perfect fit can be relied on.

The Manchester Cl-thing Depot, having such an extensive range of gods. it is impossible to give full quotations of prices (which are often mislatding); they rely solely on the value of their goods. eRd whatever price a customer may give for an article they will have full value for their money.

WHY MOTHBR 13 PROITD. Look In his face, look in his eyes, Roguish and ohae, and terribly wise— Roguish and blue, but quickest to see When mother comes in as tired as can be. Quickest to find her the nicest old chair, Qui.akest to get to the top of the stair; Quickest to see that a kiss on her cheek Would help her far more than to chatter, to speak. Look in his face, and guess, if you can, Why mother is proud of her little man. The mother is proud—l will tell you this; You can see it yourself in her tender kiss. But why? Well, of all her dears There is scarcely one who ever hears The moment she speaks, and jumps to see What her want or her wishes might be. Scarcely one. They all forget, Or are not In the notioq to go quite yet. But this she knows, if her boy is near, There is somebody certain to want to hear. Mother is proud, and she holds him fast. And kisses him first and kisses him last; And he holds her hand and looks in her face, And hunts for her spool which is out of place, And proves thaftphe loves her whenever he can; Sliat is why she is proud of her little man.

Then, turning to his father, he said, "Pa, the, engine's all out of breath, ain't it ?" A correspondent asks—" Cea a boy leave his father when he is eighteen years old ?" If a father is eighteen years old a son is justified in leaving bins, because he ought by that ter e to be able to take care of himself. • "1 wish I bad a gentleman opposite to me," said at irri- et. teele old fellow at a dinner party. A gentleman was complaining on 'Change that he had invested a large sum of money, and loet it all. A sympathi- sing triead asked ohm whether ha had been a bull or a bear. To which he replied, 'Neither; I was a jackass!" A man Ate seven cucumbers, a few radishes, a basket of strawberries, and drank part of a wineglass full of water before going to bed one night. Next day he said," A person had no business to drink water jest before retiring." On a rainy morning a small boy who has exhausted all his excuses fur not patting in an appearance at school, opens the door and says to the astonished master, "Sir, sass I can's come to school tieday --Ws raining too bard." A person overheard two countrymen who were observing a naturalist in the field collecting insects, say one to another, 1 "What's that fellow doing, John ?". "Why, he's a natu• ralist." " What's that ?" "Why, one who catches gnats, to be sure!" Persevere in whatever calling you adopt. Your progress may be slow and results seemingly meagre; but that is no reason for growing faint-hearted. Remember how the little brook persistently winds its way to the river, and the river to the ocean—both reach their destination. Two men were making arrangements to get into business. One of them said "It is understood, now, I get two. thirds of the profit, having put in the most capital, and you get . one-third." "All right," replied the other; but if we have great luck and fail, then we are to divide the profits . squally." The happiest children are those who have happy mothers. The young life which grows up in the shadow of a discon- tented, repining, and gloomy mother is like a plant en- watered by kindly dews. It is apt to be dwarfed and stunted. Even when things are croeked and temptations to be harsh come' let the mother, for her suns' and daughters' sake, try s be happy. You no doubt are well off; /eel 'hard up,' so I most fain keep the money, bat I return the pass, which is useless to me. My thanks, believe trie. are unlimited." CLEARING TEE CARRItGE —A. good story is told of the •B late Mr. Merewetber, Q.C. Wishing to have a railway carri- • age on the Great Western to himself, in order to study a brief, he was a good deal annoyed by the presence of A talka- tive curate. The Q.C. feigned insanity, whereupon the curate thought his safety lay only in soothing his fellow traveller. Passing the large madhouse at Hanwell, the curate remarked in dulcet tones, such aa a nurse would apply to a fractious child, "How well the asylum looks from the railway." Mr. Atireveether gave a bark like a dog, and replied, "Yes, but you should see how well the railway 4 looks tram the asylum." The train stopped at Slough, and the eu'ans disappeired with the utmost alacrity. Tan 'Vous° Wires Nreenenwosit.—lf a man bas ne muther or sisters to undeetake for him in f.ir0".41 MAUS; at the time esl hie marriage he not infrequently think§ more of feathering the neet for his mate than of his own plumage. -Ills Wife is apt to find, not so long after the honeymoon has Vaned, that her husband's wardrobe, as far as regards the noderlinen, needs renovating. A few sappressed groans, or a smothered something *out 'buttons," draws her atten- tion to this branch of her new duties, and she makes an in- spection, which very probably results in discoveries which fill her with dismay or amusement. Dismay, if while rea- lising the responsibility that now falls upon her as a wife, '- she feels herself incapable of undertaking it from want of experience and ignorance. Amusement, if she has been conversant with such matters for father or brothers at home, and sees no difficulty before her, but rather a wifely pride in her own skill and ability to set everything right. Few men when they buy their under linen ever think it neces- e' eery to inquire whether they are made with chain or lock. stitch machine work • probably they are told that it is all "the beat hand needlework," and pay for it accordinrly. if the work happens to be (and in the cheaper class of gtexim * it generally is) chain stitch machine work, amusing and annoying results inevitably follow. Men are not all se p Went as Job. An article is put on hurriedly or impatiently, the thread breaks, and the stitch with the least exertion runs down—erobably a collar comes half of or or a sleeve comes out eittirely, or the leg is opened half-way down. Except in the very best houses ready-made linen is but flimsily put together--buttons seem made to come off, tapes are only Sacked on slightly, and button-holes are only seamed round. AU this the young wife sees at a glance. Her husband's under-linen is in a very hal state, what there is of it, and there is very little of it such as it is. CARLYLE ow Louts Naroazox.—" I chanced to meet him a few times at the houses of people who were accus- tomed to give dinners here; and I thought that there was won then something larking in him of the blood of the old niapoletut, who was, as I read it, the great Highwayman of history t his habit being to clutch Bing or Kaiser by the throat, and swear by the Eternal,' If you don't stand and deliver instantly, I'll blow your brains out.' A profitable trade he did at this sort of thing, until another man—Arthur Duke of Wellington by name—succeeded in clutching him, and there was an end of him. This Louis Napoleon, as its is called, used to talk to me about the Spirit of the Age, the Democratic Spirit, and the Progress of the Species ; but, for my own part, it seemed that the only Progress the Species was making was backward, and that the Spirit of the Age • was leading the people downward; and we discovered that we didn't understand each other's language; that we had no key In common for oar dialects. And we parted asunder —as maybap did. Abraham and Lot—each going his several ways. After that I need to see him in this neighbourhood (I think he had lodgings in this part of tbe town), with his heeds folded across his be sat, and his eyes fixed with a melancholy stare upon the ground, and he looked to me like a poor opera stager in search of an engagement. God knows he succeeded in finding an engagement upon a stage sufficiently vast, before an audience ample enough for any man, and the whole thing got up regardless of expense. But "*I certainly expect that the day will come when the blue sulphurous flames will dart front behind the scenes and con- sume the pile with all that are in it; or that the edifice will give way in a crash of ruin, and the whole—singer, audi- ence, and all—sink into the nethermost depths of uttermost perdition, where, it seems to me, they certainly belong.. It is not easy to understand why cheese made The behaviour of the people was everywhere of a most res- in different parts of England or of the Continent, in pre- pec"dul character. cisely the same manner, should yet. vary greatly in flavour, and that cheese made by the farmer in a particular district, although made in widely different ways, should yet be of very much the same flavour. Amongst farmers an opinion has prevailed to the effect that the taste of cheese is much influenced by peculiarities of soil and herbage. Some grasses, it is said, prefer one dePcription of soil, whilst others thrive on one entirely different, so although no difference of flavour can be detected in the milk, it was yet thought that the flavour of the cheeee might be affected by the grasses eaten by the cows. M. E. Daclanx's re- searches' however, go to show that neither climate, nor soil, nor food, nor variety in the breed of the cows largely affect the cheese, nor that the flavour depends to any yel, great extent upon manipaleti6n, except inasmuch as that manipulation causes one sort of ferment or organism to take possession of the cheese. From the iavestieations made by M. Daclaux, it appears that a fungous mould of a family allied in some cases to yeast, in others to mould, pervades the cheese, and that it is the presence of the germs of one or other of these organisms in the air of maticaler districts which affects the flavour of the cheese there made. A contemporary points oat that wide results may grow out of the researches which have been made, and that the time may come "when a farmer may purchase a variety of ferments from the agricultural chemist, and may inaocalate his new cheeses with one or another, according as he wishes to produce Cheshire or Cheddar, Stilton, Parmesan, or Gruyere. It is to be hoped that other investigators will follow up the clue which M. Daclaax his afforded them, and that practical remits of an important and valuable nature may be arrived at."

afterwards Lord Northington—befriended him,: and, having obtained a brief for him as his junior, stayed away on the plea of illness, and allowed Pratt to win the cause alone. Henceforward Pratt's rise was rapid, and he was appointed Attorney-General in the Ministry of the elder Pitt. Thence he was elevated to the seat of Lord Chief Jastice of the Common Pleas. John Wilkes having been arrested on a general warrant, i.e., a warrant not specifying the name of the person, Pratt issued his habeas corpus to the Lieutenant of the Tower. and discharged Wilkes from custody. In subsequent actions for damages brought by persons who had been arrested on general warrants, Pratt used the strongest language of denunciation against the proceedings of those in power, and he pronounced a warrant to search for and seize the papers of persons prosecuted for libel as utterly illegal and void. His independent conduct gave him well merited popularity, and he became one of the idols of the people, 45 witnela the portrait of him, with its inscription. that still hangs in GqildhallaS qf the gr,3ocqde of the citizens of London. The City Was, even then, the staunch and loyal supporter of popular rights, and those who served the people might always reckon on the aid and sym- pathy of the Corporation. When the first Rockingham Ministry assumed office, a forgotten Law-lord stood in the way of Pratt's elevation to the Woolsack; bat he had become the idol of the people, and it was necessary, in obedience to the popular demand, that something should be done for him. Therefore it was that he was elevated to the Peerage under the title of Lord Camden. The Rockingham Ministry was succeeded by that of Chatham, and Cam ten's old school- fellow and lifelong friend appointed him Lord Chancellor. At that time there was no regular provision of £5,000 per annum for ex-Lord Chancellon, and, in exchanging the permanent position of Lord Chief Justice for an uncertain position on the Woolsack, Lord Camden was quite justified in stipulating for a retiring pension of £1,500 per annum, and the reversion of an Exchequer Tellership for his eldest son. When Chatham ceased to take an active part in public busimss' the Ministry reverted to unpopular courses. , Though Camden approved of the expulsion of Wilkes freen the House of Commons, he disagreed with his colleagues as to the advisability of his expulsion after the freeholders of Middlesex had re-elecled him, as also in the foolish an suicidal course which was taken in the dispute with the American Colonies. At last, on Mansfield's insinuation that he was a consenting. party to the measures for coercing America, Camden openly broke away from the Ministry. Henceforth he staunchly supported Chatham in his vain endeavours to restrain the English Ga;vernment from the folly and crime of war with the revolted colonies. The closing years of Lord Camden's life were marked by a steady and consistent support of the populaieraesc. lie pleaded eloquently for justice to Ireland; he denounced the abuses of the-Pension List, declaring that, if necessary, he was ready to give up his own, though no pension in existence had been better earned; he shared the younger Pitt's youth- ful views on the necessity of Parliamentary Reform, and strongly supported them; and, above all, he was the main cause of the passage through the House of Lords of Mr. Fox's Libel Bill, which for ever settled the question that juries and not judges should decide what was and what WAS not a libel. Lord Camden, who had been some years previously advanced to an earldom, died in 1794, at the ripe old age of 81, leaving behind him a name that will ever be precious to the hearts of free Englishmen. I pass ;now to the second Earl, who Was subsequently created a Marquis. At the age of twenty-one he received the sinecure appointment of a Tellership in the Exchequer. Two years after, he was appointed a Lord of the Admiralty, and, a little liter, one of the Commissioners of the Treasury. lit 1795, he was Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland; in 1804,Secre- tary' of State for the Colonies; in 1805, Lord President of the Council, an office which he held, with a short interrup- tion, till 1812. But all the while he was a Teller of the Exchequer. In that year a stout old Radical, Mr. Creevy, brought before Parliament the scandalous amount of emolu- ments which Lord Camden received from his office. At the time of his appointment to the post, which it must not be forgotten was a sinecure, he did not receive from it more than £2,500 a year. During the American War the profits rose to £7,000, and in 1807 to no less than £23,000. In 1812, we were in the thick 6f the struggle with Napoleon Bonaparte, and the nation was much distressed by the cost of the proldnged war; nevertheless, when Mr. Creevy, after proving his case, proposed that the profits of Lord. Camden should be limited to some fixed and settled sum of money, more suited to the present means and resources of the nation, his demand was rejected. The scandal, however, had become so great, and was so constantly denounced, that Lord Cam- den resigned his claim on the extra emoluments of his sine- cure, which Was worth at that time, according to the "Georgian Era," between thirty and forty thousand pounds per annum. It appears, however, that it was not until five years afterwards that lie resigned his full claims. Then, having received for doing nothing the enormous sum of £740,000, he agreed to take £3,083 annually for his arduous labours. As he lived till 1840 he must have received about £85,000 more.

Daring this season a plantation covering 2,000 acres has been completed. It may be remembered that the Duke of Athole'e plantations were thinned of 80,000 trees by the gale whieh destroyed the ray Bridge. When the Planter Drake began operations on a large scale, in 1774.thes Dankeld hills were almost bete. During hie life the Duke, who may be described as a tree benefactor to is country, planted 27,000,000 trees, covering 15,000 acres.—Land. INCREASE OF LIINACY.—Pauper lunacy is, according to official reports, greatly on the increase in London, and the asylums are so fall of patients that the greatest difficulty hat been experienced in providing suitable accommodation for the cases as they arise. The Board of Guardians of St. Saviour's, Southwerk, was last week compelled to send some cases into Lancashire, Devonshire, and Glemorganshire. The clerk to the guardian's reported that he had, in answer to his application, received telegrams from six or eight asylums, all conveying the same answer—" No accommoda- tion " ; and when waiting on the Lunacy Commissioners he had been informed that room might possibly be found at Ipewieh for one patient. In the end the guardians resolved to write to the Surrey justices, asking them to use all pos- sible expedition in-opening the new county asylum they are now building. Trot MILK TatrertE —Few of our native plants are more striking in appear trice than a good specimen of this plant. The beautiful milk-white veins spread thickly on every leaf, the size of the leaves themselves, and the grandeur of the whole growth are pints that must appeal to all beholders who have any eye at all for natural beauty, and few plants may more appropriately be transferred from the wild state to the beds of the flower garden. It takes up a great deal of room; but where a garden affords plenty of space this is anything but a drawback, as it is a very noble-'o king plant. It ie possihle, however, that the gardener might ob- ject to the free way in which the seed gets disuersed every- where, and we know by our own experience that one conse- quence of introducing it ie the necessity of freely weeding out the saoerflaoue seedlings that spring up all over the garden. After all, however, they do not give anything irks the trouble that grounded and many other garden-loving interlopers do, and the teil of a little preliminary hoeing is soon forgotten when the plants destined to be preserved are revealing themselves in all their beauty. The plant is a biennial, and should be looked for in hedges, banks, and on rubbish heape.—Frorn" Familiar Wild Flowers." THE ALEICANDELLA WATERWORICS.—The importance of the water supply to Alexandria, great as it is at any time, has been so keenly emphasised during the last few weeks that a few notes regaling it will be of interest. The source of the supply is the Mihrnoudieh Canal, which not only communicates with the Nile at Atfeh, but also with the Khatatbeh Canal, which is fed by large pumps, erected by Messrs. Easton and Alderson. At the works, situated at Khatatbeh, there are 10 Levant screw pampa, each 12ft. in diameter, and cleable of delivering 34,532 gallons per minute to the height of Wilt. Eight pumps are worked together, delivering 276,259 gallons per minute, and driven by two pairs of compound inverted direct acting engines of the marine type, running at 75 revolutims per minute, with a pressure of 651 b. to the square inch. There is also one reserve engine. Thee pampa, which were made fir the Behera. Irrigation Company, ran regularly from the middle of April until the commencement of the troubles at the middle of Jane. Toe excellence of the machinery may be gathered from the fact thtt the results obtained by these pumps ranged at 78 to 85 per cint—that is, the ratio be. tween the work done In lifting the water and the indicated horse-power.—Tintes.

She had 100 passengers on board, and it is feared that all except two have perished. There is a rumour in Vienna that the Emperor and Em- press of Russia are soon to go to Moscow, where the corona- tion has been fixed for October 10. A telegram from Mos- cow states that their Majesties were expected there early on Wednesday morning. From Cattaro it is announced that an offensive and defensive alliance has been concluded between Russia and Montenegro. If true, it can only be concluded that the alliance is anti-Austrian ; but in any case it cannot have any appreciable effect upon European politics. A terrible outrage has been perpetrated in Hungary. A. tax collector, who had been insulted by some of the inhabi- tants of Kopalna, fired on them, and this so infuriated the populace, that they drove the man into a house, and imme- diately set fire to the building. The man was burned to death.

Much more damage has been done by the floods in the Austrian Tyrol than at first appeared. Whole towns are flooded, and through lame tracts of country no communica- tion is possible except by boat. The destruction of pro- perty must be enormous. ,Nothing is yet said of any lives having been lost. Asan example of the retrograde action of the Austrian Governmental authorities, it is Istated that the pastor of a Protestant congregation at Prague has received an order from the Imperial Royal Ministry, communicated by the police director, that no more public religious meetings are to beheld in his church. These results, hevrever, attended a hurricane at the Friendly Islands, in the Pacific, some inonths ago, and great distress was consequently caused amongst the natives. OM MUTTON SUPPLY AND &MEP POPULATION••••-•It Is I a eerious fact for the prolacers and consumers of mutton that the sheep population of En;land diminishes while the human population increases, and it is well worth considera- tion how this serious but not irremediable condition may best be met. In the first place, with good keep, just at this season (green rape given in abundance is the best food for the purpose, but generous diet of any other kind would pro- mote the same object), given to proposed mothers of our 1883 production of lambs would probably result in an in- crease in number of lambs of 30 per cent., with correspond- 1 in increase of supply of mutton. It seems to me unac- countable that this special feeding should have so much, e.caped the observations of flackmasters as it seems to h,, done. Farmers should remember that every vfqii.bred lamb that makes its appearance it! •,ussh about 20,. at, its birth ; h'net iolleae that a fleet) farM of 300 acres, maintaining 300 ewes, which in the hands of an inconsiderate farmer pro- duce 300 lambs, would, in skilful hands, produce 500 lambs, enriching their owner and promoting the public advantage. This incrsand number might, in many cases, pay the rent of the farm with present extraordinary prices—purchased at the utnall cost of more nutritious food fora few weeks. For the benefit of incredulous readers, I give the following facts and figures :—My neighbour, Mr. John Weetrope, of Gailden Mortien, Cambs., has informed me that his flock of 200 long- woolled ewes have brought him 400 lambs—an average of two lambs each, the number of single-lambs having been balanced by numbers of triplets; and this flock has produced an approximation to this for several years past. This year I have followed in my neighbour's steps,and have raised 200 lambs from 100 ewes, forming a part of the aggregate of 320, and have sold 113 of them for £6oo—for breeding pur- poses. My twin flock are rewarded with a liberal supply of corn, for which they ate very grateful, and on clover lees always leave me a legacy of folding, ensuring a splendid crop of wheat. England expects every man to do his duty, I should not do mine if I did not endeavour to impress others on a subject which seems of so much importance to myself. Is it not as much a duty to produce two sheep as two blades of corn where only one previously was grown ?—E. KIN* FORDILLM, Ashwell Bury.

MURDER OF TIE CHIRP SECOCOENI. - The small-pox epidemic continues unabated at Cape.town. Fresh cases are constantly being discovered, principally among the Malay and coloured population, and stringent measures have been taken at Kimberley, Graaf, Reinet, Durban, Port Natal, and other places, to prevent the importation of the disease. In- telligence from Pretoria states that Secocoeni, his son, and thirteen of his followers have been murdered by Mampoer, a fugitive from justice, with the aid of a small number of Kaffirs taken from various chiefs. Secocoeni's kraal was burnt, and his cattle carried off. The chiefs faithful to the Government•are greatly alarmed. A learned Mahratta young lady has been giving evidence before the Education Commission which has just concluded its public session at Poona. This lady stated to the Com- missioners that 99 out of every 100 of the educated men of India are opposed to female education. She stated, also, that hundreds of thousands of her fellow-countrywomen are dying for want of lady doctors. "I consider it my duty," she states in her evidence, "to maintain this cause, and to advecate the proper position of women in this land." Ram- nahai Sanskrita, the lady in question, who is not more than 24 years of age. has devoted herself to the cause of female education.

TRAGEDY IN A RAILWAY TRAIN: OFFICERS SHOT DEAD BY PRISONERS.—Sheriff Cate, of Chattanooga, Tennesse, and his deputy were, the other day, taking several prisoners by railway to Knoxville, among them two murderers chained together. When the train reached Sweetwater, 40 miles from Knoxville, three men entered the car. As the train was starting they attacked the Deputy-Sheriff from behind and shot him dead. The Sheriff then fired at the rescuers. They fired back and killed him. They liberated the murderers, stopped the train, took Taylor (one of the murderers) to the locomotive. and compelled the driver to cut loose from the train, and then take them 20 miles along the railway to Lenoir Station, where horses awaited them. They then galloped into the meuntains of North Carolina. Greatly excited parties are scouring the country in search. A reward of $5,000 is offerred.

MYSTERIOUS DISLPPEARINCII IN PARlS.—AaOthey mys- terious disappearance is announced in Paris. A young notary, M. A., arrired in Paris with his wife a fortnight ago • on his bridal tour. They put up at an hotel, and, finding some friends, amused themselves by visiting the different sights. The party went to the •Brd Butner, and the gentle- man appeared to enjoy himself immensely. He returned to his hotel with his wife, and on the following morning, which had been fixed for their departure, M. A. got up very early, and alleging headache went out, as he said, for half an hour's smart walking. He has not been heard of since. He has been Missing about ten days. It is feared that he has been hired to some out of the way pica and murdered for the sake of his money. He had £BOO in notes about him, and the police are trying to trace him by the numbers of the notes, which formed part of the, dowry he had received with his wife.

Let the Churchills and the Nelsons, and even the Welles- lays, hide their diminished heads while I speak of the Pratts. The Duke of Marlborough, Lord Nelson, and the Duke of Wellington, splendidly as they were rewarded, at any rate , left an indelible record on the history of their country. One fell in the moment of victory, and the others proved their prowess on many a hard-fought fleld,. I have to tell ef a man without any record that any one cares to remember, who yet received in the course of his lifetime a million of public money. It is Safe to say that if he had never lived he never would have been missed. Though several times an office-holder, he cannot claim a place in the ranks of English statesmen. He is as utterly forgotten as the great-grand- fathers of the vast majority of those who read this page. And yet from first to last he must have recei7ed a million of money from the taxpayers of this country. We pay our Prime Ministers during their short and uncertain tenure of office a pal,try £5,000 per annum, and usually, if they choose to accept it, they are in a position to claim a pension of £2,000 when they retire; but I have to speak of a man who never did anything for his country worth mentioning, and who received a million as his reward. Beside him even the Anglo-Indian Nabob of the last century sinks into insigni- ficance. I was warned long aeo that nay materials would soon be exhausted; that after twenty or thirty families had been glanced at little would remain to be told; and yet I have dealt with no less.than seventy-eight families and have not yet noticed the Pratts. _ _ _ -

But, withal, the Pratts can boast of a singularly unique distinction, of which they may well be proud. I doubt if there is any other noble family which can fairly make a like claim. We have seen that there have been many roads to the Peerage. The Court, the field, the deck, the Bar, the Exchange, illicit love, and unlawful gain have all largely contributed to swell the ranks of the Peerage; but where shall we find a Barony like that of Camden, which was direct), obtained through the services which the first Lord Camden rendered to the Cause of popular liberty? There is not a particle of exaggeration in the eulogism which Lord Campbell has pronounced upon him :—" Englishmen to the latest generation will honour his name for having secured personal freedom by putting an end to arbitrary arrests under general warrants, for having established the Constitu- tional rights of juries, and for haring placed on an imperish- able basis the libertyrof the Press."

The very name of Camden has an aroma of antiquity about it, derived doubtless from the author of " Britannia ;" but the Camden peerage is of quite modern date. A little over a hundred years ago the first Lord Camden received his title from Camden place, Kent. The Camden estates consist of : Kent Sussex Brecon

Total 17,399 „ with a rent-roll of £16,380. We need not trouble ourselves with the early history of the Pratts ; suffice it to say they were impoverished by the Civil War, and that John Pratt, an eminent lawyer, wh flourished at the beginning of the last century, restored the fortunes of the house. In the year 1714 he was elevated to the position of Lord Chief Justice. He appears to have pur- chased the Wilderness Estate, in Kent, near Sevenoaks, and Bayham Abbey, in Sussex; though, strange to say, Lord Campbell asserts that he left his family in almost abject poverty. His son, Lord Chancellor Camden, purchased the seat at Camden Place, Chislehurst, now the residence of the ex-Empress Eugenie, and at one time the abode of Camden, the antiquary. From, this place he derived his title. Lord Chancellor Camden married the heiress of Nicholas Jeffreys, of the Priory, Brecon, through whom the Welsh estates were derived. The Brecon property is chiefly spoil of the monastic houses, Lint had been obtained by purchase by the Jeffreys family. Lord Chancellor Camden was a younger son, for whom little provision was made save an excellent education. From Eton, where he made the acquaintance of the elder Pitt, he proceeded to Cambridge, and thence to the Bar. For some time he made no progress, and, in despair, he was about to take Holy Orders, when Henley, the leader of his circuit—

div.head: TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
div.p: TRADES UNION CONGRESS.

The Trade Union Congress' opened its fifteenth. meeting in Alanchester, on Monday. .3.'nere was a large attendance of delegates, including s,veral ladies. Very little business was done beyond the election of office beaters. 112 r. Robert Austin, Manchester, was appointed President. In the report of the Parliamentary Committee, submitted by Mr. Broad- hurst, M.P., it was stated that the general trade of the country had not been brisk during the year, unless in en- gineering and iron-shiphuiirUng. In mining and building employment was •Eill slack and wages low. Increased means of production was given as the main cause in the one case, and in the other a cutting down of the profits of the commercial classes. The working men seers warned not to regard even their present limited privileges as secure, and it wee pointed out that there never was a time when it was more necessary to be watchful and alert for defence.

The Congress was resumed 'on Tuesday. In his opening address the President (Mr. Austin) referred eo the position of trades unionists now as compared with what it was some 15 years ago, whoa the Congress was started in Manchester, and in this connection mentioned that the number of unionists had increased from 150,000 in 1869 to 500,000 ibis year. Although much evil was predicted as the result ,of the repeal or amendment of unjust laws, no injurious results had arisen to person or property, but rather the reverse. Much had been accomplished by their exertions in the pest, but a great deal remeined to be done, and he hoped they would go on perseveringly until the 17 proposals for consideration at the Congress had become law. Reso- lutions were afterwards passed urging the nece,eeity of in- creasing the number of factory and workshop inepectors, reforming the patent laws, and devising further means for prevention of the loss of life occasioned by boiler explo- sions.

The Congress resumed its meeting on Wednesday. A resolution was passed in favour of compulsory inspection of boilers by duly qualified and certificated officers. The in- speclon of mines was next discussed, and a resolution was adopted .calling upon the Government to appoint an increased number of sob-inspectors in order that mines may be more frcquently inspected Mr. J. S. Marchie, one of the Manchester delegates, submitted a resolution asserting that the Employers' Liability Act had been grossly marred in its -beneficial operation by its permissive character, and in- structing the Parliamentary Committee to use their best endeavours to secure an amendment that will make it illegal for either employers or workmen to contract them- selves out of its provisions. After an animated discussion, in the coarse of which some amendments were proposed, the motion was unanimously adopted. Mr. Michael Devitt was preseut during a portion of the proceedings, his object being, it was stated, to write an article upon trades unionism for an American journal. In the evening the trades unionists of the city entertained the delegates at dinner at Iblle Vue Gardens.

When the Congress resumed its sittings on Thursday morning Mr. P. Shorrocks, one of the Manchester delegates, introduced the subject of imprisonment for debt in a resolu- tion protesting against the inequality of the law affecting debtors, "which, while it exempts persons owing £5O and upwards from imprisonment, gives power to incarcerate small debtors owing sums under £50." The resolution in the form in which it was proposed did not meet with the unanimous support of the delegates. It was discussed, however, at considerable length, and ultimately carried by a large majority. A proposal in favour of a reform of the magistracy was brought forward by Mr. Judge, a Leeds delegate, who asserted that under the present system people stood a very poor chance indeed of getting anything like justice. The seconder of the motion (Mr. Moyne) urged that the standard should be lowered, so that intelligent working men might sit as magistrates. The paid as well as the unpaid magistracy shared the strictures of some delegates, one speaker asserting that these gentlemen were quite as guilty of infringementa of the law as the an paid. A resolution was adopted calling upon the Govern- ment to make such alterations in the mode of the appoint- ment of magistrates as may secure justice to those who ap- peal to the decision of petty sessional courts. The Congress also passed a resolution in support of an amendment of the jury laws, so that working men who are calltd upon to act as jurors may be compensated for their services. Mr. G. Ship- ton, of London, introduced the subject of labour representa- tion in Parliament, and the Congress, after a protracted de- bate, adopted a resolution arging that increased labour reprerntation was desirable and even necessary in the in- terests of the working classes, and that the time had arrived when all representatives in Parliament should be paid by the State.

TRADE NOTES.

The number of bills of sale published in 'England and Wales for the week ending September 16th, was 742. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 1.026, showing a decrease of 284, being a net decrease in 1832, to date, of 1,610. The number published in Ireland for the same week was 18. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 29, showing a decrease of 11, being a net decrease in 1882, to date, of 289.—.Ke;np's Mercantile Gazette.

TSB WAGES AGITATION IN THE COAL TRADII-011 Tues- day, an important colliers' conference, representing North and South Staffordshire, East Worcestershire, and Salop, was held in Wolverhampton to consider the recent resolution of the Manchester conference' on the wages question. A resolution was carried agreeing with the 10 per cent. advance which the North Staffordshire men are about to give notice for, and instructing each district represented to at once make application for a similar rise. It was recommended, how- ever, that before giving notice joint representative meetings of employers and workmen should be held in every district. Cannock Chase district was not represented. TEE WHATIIRR AND TRH CORN TRADE.—The Mark Lane Express says :—" With fine autumnal weather the harvest has been steadily progressing in the north, whilst fair clearing up has been effected in the south. There appears to have been but little damage to the wheat crop from the weather, but barleys have taken more or less harm. The trade has yielded to the pressure of an abundant foreign supply, and it is a question whether last Monday's decline represents bottom values. Millers still look for forward rates, and at 435. may be taken to represent the equivalent of 5041b5. ordinary best red wheat, it is evident that 40s, has thus early in the season become an outside value for a very large prcportion of the English crop by imperial measure. Tne long-expected reduction in the London top price nominal of flour occurred on Monday last, but with regard to other branches of the English grain trade there is nothing fresh to note. It is, however, becoming more and more plain that fine malting samples of barley will not be very ptentiful. Trade in foreign wheats off stands in London difficult at last Monday's values, but in Liverpool there was more firmness on Friday. Foreign flour was on Friday generally. 6d. lower than on the previous Monday.—The Fariaer says—" Fair weather and good supplies tend to make trade dull. English Wae,tt ssid slowly at last Mon- day's large decline. Foreign wheat was again cheaper by Is from Monday, and sales were small and discouraging. Flour IVeIS neglected at 6d. further reduction. Malting barley kept steady in value; oth rr articles, oats, beans, peas, and maize, were offered freely on former terms. The posi- tion of the market was considered weak, tendencies being etill towards buyers."

THR LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market remains generally in a satisfactory state, but in the North of Eng- land the wages of ironworkers are again likely to be under discussion at an early date. The steel rail trade is, mean- while, being organised from the employers' side by the formation of an asssciation. Most of the leading colliery districts now show good employment, and there is little prospect of the general strike suggestel at the Manchester Conference being entered on. Railway and other large undertakings continue to give good employment to navvies, and in some parts, notably at Neath, there is some difficulty in securing the necessary complement of men. The textile trades, as a rule, show an average amount of employment, and at Oldham there is still a good deal of mill building going on. At Leicester the hosiery trade is again ve y active, and at Kidderminster the carpet looms are only moderately busy. The metropolitan industries remain fairly engaged, but few important new building contracts have been entered on. Both the letter-carriers and policemen are somewhat unsettled, and operative bakers are still organis- ing for better conditions of service. Some passing discus- sion on the introduction of Chinese labour has taken place, but it has little or no immediate significance. Recent advices from Manitoba indicate that the labour market is still active, though the season has advanced,„and the Cana- dian Pacific Railway is being vigorously pushed forware.--, Labour News.

THE PURE OF ARGYLL ON THE FOREIGN POLICY OF THE .GOVERNMENT.—The following letter has been received by a gentlemr,i in Manchester front the Duke of Argyll:— I " Inverary, September 19th, 1882. Sir.—l have no difficulty. II in answering the question which you put to me in your let- ter of the 16th. As regards the 'foreign policy of Her Majesty's present Government, I see no reason whatever to state the confidence which was placed in it by those who supported it when it was formed upon the principle of "peace at any price." If it had been so formed its, com- position would have been very different. On the other hand, no Cabinet has ever existed in this coantry whose members have had a greater dislike of war or a greater love of peace. Every war must be judged on its own merits, and not on any abstract principle apart from the circumstances of the case. But if there be any abstract principle applicable Cc such questions, I am afraid it is a principle which affirms, not the unlawfulness, but, alas! the too frequent necessity of war. War has often been, and it will often be, by far the least of two evils. The sword has often represented, and will often represent again, the cause of liberty, of civilisation, of order, and of "lasting peace." As far as my knowledge goes, I regard the war in Egypt as a case in point. Your obedient servant, ARGYLL." CLAIMANT TO AN EARLDOM —William Stephen John Fulton, late of Her Majesty's Bth Hussars, and residing in Edinburgh, presented the other day a petition to the Sheriff of Chancery, in the Outer House of the Court of Session, claiming to be served nearest and lawful heir to Archibald, 11th Earl of Eglintoune, who died, failing male issue, on the 30ih of October, 1796. The petitioner stated that he is the great-grandson of James Fulton of Fultoun, the imme- di Its younger brother of the eleventh earl, who, however, died prior to the eleventh earl, leaving a son (the petition- er's grandfather), who, when the succession opened to him by the death of his uncle the eleventh earl, was a prisoner of war, and could not claim. An agent who appeared on. behalf of the Earl cf Eglintoune opposed the petition on the ground that the ancestors of the present Earl had already been, by the Sheriff of Chancery, served heirs to the eleventh earl. Lady Mary Montgomery, it was pointed out, had, on the 27th of February, 1797, been served nearest lawful heir to the nobleman in question. The Sheriff called on the defendant to lodge written objections to the petition being granted within four months. THE BRIGHT CPILEBRATION AT BIIILMINGHAM.—A meet- ing of the Executive Committee of the Birmingham Liberal Association was held on Monday night under the presidency of Mr. G. Dixon. when it was resnlvecl .to postpone the Bright celebration until the spring; owing to the autumn session. A resolution was also passed trusting that an early settlement of the Egyptian question, and the more satisfac- tory condition of Ireland, would enable the Government to address themselves to domestic legislation so urgently needed, and requesting the Mayor to call a town's meeting in support of the Government in passing the proposed new rules of procedure. Another resolution expressed the hearty satisfaction of the meeting at the triumphant and speedy termination of the war in Egypt, and recording " its full confidence in the pledges given by Her Majesty's Ministers, that in the question involved they would have iegard to the security and development of the liberties and the self-government of the Egyptian people, the safety of our communication with Indian by means of the Suez Canal, and the maintenance of those interests which, in common with all the States of Europe, this country had in the establishment of peace, order, and prosperity in Egypt." THE HAY AND CORN DRYING COMPETITION AT READ- ING.—The Mark Lane Express says the judges appointed by the Royal Agricultural Society to test the merits of the different appliances adopted by the competitors for a prize. of 100 guineas offered for the most efficient method of dry- ing hay or corn crops artificially, either before or after being stacked, presented their report at a meeting held at the society's rooms on Saturday, under the presidency of Lord Vernon. There were eight competitors, six cif whom em- ployed the Neilson system of exhaust fans for drying in the stack, the two remaining competitors using in one case hot air appliZel before stacking, and in the other a system of ventilation assisted by hot air applied after stack- ing. The two last-named systems were only tried on hay, but a selected three of the various adaptations of Neilson 's system were submitted to an extended trial both on hay and barley, and all of them upon hay in the stack. The judges decided that none of the exhibiiors proved that they were able to make good hay in wet weather. In a few instances where fairly good hay was obtained equally good, if not better, might have been secured without the application of fans. The trials of the three selected fans upon corn was equally less satisfactory than those upon hay, none of the machines having succeeded in effectually drying the corn in the stack. Under these circumstances the judges re- ported that they did not feel justified in awarding the prize. and the stewards concurred in this decision.

"General' Booth is now, as he himself states, a licensed victualler, but he does not intend dot lug his lease to sell a drop of intoxicatiner liquor. It appears that he is bound by covenant to preserve the licence attaching to the premises. We hope the " General " will not fall into any ernbarassment in his undertaking. If he does not, as he has engaged to do, renew the licence annually for the next 17 years, he will have the aggrieved lessor to reckon with; while if he con- tinues to hold a victuallers' licence, which supposes a responsibility as well as a privilege, we do not see how he can protect himself from the possible demands of inordin- ately thirsty "soldiers." • TI/E LORD • CHANCELLOR IN DEVONSIIIRE.—The Lord Chancellor's visit to Lard Coleridge has been taken advan- tage of by the people of Devonshire to present an address to Lord Se; bor no, and in speaking at a luncheon on tke occa- sion, on Thursday, his lordship dwelt upon a feature in the Egyptian war which has not received the attention that is its due. No one desires to detract from the. high praise due to the army and navy, and to Admiral Seymour and Sir Garnet Wolseley, but the Load Chancellor is entitled to credit the Administration with much praise. The expedition was fitted out with a foresight and completeness which left I nothing to be desired, and it was consequently I ossible to ' carry it to a successful conclusion within a time that had been previously calculated almost to an hour. When tho ; troops were sent opt to Zululand, in the time of Lord : Beaconsfield's Administration, great credit was claimed for ; the promptness of their despatch; hut the expedition was badly equipped, no plan was previously considered, and the whole campaign was a succession of disastrous blunders. Liberals do not like war, but if they must fight they can do it Well. EVICTED TENANTS.—A meeting in support of the National Fund for the relief of evicted tenants was held in Cork, on Thursday, under the presidency ofAthe Mayor. Mr. O'Don- nell, M.P., in moving a resolution in favour of the scheme, said the result of his inquiries in the country was that the awards of the Land Courts were "monstrously "below the justice of the case, and even if decisions nearly approaching justice were given, the Court of Appeal stepped in and undid all the benefit the tenant had received. He told the people that if their attitude of stern resistance to the land- lords was at all relaxed, their position would be made worse, as the landlords' influence would prevail over both sub- Commissioner and Chief Commissioner. It was necessary then for the tenantry to keep up a "gentle pressure" on the commissioners, because a "new spirit of resistance and obstinate opposition" seemed to have taken possession of the landlords. This spirit was apparently encouraged by the Land Corporation promoted by Mr. Kavanagh, or, as the hon. member styled it; the "Kavanagh Eviction Com- pany." The twenty-fifth anniversary of the National Association for the promotion of Social Science was opened at Notting- ham on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. G. A. Hast- ings, M.P. The proceedings commenced with a service in St. Mary's Church, and a sermon by the Rev. J. Wilson, senior minister of Clifton College and chaplain to the Bishop of Exeter. In the evening the President delivered his opening , address. The practical business of the Congress commenced on Thursday morning. All the departments met and that devoted to jurisprudence was divided into two sections, in each of which the presidential address was delivered. Mr. A. Fox Bristowe, Vice-Chancellor of the Duchy of Lan- caster, read an able paper upon "The Amendment of the Law," in which lie traced the results of the labours of the association during the past quarter of a century. Sir John Pope Hennessy, in the Repression of Crime Section, dis- coursed upon the efforts of statesmen in recent years, and .adverting to Ireland he confessed that there was nothing in the condition of that country wilich rendered the applica- tion of the principle which British statesmen have applied successfully to other parts of the empire unsound. There was, however, clear evidence that in endeavouring to repress crime in Ireland crime itself had been increased. The general topics discussed in the different sectional meetings in the course of the day were The expediency of making the devolution of real property in case of intestacy follow that of personalty, introduced by Mr-Meryon White; the question of the marriage of English women by foreigners, by Miss Leigh, lady president of the Mission Home in Paris ; the best means of repressing drunkenness, by the Rev. J. Horsley, chaplain of Clerken- well Prison; the association of technical education with intermediate schools and local colleges, by Mr. Alderman Cropper ; infant mortality, the employment of mothers in mills and manufactories, the report of the Select Committee ' on railways, and the influence of art upon the masses of the population.
COLLAPSE OF THE WAR.

Sir Garnet Wolseley telegraphed yesterday week from Cairo :—" War in Rzypt is over." Thus he was able, on the very day which he himself fixed upon weeks ago for the conclusion of hostilities, to announce to the British , public the complete success of our arms. The General !arrived in the Egyptian capital yesterday week, having been preceded by his cavalry some twenty-four hours. Sir Garnet pays a high and well-earned compliment to this branch of the service for their rapid occupation of the city after a very long, forced march. The piece of good fortune which WAS reported somewhat doubtfully at first is officially confirmed. Arabi and Toulba, after the battle of Tel-el- Kebir, proceeded to Cairo, where they were placed under arrest by the Prefect of Police. On the arrival of our forces the rebel chiefs were handed over to us, and they are now both prisoners in cur guard-room. One item of Sir Garnet's telegram will be read with particular satisfaction. The gallant young midshipman, De Chair, who was treacherously led into Arabi's lines, has escaped the many perils of his Position among the rebel forces. He was found in Cairo all safe, and is now once more among his fellow countrymen. More of the enemy's troops were found in the capital than had been expected. Ten thousand men, Sir Garnet says, laid down their arms and surrendered to him there.

Our loss at Tel-el-Kebir is now officially stated to have been nine officers and forty-five men killed, and twenty-two officers and three hundred and twenty men wounded. An incident is mentioned as having taken place after the battle, which suggests that, although the war is over, some work may yet be found for our troops to do. While the British troops were resting at Tel-el-Kebir, after the fatigue of the engagement, some thousands of Bedonins, about three o'clock in the afternoon, swooped down upon the camp at Kassasin, expecting, no doubt, to find it empty. The 50th Regiment, which were garrisoning it, however, turned out and gave the marauders several volleys, which sent them back hastily to the desert. These restless tribes are now, it is believed, hanging round Ismailia in very large numbers, waiting for a chance to loot the town. An opinion prevails in Egypt that it will be necessary to take very energetic measures with these desert robbers before order and safety can be firmly established. On Saturday afternoon the Egyptian officer in command at Aboukir announced his readiness to surrender. In the morning Fort Aslam, which is on the Alexandria side of Karr Dower, surrendered to Sir E. Wood personally. K ifr Dower has passed into our hands,and our troops now occupy the formidable works which not long since formed an hie- rassible barrier between us and Cairo. The rebel army there had offered to surrender, and Sir Evelyn Wood proceeded to the Egyptian lines to receive the submission of the troops. When he arrived there, however, he found only a few officers waiting to give themselves up. The men, to the number of some thousands, had laid down their arms, in many cases even 'aVn off their regimental clothes, and quietly disappeared. Various theories exist as to this Isingular event, but the most probable is that the Egyptians, not caring to wait and go through the formality of surrender, walked off to homes from which they were driven by Arabi A correspondent who was present at the capitulation of Kaffr Dovrar states that the war material seized, so far as at present counted, consists of 6,000 stand of arms and com- plete accoutrements, half a million rounds of ammunition, six batteries of horse artillery, three heavy siege guns, an enormous stock of forage and provisions, 800 horses and mules, and 400 tents and camp baggage. Omar Bey, one of the Egyptian officers who surrendered at Kafir Dowar, upon being asked by a correspondent what induced Arabi to leave his best soldiers there and to face our troops with raw recruits, replied, " We were very badly served by our spies, and the continued skirmishes and feigned attacks which you made from this side deceived us. We thought that the Ismailia move vras a ruse, or at least only to secure the Canal, and that the real attack would be from here." Aboukir has yielded to Sir Evelyn Wood, and Abdallah, the commander at Damietta, who threatened to hold out in favour of the rebel cause, opportunely discovered that he never had any intention of fighting against the Khedive, and he has now surrendered. Later news from Damietta reports that Abdallah has been shot by his own troops while urging them not to yield, but fight for their Caliph, their religion, and their country. A large body of infantry, supposed to be from Bs Salihiyeh, has surrendered at Tantah, and further surrenders have taken place at other places. Indeed, it is clear that all opposition is at an end, though reports have reached Cairo expressing fears of a rising in Upper Egypt. There are signs that in a short time the Egyptians will settle down to their ordivary occupations. The Arabs, however, give no welcome to the English, nor will they sincerely rejoice at the reappearance of the Khedive. They are turbulently inclined, and have indulged in demonstra- tions which have caused Sir Garnet Wolseley to announce that if they do not conduct themselves with greater pro- priety their quarter will be bombarded. Bedouins, too, are prowling round Cairo, and some English officers who started off on a visit to the Pyramids, found it necessary to return in haste to their quarters. No serious disturbances, however, have occurred, nor are any anticipated. It is announced from Alexandria that the postal service to Cairo has been resumed, and that the telegraph censorship) has been abAished. On Tuesday, the satisfactory informa- tion reached this country from our commissariat department in Egypt, that our troops can now be readily provisioned in the country, and that it is unnecessary to send out any more preserved food. A large portion of the immense quantity of provisions provided to be sent out, will, therefore, be at once returned into stores.

In a general order which Sir Garnet has issued, congratu- lating the army on the successful termination of the cam- paign; the leading incidents of the war are enumerated, and the military courage and noble) devotion of all ranks highly praised. Called upon," says Sir Garnet, "to show discipline under exceptional privations, to give proof of fortitude in extreme toil, and to show contempt of d Inger in battle, the general officers and non-commissioned officers and men of the army have responded with zeal and alacrity, adding another chapter to the long roll of British vic- tories."

Speculation is rife as to what is to ba the fate of the rebels and the ultimate political settlement in Egypt. There is nowhere any disposition to deal severely with the rank and file of the insurrection, and the. great majority of the officers of the army, though retained under arrest, will no doubt receive little, if any, punishment lanfond dismissal. The interesting problem is as to the fate of Arabi and the other leaders, some of whom were implicated in the massacre at Alexandria, while others had planned the destruction of Cairo, and were only prevented from carrying out their diabolioal design by the speedy appearance of the British cavalry in front of the capital. Trial of these rebels-by a joint commission is spoken of, and is as probable a mode of dealing with them as any other that has been suggested. It will be for the Khedive, if he thinks fir, to exercise clemency if the sentences that may be arrived at seem too severe, and in.the use of the prerogative of mercy he will no doubt listen to English counsel. That efforts will be made to secure lenient treatment for Arabi is evident from the terms of the telegram to his mother from Lady Anne 'Blunt, who, with all the ardour of a grand-daughter of Lord Byron, expresses, her sympathy with the mother's affliction, and assures her that she shall not be deserted. At last the amusing and ridiculous negotiations with Cle Forte have been brought to a close by Lord Dufferin an- nouncing that, the rebellion in Egypt being at an end, the assistance of Turkey is not needed, andat the same time the Italian proposal for the international protection of the Suez Canal is definitely put aside by England informing the Powers that. this country will see to the safety of that great highway. Thus two troublesome questions are disposed of, and the way made more clear for the final political settle- ment of the whole question.

It is announced from Cairo that Mahmond Semi Pasha, one of Arabi's principal supporters, has been arrested in the guise of a priest. Instructions have been sent to Gibraltar and Malta to in- tercept transports with troops for Egypt, so that they may be sent home again. The Household Cavalry will be the first among the por- tions of the army not required for the temporary occupation of the country to leave, and the homeward movement will begin shortly after the review before the Khedive. _ . _ _

Sir Garnet %Iroiseley is established with the head-ouarters of his Staff in the Abdeen Palace in Cairo, and, at the re- quest of the Khedive, the Duke'of Connaught has taken temporary possession of the Kasr-en-Nuzha Palace. _ _ _

On Friday the Queen telegraphed through Sir E. Malet her congratulations to the Khedive on the overthrow of the re- bellion and the re-establishment of the Khedive's power and authority, and His Highness in reply has expressed his thanks for Her Majesty's message. A despatch from Cairo states that the report that the Egyptians had ordered the burning of Cairo has been con- firmed. From Alexandria we learn that on Sunday the Council of Ministers proposed and the Khedive signed a de- cree dissolving the Egyptian army. A correspondent informs us that the first British troops to enter Cairo were two 9quadrons of the 4th Dragoon Guards, with 50 Mounted Infantry, under Captain Darley, of the Dragoons. When they reached the citadel, the garrison, composed of 6,000 Egyptians, fled precipitately, leaving behind them many European prisoners manacled. On the subject of a future settlement of Egypt, a Berlin correspondent, telegraphing on Tuesday night, says that the regulation of the relations between England and Turkey is considered a most difficult question. Germany, the corres- pondent adds, will act the part of a mediator, but will be as reserved as hitherto. From information given by Ibrahim Bey Tewfik, who ar- rived from Cairo at Alexandria on Tuesday, a correspondent at the latter place states that orders had been given to resist the entry of the English troops into Cairo, and to burn the city if Arabi was defeated. But for the rapid advance of General Macpherson Cairo would have shared the same fate as Alexandria. The town and vicinity of Cairo are as peaceful, orderly, and busy as if war had not existed. During a journey to Cairo a correspondent noted that the appearance of the country and the people showed that, however Arabi might have impressed the peasants for the army, he had not meddled with their property. The whole country seemed prosperous. The official accounts of the engagement at Kassassin on the 28th August are published in Tuesday night's Gazette. Sir Garnet Wolseley says the conduct of the soldiers of all arms was excellent, and many gallant deeds were done. In Major General Graham's report, Major Hart, Royal Engineers; Lieutenant Pine, 4th Dragoon Guards; act' Captain Rare, brigade major, are specially commended to notice.

div.head: WELCOME TEA MEETING TO THE NEW WESLEYAN MINISTERS.
div.p: WELCOME TEA MEETING TO THE NEW WESLEYAN MINISTERS.

A public meeting for the pUrpose of giving a welcome to the newly app finted Wesleyan ministers in the St. Helens circuit, was held in the Wesleyan Chapel. Cross-lane, Earl es- town, on Thui sday evening. Previous to the meeting being held, about 130 persons sat down to an excellent tea in the schoolroom, after which an adjournment was 'mule to the Lecture Hall beneath the chapel, which was well filled. The chair was occupied by the Bev. J. M. Walmsley. of St. Helens, superintendent minister of the circuit, and he was supported by the Rev. G. Smith, of St. Helens; the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, of Earlestown ; Mr. J. Barr and Mr. J. Roberts (stewards).

. The Cuataitati observed that he wanted that meeting to partake of a true devotional character, aed he wished them to catch the true Methodist spirit at the beginning of a new Methodist year. The question was what could they do, or to put it in a practical way, "What can I do "? It seemed to him that one of the very first things they should try to do was to get into a better state of grace themselves. If people lived to God they would work for God. They wanted individual activity to keep their eyes open and look after the strangers, and to look after opportunities for doing as well as for getting good. There was another thing he wished to tell them and that was he had no right to ask God to make him what he was not trying to become, and had no right to ask God to give hitn what he was not trying to get. If they wanted to be holy they must try to be holy, if they prayed to be more useful they most try to be useful. They must have faith, prayer, and work for the Trinity in unity. If they tried to do and become what he had pointed out God would bless them. (Applause.) Mr. J. Rosmrs, on behalf of the Earlestown society, welcomed to their midst the Rev. .T. M. Fairbourn, and he thought he would be found to be the right man in the right place. He had also great pleasure in welcoming amongst them the Rev. G. Smith and the Rev. J. M. Walmsley, the chairman of that meeting. He believed that it was in the power of the church to make the minister who laboured amongst them either happy or miserable, but their desire was to make him happy, and to do that it was for their individual selves to matte it a point to live as near As passible to God. He had pleasure In qating that in Earlestown their society held its own, and that on the past quarter they had had a total increase of forty members. He exhorted each and all to do their utmost -to make their minister and his wife happy amongst them. (Applause.) Mr. 3. BARR also gave the ministers a -hearty welcome, intimating that he was doing so on behalf of some sixty or so members connected with their chapel at Golborne. He hoped they would not leave all the work to be done by the ministers, but that they would try to keep to the old Metho- dist usages and doctrines. (Applause.) He trusted the time was not far distant when the present circuit would be divided, and when Earlestown would ba the head of an extending and prosperous district. (Applause.)

The Rev. G. SMITH thanked them for the warm and hearty welcome they had accorded to him and his colleague, and proceeded to remark that it would be a very painful and hard thing for him to do if in working in the Methodist miniEry he thought he had not the sympathy and support of the Christian people. They had notcome into the circuit to try to suit or please everybody. They had come to de- liver a glorious message, t ) try to do good, to try to help them to live a better life, and they had come also to be helped by them to live a better life themselves. Before he decided upon coming to the circuit he wrote to some of their friends, and amongst them was their old and respected minister Mr. Fwell, who wrote that the people at Earles- town were intelligent, kind, and appreciative, and that he would be very glad to labour amongst them again. If they were only right in their principles, aims, and dispositions, then they could go ahead as much as they possibly could. Let them all work unitedly, lovingly, and prayerfully, and this would undoubtedly be a grand and glorious year. (Applause). Mr. E. NEwmaN, on behalf of the local preachers, gave the ministers a hearty welcome, and said that if they deter- mined to work upon the lines laid down success would attend their efforts. The Rev. J. M. FAIRBOURN, the new resident minister in Earlestown' then addressed the meeting. ile remarked that his mind had been wandering to the past, and he had been thinking after all the former Methodist days were not better than these. His first and most important duty in that circuit would be to preach. He might he mistaken, but he thought it was the primary duty of every minister of the Lord Jesus Christ to preach. The religious worllhad been divided into two divisions, not Protestantism and Roman Catholicism, but Evangelicalism, and the Hierarchial system. On the one hand they found altars, sacraments. vestments, and the like, but on the other side they found few ordinances, a simple service but a great deal of preaching, so that he thought he and his colleague would have to be very attentive to the preaching. He should not preach at any of them, and he did not want any of them to pray at him. it would he his duty to ascertain to the best of his ability the truth of God and to declare it. He had unbounded confidence in the power of God's word, and that seed which was faithfully sown and watered by the dew of the Holy Spirit must surely grow. The next in order was the pastoral office. He did not set up to be a famous visitor. A part of the minister's work was to make other people work, and he supposed that to some extent would be his post and office. Hekusted that at the end of his stay amongst them the feeling would be as amicable and friendly as it was at that moment. (Applause.) a helar.rtNyEl7oMteAoNf tea, and also to the choir for attending that evening. The ttlilleannkpsrotpootshede,laadnidesMwrh. oJ.bCar anstsecdoantdiehde, motion was carried with acclamation, and the meeting con- cluded with singing and the Benediction.

MUSICAL HONOTTRS.-IVessrs: John Brinsinead and Sons have been appointed pianoforte manufacturers to the of King Portugal, and Mr. John Brinsmead has been elected an hon- orary member of the Musical Academy of .•.;anta Cecilia, at _ . Rome.—Deily Chronicle. ATo View or AFFAIRS —Lord Ferersham, respond- ing for the House of Lords at a luncheon in connection with the Easingwold Agricultural Show, alluded to the Entailed Estates Bill, and claimed that the House of Lords had proved itself more Lib.ral than a Radical House of Com- mons. Viscount Castlereagh spoke congratulatingly of the successes of our army in Egypt, but feared grave political differences would arise in connection with Eastern affairs. Colonel Denney, M.P., also spoke. THZ WORD "DOS."—Sonde erroneously sup. pose that it comes from the French word "dormer!' give. implying a demand, or something due; but the true origin of this word is from one John Dunn. a famous bailiff of Lincoln, so extremely active and dexterous at the manage- ment of his rough business that it became a proverb when a naan refused to pay his debts—Wby don't you Dunn him? that is, Why do you not send Dann to arrest him? Hence it became a custom and a proverb, and Is as old as the days . of Henry VII.

A LTRISC 11 A 31. A DANGF:IIOI;3 PCBLIC-110USE.—A singehe the granting of a license was nride by tlyt A, 'trio- cham &.ssions on Monday. Mr. Cave appiied fcn, thhe V. fer of the license of the Orange Tree Inn, wiiMir ii Magistrates had withdrawn in consequence ef the unaatia-; -factory conduct of the previous tenant. rolim Superinten- -dent Leighton informed the Bench that there was a large crack in one of the walls-, which was "bulge," and the house- Might come down. The flooring boat ds were rotten, and in his opinion the house was dangerous. The Surveyor ' of the Altrincham.
