div.head: S IiTON.
div.p: A S IiTON.

DRUNKENNESS--At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, before J. Prescot and F. S. Gerrard, Esqs., Sarah Johnson, of Ashton, was charged with being drunk and in- capable in Bolton-road, Ashton, on Sunday morning.—P.C. Hudson proved the case, and the woman was fined is. and costs, but in default of payment went to prison for seven days. THE ABRAM Wisaltn SCHEME.—The work in connection with the formation of a reservoir at Stubshaw Cross, in ac- cordance with what is known as the Abram Water Scheme, was commenced at the beginning of the present week. The project comprises the supply of water to the township of Abram, the service pipes, &e.„ being laid through the town- ship of Ashton. MBETING OF RATEPAyEs.—A. monthly meeting of the subscribers to the Ashton-in-Makerfield Ratepayers' Associa- tion was held at the Robin Hood Hotel, Bridge Foot, on Thursday evening, last week. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. Peter Aspirin! presided. The minutes of the last meeting were approved. A discussion afterwards took place as to general affairs in the townshio, the proposed expendi- ture at the gasworks being principally discussed. THE LODGE-DANE FLORAL AND BORTICUIATURAL SOCIETY. —The thirty-seventh annual show of flowers, roots, fruits,and vegetables ita connection with the Lodge-lane Floral and Horticultural Society was held at the house of Mr. Enoch Sankey, the Colliers' Arms, Warrington-road, Ashton, on Saturday last. There were seven exhibit4rs, and the classes exhibited numbered 47. Though the number was compara- tively small, the fruits and vegetabies were of a most ex- cellent quality, and the judges, Messrs Wm. Clark (Ashton Heath) and IVm. Kay ( Elaydock) had some difficulty in de- ciding upon the merits of the respective classes sent in for competition. The show was visited by a large number of persons. Sr. THOMAS'S SICK AND BURIAL SOCIETY.—The sick and btu ial society connected with St. Thomas's schools. Ashton, is in a very flourishing and satisfactory condition, and while the number of its members is large, there is, in addition, plenty of funds in hand. The annual tea party and dance connected with the society was held in St. Thomas's schools, on Monday evening. About 40 members sat down to a sub- stantial tea, the members of the St. Thomas's Brass Band, who had kindly promised their services, being served in addition. Tha room was afterwards cleared for dancing, when an additional number of ladies and gentlemen, alto- Eether about 130, attended. The band, conducted by Mr. Thomas Livesley, creditably rendered the selections, and the party very pleasantly and enjoyably spent the evening. The company broke up about tw,.elve o'clock.

C ULCHETH. POACHING AFFRAY AT CIII,CHETH.—On Wednesday night about half-past eleven o'clock, a serious affray bEtween poachers and keepers took place at Risky, Culcheth, about five miles from Leigh and Warrington. Nine keepers lay under a hedge in wait for the poachers, several of them being asleep, and owing to the prevalence of a high wind a gang of five or six men came suddenly upon the scene, the keepers awake having no time to rouse their slumbering companions. Samuel Watkins, a keeper, was knocked down four times, and had he not had a shield of twigs would have had difficulty in escaping with his life, the poachers using both sticks and stones. The scuffle, which was a severe one, ended in the capture of two of the poachers, Albert Smith and George Harrison, of Hollins Green. The prisoners, who were very badly- beaten on the head and face, and had to be attended by a doctor after being taken to the police station at Leigh, have been remanded.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

CONGREGATIONAL CIIAPEL CHOIR.—The annual sermons in aid of the choir fund were preached in the Congrega- tional Chapel, Golborne, on Sunday last. The preacher was the Rev. R. Lambert, of Poulton, near Blackpool, formerly of Wigan. There was a pretty good attendance at each service, and the collections amounted to SS 15s. SHOCKING RAILWAY AccinENT.—A shocking accident happened on the London and North-Western Railway, on Saturday, a labourer named John Bate • being killed, and another workman, John Bridge, seriously injured. The men were employed on the railway, and were walking along the line from Golborne towards Wigan. They stepped out of the way of the approaching luggage train, but were knocked down by the light engine passing on the other line, which they had failed to notice owing to the heavy fog. Several other workaren had narrow escapes. GOLBORNE CHURCH DAY AND SUNDAY SCHOOLS.—Special sermons were preached in St. Thomas' Church, Golborne, on Sunday last, and collections were made in aid of the funds of the parish day and Sunday schools. The morning preacher was the Rev. George L. B. Wildig, M.A., incum- bent of St. Luke's Church, Liverpool, and in the aftei'noon and•evening the pulpit was occupied hy the Rev. Johe N. Quirk, M.A., incumbent of St. Thomas' Church, Douglas, Isle of Man. There were large attendances, and the collec- tions amounted to the sum of £43, but this has since been increased by subscriptions received. ° THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY AND GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MOVIIMEKT.—A week's mission in connection with the Blue Ribbon Army and Gospel Temperance Movement was com- rnenced in the Congregational School, Golborne, on Monday evening. The meetings are being held in conneetion with the branch of the Bine Ribbon Army established at Edge Green, and are being conducted by Mr. T. Rosbottom, the veteran temperance worker. For a short time previous to the commencement of the first meeting, the Edge Green B:ue Ribbon Army , band paraded the principal street in the village, and attracted a large number of persons. , SINGULAR BAGATELLE COMPETITION. Last weer:, and during the present week' considerable interest has been manifested in a bagatelle handicap, which is being played at the Liberal Club. Thirty-seven competitors entered in a contest, based on the American principle, by which each ?layer must oppose every man in the handicap, the one winning the most matches taking the first prize. It will thus be seen that the contest will take some time before it is concluded, and the table is used continuously each evening; from 8.20 to ten o'clock. The handicappers in their deci- sions appear to have given satisfaction, although their task , was a difficult and arduous one. DWELLINGHOUSES FOR SALE —A large nu-nber of persons interested in matters relating to property assembled at the New Inn, Golborne on Wednesday evening, on the occasion of an announced sale by auction of eight leasehold dwelling- houses, situate in Church-street, and Back Church-street, Golborne (the gross annual rental being X 59 3s), together with the land forming the site, and containing about 1,480 square yards. The lease was dated 26th July, 1353, and the property was subject to an annual rent charge of £6 3s 4dll The auctioneers were Messrs. Provis and Company, of Man- chester. The bidding commenced at £250, and this was briskly advanced to £605, at which point the property was withdrawn. The reserve sum was not announced.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

WESLEYAN Cr:renal, S-E—rt-siore-s.------The anniversary serviees in connection with the. Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Hay- dock, were held on Sunday last, when two sermons were preached by the Rev. G. Smith, of St. Helens, the newly- I appointed minister. There were good attendances, and. I a collection was made at each service in aid of the trust I fund. SALE OF WORE AT ST. JAMES'S SCHOOL.—The sale of the werk completed during the past year by the scholars attending St. James's day schools, was held on Monday evening in the schoolroom. The sale is looked hpon as an annual affair, and the one held on Monday evening was in no way behind its predecessors. The children have been taught by Mrs. Sherlock (wife of the Rev. H. Sherlock, vicar), Mrs. Brooks and Mrs. Walden, who were also in charge of the articles, which were neatly arranged on tables around the room. The goods chiefly comprised pinafores, children's frocks, shirts, underclothing, many a them being exceedingly well made, and evidencing no small amount of careful training. During the evening there was a goodl attendance of persons interested, including the Rev. H. I Sherlock. It is satisfactory to note that neatly, if not quite, all the articles were rapidly disposed of. RIGHT OF ROAD DISPUTE AT PARR.—A scene of AN exciting nature, arising out of a right of road dispute, was witnessed on Saturday week at Parr. It appears that near the Redgate Bridge a Mr. Jackson owns some property which was reached by going along the towing path of the London and North-Western Company's canal. When the Blackbrook extention was made, about two and a half years ago, the company put up a gate on either side of their line, which, it was allege, blocked up Mr. Jackson's right of road. On the 26th ult. it was discovered that the gates had been cut down, and they were re-erected by the corn pany's workmen. On Saturday last, however, a body of seven men, apparently colliers, went to the place with saws and hammers, cut down the gates, pulled up the stumps, and then threw them aside. They afterwards adjleurned to a neighbouring public-house and partook of refreshments, but in the meantime a number of the company's servants, under Inspector Winters, of "the traffic department, replaced the gates. No sooner was this accomplished, however, than Mr. Jackson's workmen returned and again cut them away. The railway men in their turn , re-ected them, and this was continued until the eighth time, when a railway detective took the names of the opposing parties with a view to legal proceedings, and withdrew their men. The gates are now Ifing down, and the roadway is left open. -A good deal of excitement prevailed in the immediate neighbourhood of the occurrence.

LOWTON. LOWTON PRIMITITE. METHODIST CHIPEL.—The Primitive Methodist Chapel anniversary services were beta on. Sunday last, when two sermons were preached by .the Rev. Miles Dickenson, of Earlestown. The congregations were large, and the collections, which were in aid of the trust limas, amopnted to over £lB. Cron/ Ptc..Ntc.—The teachers and choir connected with St. Luke's schools and ,church, Lowton, recntly held their. annual pic-nic, the place chosen being Chester: The weather was extremely fine, and the day was most pleasantly spent in viewing the places of interest in the far-famed city. The party numbered about 35 perBous, and also visited Eat"'
HAII, the seat of the Duke of Wfstm7nster, and saw Cie splindid gardens awl conservatories, in addition to hum the lower moms and ca:rancl Lall of the magnificent inanson.

It w.ta• poin7td4it that the company aff,arded great facilities for h car,tialf, sof milk, but as it was impo:isible to check the cyuantities eom-n ,N. -ed by each farmer the latter had taken advantage of that .ct. False declarations were commonlY made,. and in the ease* brought Ipfore the magistrates a 1..? defendants had understate, I their consignments to a very large extent, in one case of norly 50 per cent. This was admitted, the excuse being that margin of profit was so sooth that if the charge of one peony per gallon were paid for carriage the profit would dieappear. Fines of and costs were imposed upon the defendants, ono.of whom had to pay £l3.

LYMf. CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY CFEOOL.—TheRev. R. Craimp M.A., of Salford, preached the anniversary- sermons in aid of the above school on Sanday morning and evening last. The services wete well attend,d, as was that in the after- noon' when Mr. W. R. Benn, of Loudon, addressfd the teachers, parents, and scholars. The collections amounted to L2O.
_PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPE,L.—At this chapel, on Suuday last, the Rev. W. Rowe, of Chester, ereached two sertnonQ, which were well attended.
RAINHILL.

AN I.lNr.nolt "SPREE" AT RAINTIIILL.—On Tuesiay, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, two men, named Patrick O'Brien and Michael Costello, were charged on remand with having stolen a fowl, valued at 25., the property of Mrs. McLean, poulterer, Prescot. It appeared from the evidence that Frederick John McLean, the son of Mrs. McLean, had been e•oing his round with a cart in which were several dead ' fowl, drc. Having occasion to go into a gentleman's house near Rainbill, he left his cart in the road, and whilst away from it the two prisoners took the fowl. They went into a public-house at Rainhill, threw the fowl on the fl-c, and asked the servant to cook it for .them. She refused, and after some time they left the premises together. Informa- tion was given to the police officer stationed at Rainhill,Sbut before he had time to apprehend the prisoners they went to Mrs. McLean's shop,told'her they had taken the fowl for a drunken "spree," and paid her the price of it, which was 23. They were, however, apprehended on the charge of stealing the fowl.—Mr. Swift, who appeared on behalf of the prisoners, said that the fowl had only been taken as a "spree," and without any felonious intention, in proof of which he poinfed to th&r conduct after they had taken it. —The Bench, however, thought the charge was proved, and sentenced Costello, who had been previously convicted of the theft of a goose, to two months' hard labour, and O'Brien to one month's hard labour. RAINFORD.

A SCUFFLE IN A PUBLIC-HOUSE AT RAINFORD.-011 Mon- day, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, Mark Burke was charged with baying been drunk and refusing to quit licensed premises, and also with further charges of breaking glasses and of assaulting a barman named Daniel Yates. Mr. Thomas, solicitor, said he appeared on behalf of Mr. Middlehurst, landlord of the Bridge Inn, Rainford, upon whose premises the offence bad been comutittei. The number of glasses which had been broken was 16, and their value 45 9d. It appeared that the prisoner, whilst drunk, had gone into Mr. Middlehurat's house and asked the bar- man to supply him with drink. The barman refused, and defendant became violent and struck Yates, and afterwards struck a man named Baxter. Baxter closed with him, and they fell togetaer, and whilst struggling on the floor the tables were overturned and the glasses broken. The 'an,'" lord did his utmost to get the defendant off the premises, but it was not till his mother and brother came and took him away that he succeeded. The summonses had been issued in order to be a warning to others, as disturbances of that kind on licensed premises jeopardised the license, and he (Mr. Thomas) would ask that a severe tine should ba imposed in each ease. Mr. Middlehurst and the barman Yates having corroborated this statement, defendant was fined lOs and costs in each case for refusing to quit and assaulting Yates. The charge of breaking the glasses was dismissed.

div.head: SANDBACH.
div.p: SANDBACH.

FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT SANDBACH.—Mr. Blunt, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Commercial Hotel. Sandbach, on Tuesday evening, touching the death a Ralph Kettle, a passenger, who was killed as he was crossing the line at the station.—Jessie Hodgkinson said that as the 7-35 p.m. train was shunting back, she saw a man at the rear of it walking across the footpath. He disappeared as the train passed. Thomas Wood, booking clerk, said that as the train was in motion he heard a "crunching" sound under it, and on going to look afterwards with a lamp he found the body of the deceased lying across the line. One leg near the foot was crushed, the other from below the knee to the hip was frightfully mangled, the right hand was cut off, and the head bicily injured. It was stated that the deceased had pledged his wach before be left Nantwich, and that although he had obtained a sovereign upon it only 7s. were found upon him.—A verdict of accidental death was returned, added to which was a recommendation that a ftot bridge should be provided at the station.—The Deputy Coroner promised to bring the matter to the notice of the Home Secretary.

WIGAN. CREDITORS' MEETING.—The first meeting el the creditors under liquidation proceedings instituted by Robert Cornish and William Lawton, of Wigan. coachbuilders, was held the other day at the offices of Mr. W. Ashcroft Byrom, solicitor, Wigan. The statement of affairs presented hy the receiver, Mr, George J. Healy, accountant, showed liabilities £931, and assets, less preferential claims, .£338. No offer being forthcoming, it was resolved to wind up the estate in liqui- dation, Mr. Healy being appointed trustee, with a commit- tee of inspection. The principal creditors were represented by Mr. Healy, Mr. H. Vaughan, jun. (H. Vaughan' Son, and Co., accountants), and Mr. Byrom, solicitor, who was entrusted with the registration of the resolutions. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. The Conservatives of West Cheshire held two demonstra- tions on Tuesday—the first at Kingsley and the second at Frodsham. It was incidentelly stated' that the number of meetings hold in connection with their cause of late was 14. The Nantwich Local Board approved at 10 meeting on Friday of the plan and the proposed new brine baths, the swimming bath of which will be upwards of 46 feet in length. The example set by the Crewe Town Council in applying to the Post-office authorities for an improved Post Office pas been emulated by the authorities at Nantwich, who de- cided at their meeting on Friday to m dee a similar applica- tion. AN EXTRAORDINARY CRIMINAL.—A child named Taylor, aged nine yeats, whose head only just appeared above the table, was sentenced by the Chester magistrates to 14 ,lays' imprisonment and four years in a reformatory, for stealing jam. Al:hough of such tender years, he has alre irly com- mitted four felonies. He has one brother in gaol and another in a reformatory. On Thursday the tenantry on the Eaton a d Chester Estates of the Duke of Westiniester preamted to the Duchess a diamond ring, in celebration of her recent mirrfage. The Duke, in reply, referred to the pleasant relations which had always existed between himself and the tenantry, and-trusted they would so continue. DISGRACEFUL ASSAULT ON A LADY.—At Haleeowen, on Tuesday, a farm labourer ntmed Leyshon was charged with assaultiog a lady named Emily Morris. When walking through one of the principal streets in Halesowen, coin- olainant was overtaken by defendant, who jumped upen her back and attemp'ed to kiss her. He was vet y rough and she was knocked down. Prisoner, who said he was larking, was, in default of paying a fine, sentenced to 21 days' imprison- ment. PRESENTATION TO THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF WEST- -111INSTER.-I'he presentation by the city of Chester of two testimonials to the Duke and Duchess of West- minster, in celebration of their marriage, took place at Eaton Hall on Saturday. The testimonials consisted of a magnificent diamond bracelet, subscribed for by the ladies of Chester, and an illuminated address from the Cor- poration. The Duke, in returning thanks, gracefully alluded to his connection with the city, and assured his hearers that at all times everything which concerned its highest and best interests should have us hearty support. The bracelet was presesated to the Duchess by Mrs. Howson, wife of the Dean of Cheater.

'party, but, on 'no other hand, to the nhagrin of the detractors of the Government,, and especially of Sir Garnet Weiseley, the rebellion has been successfully stamped out, and it can no longer be said that a Liberal Government is afraid or powerless to protect British interests. Now that we have oenquered, the question arises what is to be done with Egypt, Oar interest in it, it is manifest, must now be greater than it has hitherto been, and we sincerely hope that no sentimental feelings will induce the Government to bate one jot or tittle of the influence we are entitled to exercise in Egyptian eouncils. We have conquered single-handed, and we are entitled to reap the fruit of our vietory. It has been suggested that the future of Egypt should be settled in European Conference, as was the treaty of San Stefano. There may be a great deal said in favour of such a Conference, and so thoroughly disinterested has been the action of Bugland in this war that we do net for a moment doubt the final settlement will be submitted to the combined Powers, but we may remind those who are so eager for such a course being adopted that other Powers have not been careful to set an example in this respect. A European Conference did not decide the fate of Bosnia or of Tunis, and if it de- cides the fate of Egypt it will be because of the mag- nanimity of the,English Government. France, whose loot skulked away when Admiral Seymonr proceeded to open fire on the Alexandria forts, is now desirous of the Joint Control being re-established. It is some- what cool of France to make such a request, seeing that she allowed England to do all the work of the eainpaign ; but there is, we should think, little fear of the request of Franca being complied with. The Control has been the cause of too many difficulties and eomplioations in the past to be of any efficacy in the future; and its abolition may, therefore, be accepted as a foregone conclusion. We may be sure, too, that the Sultan's influence will not in any way be aug- mented; it may, however, be curbed. The Sultan has shown an extraordinary capacity for abusing the titular power he now possesses, and consequently his position does not call for any special consideration at the hands of England, except to curtail his authority. From the strong arm of England alone can Egypt and the Khedive hope for any assistance at the present jatiacture, and this England is prepared to extend, in no selfish spirit, in order that the resources of the sountry may be developed. The sole object in inter- vening in Egypt at all, as has been again and again avowed, was to destroy the military faction which was ruining the country, and to restore the people by degrees to the enjoyment of the privileges of self-government. Mr. Gladstone has frequently declared it to be one of the most sacred duties of Her Majesty's Government to use whatever influence they pessess for the purpose of promoting the advancement of the people of the country; and we need scarcely say that the expendi- ture of her blood and treasure in the war which has now closed has established for England a moral claim. to participation in the future government of Egypt which no Power will dispute. How England's in - fluence can best be exercised is now the one question which has to be solved. The aspirations of the National Party, such as it is, must be respected, and along with this there must be a regular system of representative institutions ;established. Were all the Powers of Ruralise to share in the Government, opportunities would be created for interminable Intrigues, one Poser trying to gain asi ascendancy over another. These would lead probably to ;further difficulties, and cer- tainly they would retard the progress of the country itself; but if left to the disinterested tutelage of Eng- land, Egypt would, we believe, soon recover her lost ground and make rapid strides towards advancement. In the controlling influence of England alone rests our hope for the future of Egypt, and though such a eontrolling influence would give rise to jealousy on the part of other Powers we feel sure that they need have nothing to fear. Besides, they chose to allow England to fight by itself, and they ought to be satisfied with the security England's presence on the Suez Canal affords for the protection of that great !highway. We may add that. one of the inevitable results of the war will be to more firmly establish the Government in the confidence of the country, and we are glad to find that this fact is recognised in sources not usually guilty of saying anything in favour of a Liberal Administration.

WIDNES POLICE COVET.—Yesterday, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and J. Brock, Elizabeth Bushell, who made her Bth appearance, was committed to gaol for a month for being drunk and disorderly on the previous day.

TZEFT OF i CUPBOARD POOR AT WIDNES.— Henry Bartley, 56 years of age, was brought up on remand at Widnes Police Court, yesterday, on a charge of stealing a cupboard door, the property of Joseph Sherlock, of St. Helens. The particulars of the case have been previously given. The prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, and ordered to pay the damage (7s. 61), or in default a fortnight's im- prisonment.

THEFT OE' A LOAF AT WIDNES. -At Widnes Police Court yesterday, before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. J. Brock, a young girl named Hannah Nixon was charged with steal- ing a 21b.loaf from the shop of Francis Lawrinson, grocer, Waterloo-road, Widnes. Mr. Lawrinson stated that on Wed- nesday afternoon, at four o'clock., the prisoner went into his shop and made some purchases. As she was leaving he saw the loaf (produced) under her apron. He accused her ef stealing the loaf, when she stated she had got it from the ' next house. He found that this statement was false, and eventually the prisoner admitted her guilt. She was fined I bs and costs.

MAN DROWNED LT RVNCORN Docis.—On Thursday afternoon there was recovered from the Bottom Locks Basin, Runcorn, by P.C. Wallace, the body of a sailor named •Samuel Mitchell, who resided at New Quay, Cornwall. The ;deceased was math of the schooner" Saint," which is at pre- sent moored in Runcorn Docks, and on Wednesday evenine. ' about 9 o'clock, he was seen in the town. He afterwards appears to have returned on board. About 11 o'clock the .captain heard the deceased ascend from the cabin to the deck, in consequence, he thought, of Mitchell being seized with illness. He, however, considered there was nothing strange about this and went to sleep. The following morn- ing he discovered that the deceased was not on the boat, and suspecting that he might have been drowned, gave informa- tion to the police with the result previously stated. RUNCORN LICENSING SESSIONEI ADJOURNED MEET.. ntn.—The adjourned meeting of the Licensing Sessions for .the Runcorn district was held in the Town Hall, on Monday morning. The magistrates present ,en the Bench were Mr. Henry Reynolds (chairman) and Mr. E. A. Thomas. In accordance with the -usual custom, those persons whose ,names were on the black list appeared personally to apply for the renewal of their licenses. The list was a light one. The landlords who appeared were—Samuel Burrows, of the Royal Oak public-house, Weston, who had been fined 40s. .and costs 14s. Oct., for selling drink during prohibited hours, •on the 10th December.; Edward Hill, of the Dog and Partridge, Runcorn, who had been fined 403. and costs 215., for permitting drunkenness on the 30th August,lBBl ; James lEaguley, of the Queen's Head, Runcorn, who had been fined 20s. and costs 15s. 6d., kr permitting drunkenness en the 25th March ; Wm. Hulse, of the Village Inn, Weston, who had been fined 20s. and casts 95. 6d., for selling during pro- hibited hours.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said he had no objection to the renewal of the licenses: whereupon Mr. Reynolds remarked that the licenses would' ,be renewed on this occasion, but the applicants had better take care that their names did not again eccur on the blank list, or their licenses would be taken from them.

A MAN DROWNED IN TEE WEAVER AT SDITON.-Art inquest was held at the Aston Arms, Sutton, ea Wednesday, by Mr. J. E. Worsley, deputy coroner, on the body of an Irishman named Michael O'Hara, who was drowned on Sun- day night, the 10th inst.—Deceased was 35 years of age, and a farm labourer employed by Mr. Wm. Griffiths, of Weston. On Sunday, the 10th inst., deceased, in company with about half a dozen friends, went up the Weaver in a small boat as far as Pickering's Locks. They arrived at a public-hod-se close by about seven o'clock p.m., and they remained for about an bony. Deceased started to walk home in company with Martin Radkin and two females. He, however, became so incapable on the way that they were obliged to leave him. After the_ party had proceeded some distanee they were over- taken by a man named Murphy, who had been In deceased's company. They asked him if he bad passed O'Hara on the road, and he replied "No." The deceased was not again seen alive, and his body was found floating in the river Weaver by John Molyneux, captain of the flat "Thomas," with the bead split open, but this injury was supposed to have been caused by the screw of a passing steamsf,, The jury returned a verdict of "Found dead."
SANIISY Cittraort BAZAAR. —The receipts at this bazaar, on Saturday, amounted to £96 9s. 10,1., making the total receipts for the week DOS Is.

SERMON TO CILILDRIIN AT RIINCORN.-011 Sunday morning, at Halton-road Wesleyan Chapel, the Rev. George Hack preached a special sermon entitled " Bread " to Sunday school scholars. There was a large number present.

WIFE BFATING AT ItTINCOUN.-At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. John Bruudrit and Mr. R. M. Brooke, a boatman named James Armstrong was brought up in custody to answer a charge of assaulting his wife Eleanor, at Runcorn, on Monday.—lt appeared that P.C. Price, who was passing at the time, saw the prisoner come out of his house, rush at his wife, who was standing out- side, and brutally kick her several times.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and said his wife had provoked him.—He was fined 40s. aad costs 83. GI, or, in default, one month's imprisonment with hard labour.

A DREADYITL FALL AT WESTON. —ln a quarry situate off the Weston Highway, a woman namel Ellen Hart was discovered, suffering from serious injuries, at an early hour on Sunday morning. Her injuries had evidently been caused by falling into the quarry, which reaches a depth of 34 feet, and it is a matter of extreme surprise that she was not instantly killed. Mr. Capper, publican, b-ought the woman in a conveyance to Runcorn police station, where she was seen by a doctor, and subsequently she was conveyed to Dutton Workhouse. The woman, we understand, was in Runcorn on Saturday night, in a state bordering on intoxi- cation, and the only explanation of the somewhat mysterious accident is that she aimlessly wandered to Weston, and, in the darkness, fell into the quarry.

ALLEGED ROBBERY FROIL A. WIDNE3 BARMLN.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Police-court, Margiret Rooney was brought up in custody on a charge of stealing a silver watch and chain, valued at £3 35., from the person of John Holden, barman of the Albert Hotel, and living in Albert•road.— Holden stated that about twenty minutes past seven on Tuesday morning he went to the Castle Inn publichouse, where he remained until eight o'clock. Whilst walking on Albert-road, on his way home, he met the prisoner. Having had some drink, he went into a field off the roid, and lay down. The prisoner followed him there. He fell asleep, and, when he awoke, about eleven o'clock, he missed his watch and chain, which he had upon him when he fell asleep. The prisoner had gone away. The prisoner was remanded for a week.

Brooke, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, James Thompson, a seaman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in High-street on the pre- vious day, and also with assaulting P.C. Mellor whilst in the execution of his duty, at the same time and place. Francis Clarke, clogger, Ellesmere-street, was chlarged with attempting to rescue Thompson, and with ASsatiltiDg Morris.—P.C. Mellor, it seenaz,, was MI ditty k High-street about ten o'clock on the, prisoners come o 1 night in question, when he saw the proceed :4 of the Holyhead Harbour beerhouse, and the street. Thompson, who was drunk, made ee of bad language, and Mellor requested him to behave himself. The t onstable followel the prisoners some dis- tance, and when they had got near the cocoa rooms, Thomp- son struck him. A struggle ensued, and Clarke attempted to rescue his companion. P.C. Morris now came to the as- sistance of his brother officer, when he was struck by Clarke, and eventually both the prisoners were apprehended.—For being drunk and disorderly Thompson was fined 10a. and costs 7s. 4d., or, in default, 14 days' hard labour ; and for the assault he was fined 20s. and ss. costs with the alterna- tive of a montlesfurther imprisonment.—dlarke was mulcted in the penalty of 20a. and costs 78. 4d.—Thompson went to gaol.

RUNCORN NwrioNAL ScnooLs.—The annual sermons and flower service in behalf of these schools were held on Sunday, in the Parish Church. In the morning the Rev. George Bond, vicar of Farnworth, occupied the pulpit, and in the evening the sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Barclay, the vicar. The children's flower service held in the afternoon attracted a large congregation, and the sacred edifice was crowded. The scho!ars from the national schools, Newtown mission school, Weston schools, and the Sunday school of the Mersey Missions to Seamen, most of whom carried flowers in their hands, occupied the centre of the church. A large number of the parishioners had also brought offerings of flowers, which at the close of the service were placed on the altar steps, afterwards to be sent to gladden the heart of some poor p client in Widnes Accident Hospital, Chester Infirmary, and the various Liverpool hospitals. Hymns, chosen for the occasion by the vicar, were sung, and it is a fact worth mentioning that Master Charles Clark, a boy choriste;, read the lesson for the day. The Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A.., preached a highly instructive and interesting sermon on flowers, and the lessons they taught. The collec- tions amounted to .£26 lie. 9th

TRAMPLING THROUGH THE Okra. A young lean, named Jno. Allman, was charged at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, with unlawfully and wilfully damag log growing oats, the property of James Dunbavin, by trampling down the same. It appeared that in the com- plainant's field is a pit, which contains fish, and the only way by which it can be reached is through a crop of oats. "Fishermen," in the prosecution of Unit pastime, had not scrupled to trample through the oats, forming a kind of beaten track. The complainant, determined to make an example of the first gentle craftsman upon whom he could lay his bands, and, on the Bth inst., he discovered the defendant on the edge of the pit. As he could not hav'e arrived there without walking through the field of oats, he was summ,ned for committing damage to the extent of Is., although the complainant said this was far below the actual amount.—Defendant pleaded that he only walked on pits which had been already trampled upon, but Mr. Rey:

fields said he had no business there whatever, and fined him '23 6d, and costs 103 6d. and ordered him to pay the damage, or, in default, seven day's hard labour. FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.--.411 Saturday MOM.. -hag, jamos Rydehead, joiner, residing at 13. Halton-view, met with an accident at the works of Messrs. Sullivan and Company, which resulted in his tleath. It appeared that Rydehead was erecting en the top of an acid chamber, at a height of 41 feet from the ground, a platform for the plum- bers-to work upon, when he fell to the ground, and was picked up insensible. Midway between the top of the cham- ber and the ground is a platform in which was a hole 16 inches wide, and the deceased, who was a stout man, strange to say, fell through. The hie/west en the body was held on Tuesday, at the George Inn, before Mr. Coroner DritEeld. Mr. ]J. Brock, J.P., watched the inquiry on behalf of the ffirm—Eleanor Rydehead, widow of the deceased, said her husband was 45 years of age. Ilehad been in his employ- ment at Messrs. Brock s for a period of three or four years. He left home in the best of health about six o'clock on i3aturday morning, and about eleven o'clock she heard of, -the accident. When she was going to the works she !net a cart conveying her husband to the hospital, and she followed, it. She saw him in the hospital. He was unconscious.l She saw him many times during Sunday, in the evening of', which day ho died, without even regaining consciousness. In answer to the Coroner she said ahe had heard that so , stout a man ac her husband ought not.to have been sent to the job he was doing on Saturday morning. He, however, did not think he was too stout to do the work.—Ellen Thompson, nurce at the hospital srro.dsm, said the de- ceased was received into the hospital at a quarter to twelve on Saturday. He was seen by Dr. O'Keeffe. His head was very badly cut, and he had serious injuries to his body, although there was no external wound. No bones werebroken that she was aware of. Relived until 7-40 on Sunday evening. Everything that could be done for the deceased was done, end he was attended l‘ir four doctors._! Alexander Thorborn, living at 15, Mersey-road, Moss Bank, said he was a labourer at the works in question. The acci- dent by which the deceased lost his life occurred about half-past ten on Saturday morning. He .(witness) was at the time spreading some wood on a kiln, when he saw the deceased falling. He fell quickly and .heavgy. Witness called aid to the deceased, who had been on the acid chamber engaged in come occapation.—Robert Bur- r_ell, of Grove House, Parnworth, foreman joiner at the works, said the deceased was one of his men. He did not see the accident, and the deceased had been conveyed to the ieiner's shop-when he saw him. Witness fetched some brandy, and sent for a doctor. Dr. O'Reeffe arrived with all speed, and ordered his removal to the hospital. Drs. Brown, McDonald, and Shaw examined him at the infirmary. He thought deceased had fallen from the top of a vitriol chamber. Deceased had worked with witness for three yehrs, and during that time be had assisted to build five chambers, and was thoroughly conversant with the work. He had been working on the same chamber for a fortnight previous to the accident, and the bole he fell through he cut himself. He was working alone at the time of the accident. He had cut the hole two days previously. The top of the chamber was about 41 feet above the ground. Ito tools fell with the demised, who was employed to make a-scaffold for the plumbers to work on, the hole being made to haul the boards up—Mr. Brock produced a plan of the chambers, which he explained. It could only be conjec- tured hew the deceased came to fall. The marvellous thing was that the deceased had, in his fall gone through a hole only 15 inches wide.—A juryman remarked that theileceased was 45 inches round the waist,—.4- Yerdict QI azei.Jenta.l death was reco:dod.

RuNconw SCIENCE &Hoot, NN. 449.—The preliminary meeting for the ensuing season will .be held in Bethesda Schoolroom, on Friday evening next. Mr. J. R. Frith will preside.

RUNCORN BRITNSWICY METELL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.— The usual weekly meeting of the Brunswick Mutual Im- provement Class took place on Wednesday evening in the School-room, Brunswick-street. Mr. T. Simister occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. of members. Mr. Thomas Simkin read a paper on "Scott and his Poems." The essayist gave a brief and interesting sketch of the poet's life, and towards the close of his paper read, with great taste and skill, several extracts from "The Lay of the Last Minstrel," " Marmitin," "The Lady of the Lake," and the "Lord of the Isles," and was frequently applauded. A cor- dial vote of thanks was accorded the essayist at the close of the meeting. PROPOSED ALTERATION TO THE UNITED METHODIST FREE CHEMCII, RUNCORN.—The annual tea meeting in con- nection with this church was held in the Schoolroom, Elles- mere-street, on Monday evening, and it was attended by about 80 persons. Afterwards a public meeting, presided over by the pastor, the Rex. J. Billington, was held. The deliberations of the assembly were occupied in the settle- ment of the question as to whether a spirited effort should be made to wife off the debt of £370, which existed upon the church, or whether it was advisable to repair and beautify the sacred edifice. The chairman, Mr. Edward Jones, Mr. F. A. Clarke, Mr. G indy, Mr. M. Timperley, addressed the meeting, and were imanimously in favour of beautifying and improving the church, it being agreed that they would secure better congregations, and thus be in a better position to liquidate the debt. Ultimately Mr. Gandy moved, and Mr. Timperley seconded, a motion to the etf,ct that in the opinion of the meeting a special effort should be made to reseat andoirnprove the chapel, ant it was adopted unani- mously. It is intended to hold a bazaar abut April next to raise the money with which to carry out the improve- ment.

RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY COMMITTRE.—Ths monthly meeting of the above committee was held in the Commissioners' Board-room, on Thursday evening, and there were present—Dr. McDougall (in the chair), Dr. Steele/ Messrs. J. Simpson, G. Rhodes, T. Riley, W. Handley, P. Briscoe, G. S. Hazlehurst, F. A. Like, J. R. Frith, and W. Brookes (secretary.)—lt was resolved, on the motion of Dr. Steele, seconded by Dr. McDougall, that the Rev. Canon Barclay be re-appointed chairman for the ensuing year.— On the motion of Dr. Steele, seconded by Mr. Simpson, Dr. McDougall was re-appointed vice-chairman.—The following letter was read by the Chairman:—" Halton Lodge, Septem- ber 11th, 1882.—T0 the chairman of the Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners.—Dear Sir,—l have the pleasure to present to the Runcorn Free Library the accompanying 13 volumes of 'Engineering,' which I have no doubt will be useful to the scientific readers.—l remain, dear sir, yours truly, Charles Wigg."—On the motion of Mr. Simpson,' seconded by Mr. Hazlehurst, the best thanks of the committee were given to Mr. Wig g for his valuable present. The Librarian reported that 1,471 books had been issued during the month of August, being an average of 163 per day, classed as follows :—Theology, 38; political economy, ctc., 15; science and art, 64; history, travels, and biography-, 319; poetry and the drama, 32; prose fiction, 915 ; miscel- laneous, 88. Books presented during the month Homanism Weighed, written and presented by the Rev. Wm. Preston, M.A.; Engineering, 13 vols., by Mr. Charles Wigg ; John- son's Idler, two bijou vols., and several novels, by Mr.l Oliver Leak; Guide to Employment in the Civil Service, ' by Mr. T. C. Williams; and several pamphlets of local in- terest, by the Committee of the Warrington Library and Museum.—On the motion 9f Dr, steele. seconded by Mr. Frith, a. cordial. vote ot thanks was given to Dr. McDougall for ll:tying presented to the committee a handsomely-framed copy of the rules and regulations, printed on parchment, containing the autographs of the fist committee and Sir J. A. Picton, which now graces the walls of the reading- room.—lt was resolved, on the motion of Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. Simpson, that Messrs. Rhodes, Handley, Frith, and Lake be appointed a committee to make arrangements for a series of lectures during, the winter months.

LECTURE BY TILE REV. .1. D. Thomas, OF RUNcoitN.—The annual meeting of the Rev. J. D. Thomas's children's class was held in Bethesda school-room on Monday evening, when the rev, gentleman delivered- a very interesting lecture on "Hymns and hymn writers." Mr. Thomas Handley occupied the chair. There was a good attendance, the room being half filled. The lecturer remarked that if the; physical benefits spoken of by Carlyle were to bs ob- tained by the free use of their vocal powers, then they ought to sing with all their might. But the singing of psalms and hymns and spiritual songs had a much more important influence on the life of the Church of God since the days when Moses sang his ode of triumph after having crossed the Rd Sea. Psalms and hymns had been multi- plied at an enormous rate; and still they came, and if they did not actually fill the world with their bulk, they were likely soon to fill it with the sound of their music. All of them had not, however, been in,pired by the achievement of brilliant victories. Some of them, and perhaps the sweetest, were inspiged through circumstances of a most de- pressing character. Ag there were flowers which emitted their odours only when they were crushed and bruised, so there were souls who sung their sweetest songs to the Lord when His chastening rod was upon them. Mr. Thomas then related the circums!anvs which had led to the composition of a number of the Lyrnns in the Congrega- tional hymn book, and the songs and solos of Messrs. Moody and Sankey, giving a number of delightful inci- dents connected with them in a very instructing manner. After the discussion of the last hymn, the class, aided by a few meinbers of the church choir, gave a pleasing musical rendering of them. Miss Clara Barrow sang the solo of " When peace like a river; " Miss Emily Ainsworth, I "Come, father, pray with use to-night;" and Miss Polly I Abrams, "Meet me at the fountain." The youthful song- sters acquitted themselves very creditably. Mr. F. Fair- hurst conducted, and Mr. George Lacy presided at the harmonium. Previous to the lecture Hedley Powell re- cited the piece "Charity," and Robert Gornall ' The village lacksmith." Mr. Thomas announced that his class numbered 83 members, and the average attendance during the season amounted to 50. On the motion of Mr. William Handley, seconded by Mr. Slade a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Thomas for his in- teresting lecture.

-SAD BURNING FITAITY AT WARRINGTOIC—Mr.CJrODin 13.n0d h(ld an ingeiry at the White ,Hart Inn, Sankey- street, on Wednesday, touching the death of Sarah Hart, 56. a widow, who lived at 8, Litton's-row, off ;Morey-street, It appeared that the deceased had for some tient been sub- l'ect to fits, and on Thursday morning she was heard in the 'kitchen by her daughter-in-law, who on going down stairs 'found her with her head on the bars of the Ere-place badly burned.- The chair on which deceased had been sitting was ,overturned, and MTS. Hart believed she had fallen with her 'face on the fire whilst in a fit. A verdict was returned to the effect that deceased came to her death accidentally.

A LATCHFORD IAAN DROWNED AT Lie) -Mr. Wors. ley (deputy coroner) held an inquest, on Thursday, at the Bridgewater Arms, Lymm, touching the -death of William Bradshaw, a driver in the employ of the Bridgewater Navi- gation Company, and who resided at 10, Beatrice-street, 'Latchford. Deceased, who was 54 year.; of age, left home Ito go to work at an early hour, cm Monday morning. He was seen by Thomas Wood, captain of the fiat, about eight p.m., on Monday night, near Oughtrington Bridge. Deceased then shouted to the captain ' that he was taking his horse to the stable, and he heard I him go away with the horse in the direction of the stable. He was not afterwards seen alive. The estler informed the captain that the horse had corne.to the stables by itself about 8-15 on the•following morning. Wood was despatched to Latchford to eee if deceased had got borne, but on arrival •he found he was not there. On Wednesday morning a man I named John Bate, -who works on the canal bank,commenced to grapple for the body, and found it between Lymm and •Oughtrington Bridges. P.C. Chatterton examined the body, but found no marks of violence upon it. A watch was ,found in the deceatod's pocket, which was stopped at three 'minutes to nine. A verdict of "Found , drowned" was {returned.

A COAL DRALRZIAINED FOR DEFRAUDIVIG Titel Henry Al!mark, a coal dealer, residing at Salford, was ,oharged at the Warengton Police Court, yesterday, with telling a bag of coal without weighing it; and John Wilkin- con and John Mannion; who were employedly the defendant, wore charged with Aiding and abetting.—Mr. Whittle, deputy town clerk, prosecuted on behalf of the Corporation. —The case was brought under the Weights and Measures Act, iS7B, which stipuleicd that coal, &ea shall be sold by weight and not by measure. In consequence of complaints of short weight, Mr. Plate, market inspector, has been on the look out, and on the llth inst. he saw the defendont in Allen-street, and noticed Mannion take a bag of coal out of the tart and deliver it to a woman named Mrs. Gibson. He took it alp an entry and placed it in the yard. Mr. Place followed the lad into the sard and asked Mrs. Gibson whether eke ordered a hundredweight, and she said " yes ; I have paid him for a hucdredweight." The lad, in answer to Mr. Place, said that he did not weigh the coal. Mr. Plate took the cart, Wilkinson, and Melanin( to the Town Hall, where he weighed the coal. There were about 21 bags in all in the cart. One of the bags was 34i lbs short of a hundred weight, and another 314 lbs short. The bass were all full, and none of them would weigh a cwt. They appeared only to be cwt. bas. Mr. Place told Wilkinson he must not sell any more cos without weighing it. The defendant said that he gave his ;men instructions to weigh the coal, and they always carried a pair of scales for that purpose. The cut was always sup- plied with a quantity of loose coal so as to make up weight of any bag which was deficient. The bags were bought for ' cwt. hags—Mr. Place stated that the two defendants had only about 50 lbs of lease coal at the bottom of the cart, which was not sufficient to make up the deficiencies in the two bags he weighed.—Allvrark was flened 403 and costs, but Wilkinson and Mannion were discharged, as they were acting und9r the instructions of their employer.

div.head: WARRINGTON LEA.GUE OF THE CROSS. CARDINAL MANNING AND MR. McMINNIES,
div.p: WARRINGTON LEA.GUE OF THE CROSS. CARDINAL MANNING AND MR. McMINNIES,
ON TEMPNRANCE.

His Emine.nce Cardinal Manning paid his second visit to Warrington on Monday evening, and delivered an address in the Public Hall, under the auspices of the Warrington League of the Cross. There was a very large attendance, and many of those present wore the regalia of the League, while banners and mottoes bidding "Welcome to our Car- dinal Prince," wishing Success to the League," and "Long live his Eminence," were displayed in various parts of the hall. Exactly at the time fixed for the commence- bent of the proceedings Mr. .1. G. McMinnies, M.P., who was announced to preside, made his appearance on the plat- form, accompanied by Cardinal Manning, Rev. A. B. Pozzi, 0.5.8. (chaplain of the League); Rev. T. B. Feeny, 0.5.8., Rev. J. C. Almond, 0.5.8., Rev. T. 0. Furniss, 0.5.8., Rev. J. C. Cody, 0.5.8., Rev. J. Thompson, Councillors C. Broadbent, J. Croslield, F. Monks, and P. Caldwell, Mr. R. Hind, Dr. Fax, Messrs. J. H. Gornall, T. Wallington, G. T. Moore, Marsh, T. Flood, John W. Hall (1.0 G.T.), J. Mullins (president of the-League), and others. The Cits.rxmAN, who was cordially greeted, said :—Mv Lord Cardinal, ladies and gentlemen,—Two things occur to me to say to you to-night in the very few observations I shall have to make. The first is the magnitude of the evil against which, as temperance reformers, you are contending, And the second is the great encouragement which it seems to me the state of public opinion and public practice ought to give to you as temperance reformers. (Applause.) A great orator and statesman of our own day and country said not long ago that if you could abstract from all the misery, all the poverty, all the crime, and all the distress that affects this country, all the misery, all the crime, all the poverty and all the distress that arises from intemperance the country would be sa improved as that hardly any of us would know it. And the testimony of men most likely to know the condition of the country is all of the same kind. , Magistrates, from the judges downward. medical men, ministers of religi in, those amongst us who are best acquainted with the social condition of the country. all bear witness of the same kind ; and those of us who mix much with society are quite prepared to accept the verdict of these men, and to say that perhaps the greatest curse that affects this country is thts curse of iutemperance. (Applause.) At the same time, Ido believe' that there are circumstances in connection with the sentiment and practice of this country which are very encouraging to those who wish to put an end to ,this great curse. I remem- ber the time when a host was considered a very good fellow I indeed, if, at the end of his entertainment, half his guests were under the table—(laughter and applause)—and the perfected pattern host was the man who locked his door so that his guests should not escape until , they were in that state or very near it. I remember the time, too, when it was a common thing for tradesmen, after their hours of business, to repair every night to their accustomed tavera and to drink there until late. I have known members of Parliament, and men who aspired to be such, to indulge in this practice. The change that I think has taken place in this matter is not confined to the middle or the higher classes. I believe that working- men are very much better in this respect—(hear, hear)— than they were when I was born. (Applause.) I have been practically a workingman for 40 or 50 years. I was apprenticed to the cotton trade when I was very young for seven years, and I am an employer now, and have been for many years, of 1,000 to 1,500 men in that trade, and my experience is that the habits of the people with whom I mil connected in this way are very much improved to what those habits were when I was apprenticed to that trade. (Applause.) I speak of my own trade because lam best acquainted with it; but I WAS talking on this subject only yesterday with a man who, if I wete to name Lies, you would say was not in the habit of making reckless or any statements that had no foundation, and he told me that he had been 35 years in the iron trade, and his experience—l dare hardly put it into figures, it seems to me to be so astounding, but his experience at any rate was the same in reference to the iron trade as mine is in reference to the cotton trade. (Applause.) I remember that in a town that I am a good deal acquainted with, there was a club con- sisting of eight members. I think it was called the Octagon Club, and the custom was for the members to dine together once a month, and the custom also was that every Member of the club had three bottles of port wine put under his chair after dinner—(laughter)—and he was expected either to drink it or take it home with him. (Laughter.) Well, I have been told that the members of that club did not carry home that wine in the bottle. (Laughter.) Such a thing now is impossible. I do not know any man living to whom three bottles of port wine would not be as fatal as a dose of prussic acid. I do not know anyone who would drink three bottles of wine, but that was the custom in reference to this cub, and that club existed 50 years ago. Well, now, ia reference to this par- ticular question of the improvement in the temperance habits of the people, the national revenue gives us some evidence. The revenue from intoxicating drink is diminish- ing, and temperance reformers will have to pay for their exertions in an extra income tax—(laughteri—unless they can persuade the7paople of this country that they may be governed with a less expenditure than £85,000,000 sterling a year. (Applause.) Now I saw a very remarkable illus- tration of what I am contending for—that ha the improved habits of the people—in Preston a fortnight ago. (Ap- plause.) I dare say you have all heard of the Preston it is a celebration that is held every 20 years, and it is a great holiday. It was a great holiday a fortnight ago. Everybody abstained from work for a week—in the neigh- bourhood of Preston, I mean—and it is said that on two idays during that week there were a million of people in the town. I believe that you (Cardinal Manning) assisted one day in that celebration. (Applause.) Well, the testimony of everybody who is likely to know —the policemen, the magistrates, and the outside visitors—is that it was remarkable for the sobriety of the people. (Applause.) Lord Winmarleigh told nee himself that he had been there every day for a week, and he had not seen a drunken man. (Applause.) He said, moreover, that he joined in the procession to the church, the way of which was kept without the aid of a single policeman. (Applause.) Ido not mean to say that there was not a drunken man in Preston during that week, because there were many,—two many—but there can be no doubt at all I think from what I hear that the sobriety of the people was most remarkable. I spoke to an old resident of Preston on this subject, and he said "I have attended three Preston ; Guilds, and I can assure you that there was less intemper- ance at this Guild, when Preston had 100,000 inhabitants, than at the first Guild I attended, when there were only 30,000." Well, this testimony, you will observe, does not apply to Preston alone. So many people came to Preston during that week that it is hardly an exaggeration to say everybody in the county was in Preston that week, and whatever you may say about the sobriety and order that prevailed in Preston during the Graild you may say that it characterised a large number of people who were not in- habitants of Preston. (Applause.) Now, why do I say these things and take this toner Not because I wish to minify or make light of the evil against which you are contending- Quite the contrary. I admit it in all its force. But 'Meat I should like to say is this: that there has been a great deal in the habits of the people, and in the changed habits of the people, that ought to be encourag- ing to you as temperance reformers. (Applause.) Not long ago a friend of mine, who has done, perhaps, as much to forward temperance in this town as anybody, except his wife, said to me that ho thought the whole thing was a failure. He -said, "I have seen one thing after anether— teetotalsacieties, total abstinence societies, bends of hope, leagues .alliances everything, and we are as bad as we were when we began." He spoke with great despondency. Now, I think this is a great mistake. -,I think it is a great blunder, I mean this despondency, because it does not rest upon the solid 'foundation of facts. The real truth is that you have got reason to be encouraged in your work, in consequence of what, at any rate, I remember during my time. I dare say that the various temperance soeieties that we have are not all of them doing as much as we -should desire, not all of them doing as much as those who founded them toped for, but there is no doubt at all in my mind, and 1 hope there is no doubt in yours, that they are all working together for good,eand they are bringing about that time when -you who are engaged in this work mly see the result of your labours and be satisfied. (L9ut applause.) Well, now, I know perfectly well that you don't come here to listen to me, and I am not going to take up any more of -your time. I have now the great honour and • pleasure of asking his Eminence to address us. (Ap- plause.) Cardinal Mammra, who was enthusiastically received, expressed his pleasure to be once more in Warrington and in that place. (Applause.) Since he entered that ball one conviction bad grown upon him, and that was that the League of the Cross in Warrington had become solid, strong, and numerous, far beyond what it was when he last was in that place. (Applause.) He rejoiced to know how many members there were already enrolled, but being a man cf discontented mind he should not he satisfied after be went away without a very much larger number being enrolled that night. (Applause.), He was also exceedingly glad to see before him guards of the League of the Cross. planate) As he said the other'day at Widnes and at Laver- pool, it made laim feel to be at home again, •for in London he had the happiness of seeing that sash and those medals and insignia wherever he went ; and he hoped the number would be multiplied in Warrington, for there were signs of a great and good work, a work that would be for the glory of .God and the salVation of souls. (Applause.) He was especially happy to see the young guards and the young girls and women enrolled in the League of the Cross. (Applause.) It was a fine thing to see the >harvest field full of ripe corn, and it was a beautiful thing to see the garner full of good grain for the next year. (Applause.) The members of the League of the Cross who were grown to manhood and womanhood were the harvest standing in the field, the young guards and the girls were the good seed in the garner who would grow up to fill their places, and .there would be another harvest ripe, matured, multiplied thirty-fold, sixty-fold, and a hundred-fold, ho hoped, when they who began the League of the Cross were gone to their rest.
