div.p: paper—though he did not always agree with it—and which, with the intention, he feared, rather of discouraging their work, for it had never spoken a word of encouragement on the subject of local option or popular veto, summed up its argument in this way. It said there had been efforts made now for half a century, efforts of temperance socie- ties, efforts of temperance reformers, efforts of politicians, efforts of statesmen, and what had they come to? It was acknowledged everywhere that the places where intoxicat- ing drink was sold were increased three-fold; it was acknowledged that the arrests fer drunkenness were doubled; it was acknowledged that the capital invested in the distribution of intoxicating drink had risen from, he hardly remembered which figure it was 50 years ago, but since the year 1860 it had risen from £88,000,000 to £130,000,000. Therefore the zonclusion was drawn, notwithstanding all these efforts, the evil was increasing. He said "Thank you for that proof. One great difficulty is this : to convince men of the existence of an evil of sufficient magnitude to rouse them up to make an effort. (Applause). You as an antagonist have strengthened our hands, and I thank you for it." Ho was net going to speak in a discouraging tone, for to tell the truth his intention was quite the reverse, and that for this reason: In the month of August last or the beginning of the present month, the jubilee of this great temperance movement was kept in London, and in the course of the month preceding that there had bsen two great festivals— one of the Church of England Temperance Society, and the other of the League of the Cross, and then finally one gathering of all the temperance societies at the. Crystal Palace. These three great festivals had no existence and couhl have had no existence 50 years ago—(applause)—for the movement which they represented had no existence it- self. (Hear, hear.) There were two men still among them, one in Preston, Mr. Livesey—(applanse) in his 89th year, and one in Manchester, Mr. King, who is in his 87th year, whom be thought they might congratulate. They were two of the first Seven Men of Preston, of whom they had heard a great deal lately. (Applause.) Those seven courageous men, at a time when it was a reproach and a rebuke to be a total abstainer, came forward to bear that reproach and that rebuke, and they set an example to others. There was encouragemext for everyone of them, and he hoped before he sat down to follow that example, and he trusted some more would take the pledge. While seven men began the work, who could count, or who could imagine the number of total abstainers throughout the United Kingdom to-day? (Applause.) They had seen iudeeed the harvest spring from very small sowing of the seed. After them came the work of Father Mathew. (Cheers.) What he did in Ireland, in England, in Scotland, and in America all know. After Father Mathew came the United Kingdom Alliance. What that United Kingdom Alliance had done, was doing, and would do nobody knew better than the hon. chairman of , that meeting. (Cheers.) When that work began 50 years , ago the people bad not been roused out if their sleep, and it was the drowsy sleep of intoxication. They were now all alive and the temperance movement sprang from the people. Let it never for one moment be imagined that it was individual men who were moving the mass of the people to-day. They were leading them he admitted, but if the mass of the people were not rising up to an aspiration of their own, there would be no army for those leaders to guide. (Cheers.) Why had the people risen up? They bad become conscious of their own miseries, dangers, and degradations, and they were crying out to be delivered, and to have the power given to them to deliver themselves from a domination of which he would presently speak. Next, there had been a great public opinion created. (Hear, 11:ae) He recollected the day per- fectly well, it was not more than 15 years ago, when any man who had the courage to speak on the subject of the intoxi.- , cation of this country was assailed by every newspaper that he could remember, with one exception—for he believed it i then existed—and that leis the Alliance News. (Hear, hear.) The whole public opinion of this country was poin:cd down , upon the efforts of those who were endeavouring to prove to the country that drunkenness was increasing every year. They denied it in the most absolute way. The chairman's was only a hopeful estimate of what had been done by the , counter movement, which these newspapers were checking. The chairman also said that they had at lost converted the doctors. They had died hard. (Laughter.) The doctors were the most dangerous of their opponents, far worse than the publicans, for the publicans nobody believed, but the doctors everybody believed. (Laughter.) All the valetudinarians, all the I patients who did not like physic but did like champagne, were entirely convinced the physicians were right in saying that no man could live without a stimulant, that it was part of necessary food, and that it was the most powerful medi- cine to keep them in health and strength. He was happy to say that had gone, that one more superstition was swept away; and the physicians and surgeons, the highest authorities both in medical and surgical practice, were at that moment in the openest way declaring not only that intoxicating drinks were unnecessary as ordinary food, but even the practice of medicine could dispense with them. In some cases they might be used, as he often said, just as, when they pulled a man out of the Serpentine at London, and carried him into the Humane Society's house, they put hot bricks to the soles of his feet. But he did not imagine that any men would say the appli- cation of hot bricks to a man's feet ought to be an ordi- nary practice in a man's life. Further than this, he was going to say we had all over the country the teachers of religion and the pastors, and these who filled the highest offices men could hold, also going forward with great deter- mination—(bear, hear) '--and he might say that upon them depended the future guidance of this work. If they would etind firm and go forward the people would follow them. (Applause) There were many more very hopeful signs, upon which he need not dwell ; but he wished to ray a few words upon some of their 'Lingers and some of their hindrances. Their dangers at this moment were, lie thought, chiefly social dangers; he meant the dangers of private life. There was a great dead resistance by those whom they could not rouse to listen to them, and it was like an earthwork, which was of all fortifi- catioes the strongest, for this reason, they might knock a stone wall to pieces but the heaviest artillery buried itself in an earthwork. He believed in society there were earth- works thrown up all around against which everything they could say seemed to have very little effect. Habit, custom, liking, self-indulgence levity, indifference, ignorance, and unconsciousness seemed to him to pervade the great mass of the people who had not yet been roused to look into the m matter ; for let the never deceive themselves by thinking that they, temperance reformers as they called them—which was a very high and dignified title—had as yet penetrated all the strata of society. They had not done that yet ; there was an enormous resistance et interest everywhere. He said just now there were 130 millions of money every year engaged in the production, sale, and distribution of intoxiciting drink; and he meant to say that those who were interested in maintaining and extending this traffic were very numerous, widespread, scattered all over the country, and had centres of influence everywhere; so that i ihe might say , the power of that great capital spread like a net over the face of the whole land. The chairman , said that the revenue showed signs of an improvement. It was quite true in the last three years instead of 33 millions being raised by taxes on intoxicating drink the amount had fallen to 29 millions. He had bad to tell his friends not to imagine that that reduction was caused by thoee who drank water. Bedtimes, depression in trade, depression in agri- cultural employment, diminution of wages, and a consequent diminution of the amount of money to tee spent in intoxi- cating think had marked the last three years. He was afraid, therefore, he must believe that the amount of reduction in revenue brought about by the temperance sec'eties was a small amount. He said this not to discourage them, but do not let them deceive themselves, for that would be worse. , Mr. Lyon Playfair, who went as a commissioner to all the manufacturing districts some years ago, drew up a table by which he proved that in those districts where wages were high drunkenness increased, and where wages were low drunkenness diminished. Therefore he was hound to be- lieve what he said was strictly true, that though some effect had been produced, it was not much more than a dint upon the surface. They had not yet broken from this enormous evil. ( Ipplause.) He was sorry Lancashire had not a good reputation in the matter of intoxicating drink, and he had that from Lancashire men. He was told , that the amount which . had been expended in , 'Lancashire on intoxicating drink in one year 1 dmoigmhotrbeetbseatadoqwuonteathlis authority, ifmner.owneivli.iamHeHwoyonibl,dwnhoot I be believed was a Lancashire man,—(hear, hear) and millions o 1 whese accuracy in calculation could be depended upon. That gentleman said this was a great misapplication of jcapital; it was a very bad investment of that large sum of I money. If they were to spend 18 millions of money in i digging wells and filling them up again everybody would say that was a great waste. But we spent 18 millions of ' money in the production and sale of intoxicating drink, which, when consumed, was gone. If that 18 millions of money were spent—six millions in tilling the ground and obtaining corn and bread; six millions in weaving cloth, and six millions in building houses there would not be a hungry i I mouth, there would not be a bare back, and there would not I be a workingman and his family without a good roof over I their heads. (Cheers.) Moreover, in thus applying 18 I millions of money, besides the profitable labour they ob- tained in the form of produce, they were employing every 'unemployed hand in the land; and there would not be such I a thing as an unemployed workingman. He said this be- cause he confessed one argument of the chairman alarmed Ihim for the moment, when be said they would have to bear ,an increased income tax, and perhaps should have 'to bear the imposition Apf some other tax; but his answer was that their income would be greater. There would be more money in the land and more prosperity, and they would be able to endure greater taxition without any sensible burden. Well, the , first great obstruction was this great capital. The next he 1 WM afraid was in what he might call the social habits, cus- toms, tastes, and indulgences wleich spread themselves very widely and very stealthily through all classes. He never I would believe that intemperance was a characteristic of the I workingmen, but it spread all through society from the highest to the lowest. There was another danger which resisted them, and that was levity. There was no subject that had provoked a joke oftener than the subject of drunkenness. There was something grotesque, he admitted, in the actions and articulation of a drunken man. Eat whit was there lauehable in the sight of a man, :created in the likeness and image of God, when he had turned that glorious and bright image into the likeness and image of a beast? And if that be ti ue of man, how much more was it true of a woman, who by creation was delicate, of tende: fibre and organisation, of affectiorsee generous, and noble nature, different altogether from the strength and th solidity of man? When they saw a character of that kin, i

with its reinement and its beauty disfigured, degraded by drink, was there anything to laugh at? And yet there were some who made jokes of it. Now he would like lo put the question to any such man In this way: He saw a drunken woman and laughed. If it had been his or le mother would he have laughed ? He saw a young woman drunk; would he have laughed if it had been his sister? 'Would he have laughed if it had been his wife? They should remember that there were husbands, fathers, and brothers at home whose hearts were broken by that that they joked at. He had said he 'believed a great many people were not at this moment roused up to be iri earnest, simply because they did not know eneuela of the subject, but he took the responsibility to inform theee they could not go on shutting their eyes, closeag their ear, laldnraefusing to read without becoming culpable. They were to enquire. They read in the Holy Gospel of the rich man who fared sumptuously every day, and there lay at his threshold a beggar full of sore's. Theyrememb-ted the end of it. But they did not read that that rich man ever refused to give bread to the beggar at that door, or that the beggar asked him; but he lived on in prosperity and men n that self-indulgence all his life unconscious of the misery was round about him. S) he believed there were did not know the extent of this evil; but they were whbound to enquire, and the day in which they came to the knowledea which temperance people already possessed he was confident , they would stand side by side with them. (Cheers.) As he said at the beginning they had made great gains. There was a time when an attempt to obtain legislation on this subject teas refused in the most peremp- tory manner. They were told that intemperance was to be corrected, not by Acts of Parliament, not by legislation, but by religion, by education, by refinement, and he knew not what. Now, nob ady knew better than the chairman what part the Legislature had had in creating this evil-(hear, bear) —and the whole system of licensing laws. The fact was the Government was a sleeping partner in the drink traffic. The 33 millions of money that had been received by them he held to be the share of the sleeping partner. The Legisla- ture, therefore, must undo what they had done. (Cheers.) He need use no other argument. Tney had done it by giving legalised facility all over the land to multiply without limit the places of distribution in which intoxicat- ing drink was sold. (Hear, hear.) They must put a stop or a check upon themselves. How could that be done? Don't tell him by magistrates! For 300 years, ever since Edward VI., the magistrates had been endeavouring by licensing laws to limit this evil. The licensing, laws were introduced as a limit and a check upon the evil. Three hundred years' experience has proved how far this power of the magistrates to grant licenses bad had the effect of check or limit. Don't let them be told that the police could deal with it! His answer was they had no right to put the police in the country in the position of having to cure the evil which they of the Legislature had created. (Cheers.) The Goverment should undo the evil they had done. Don't burden the police with that which he would call an intollerable and an impassible work. Well, how could it be does? He knew of only one wav,which was perfectly constitutional, in perfect harmony with all the spirit of our laws, which was also just in the highest degree, and still was alone adequate to cure the evil. He meant to give to the people themselves in every locality— city, borough, town, and village—in England the power of - saying whether or not they desired public-houses in the midst of them. (Cheers.) Trial by jury was the essence of our English law, and what did it mean? That a man had to be tried by his peers, by men like himself in interests and circumstances, who were best able to judge of the truth of the facts. He asked then, who were they that could judge whether or not public-houses were desired by a population better than the population themselves? (Cheers.) Who could more justly have that power than those who suffered most from public•houses, those who had to pay for the evils that sprang front them, these whose homes were wrecked, whose happiness was destroyed, by public-heuses put down in the midst of their own residences ? The poor workingman had no remedy whatever. The rich man would clear his ovsn estate of any public-houses which fell then in the midst of the poor man. He said then give the poor man by law that which the rich man bad by right of property—the power of protecting himself. (Cheers.) Let the magistrates have the power of licensine, but let the people of every locality have the power to say "we don't want it, and therefore, no ; we will have no public-house in the midst of us." (Cheers.) He con- gratulated the chairman upon the fact that Sir Wilfrid Lawson, who was thrown out of his seat at Carlisle over the Permissive Bill, and then by a reaction of honest English- men was put back again—(cheers)—who had laboured like a fearless and honest champion in this great cause, had at last through the work of the United Kingdom Alliance—for to that alone he could ascribe it—obtained the support of some 240 members of the House of Commons, and had twice over carried the Local Option Resolution—once by some 26 votes, and another time by some 40 or 42 votes. He could not mention this without expressing his great regret to know that Mr. Hugh Mason, who seconded that motion on the first occasion, lay dangerously ill. (Hear, hear.) Might his life be prolonged to continue the good work. (Cheers.) He hoped when this question Came again before the House of Commons every man who was elected at the last general election on the understanding—he might say the promise— that he would vote for the Local Option Resolution would be found in his place. (Cheers.) Legislation was out of the reach of those present, but there was something within the reach of their arms, which mid be done by an act of their own will, and they could each one contribute to this great movement personally by one of two things: either by living up to the line of strict temperance by measure and rule, or by doing at the League of the Cross did. (Cheers.) To all those who lived up to the strict rule of temperance he wished 'God ' speed," perseverance, and strength to resist. So long as the sweetness of the taste was on their lips there would be a dreadful temptation which might catch them unawares. The safer course, be would not say absolutely the better, and yet perhaps he might, was that which_the League of the Cross had taken. (Cheers.) He protested against the notion that the League of the Cates as a to neerance movement confined itself to the saving of drunkards. He rejected abselutely the notion that bad gone out all over England that they were only endeavouring to give the pledge to those who needed it. That would be a very low view indeed. He be- lieved that it was the aspiratioa all over England, in Scot- land, and Ireland for Sunday Closing Acts. Scotland, Ireland, and Wales had got them; he hoped he Might say Cornwall, and should be able to say Yorkshire; and when England was set on fire in two or three places he believed the conflagration would be universal. (Cheers.) He looked upon this great temperance movement as a rising t,ip the people to clean away the foul stain emit the name of our courety. (Cheers.). Tee, Chinese had the strictest and severest laws again"..:. Intoxication and against the opium which we :tweed upon them. The poor Hindoos had petitioned our Government to withdraw intoxicating drink kud not to tax it, because as long as they taxed it they became interested in its sale. We, Christians, were the only people who had this burning shame upon our brow. The ielabornmedan world was bound by its law not to drink intoxicating drink. They might break that law, and many did. Notwithstanding, the Mahommedan world, the Hindoo world, the Chinese world had not upon them, as peoples, the burning shame that was branded upon the brow of the Christian nations of the world. (Cheers.) He Was ashamed to say that among the Christian nations of the world, he believed there was not one that was more deeply branded than we were ourselves—(hear, hear)—and there- fore he thought this temperance movement was an aspira- tion and a rising up of the whole people to wipe away this stain. Was it not a wonderful thing that such a people as we should be under the domination of so low and so base a habit? What was intoxicating drink? A drug, a poison- ous drug, which we manufactured bf brewing and distilling, and then we fell down and worshipped it. We made it an idol, and it was the worst kind of idol, for the idols of wood and stone could not enter into the bran or heart, but intoxicating drink entered into the whole man ' and embruted and destroyed him. And tbis we did—a wise, understanding, and great people, having all manner of science and the greatest prosperity of any people in the I civilised world. In conclusion his Eminence urged them to take up this light self-denial, and remarked that if their example shculd save one soul, surely that would be a suf- ficient reward. (Loud cheers.) The Rev. A. B. Pozzr proposed a vote of thanks to his Eminence for the great honour and service he had done them that evening, and in doing se alluded to the readiness with which the Cardinal accepted their invitation. Councillor Brueeneserr seconded the proposition, and re- marked that all must acknowledge there was nothing that weighed so heavily upon the prosperity and welfare, mate- rial and spiritual, and upon the happiness of this country, as the vice of intemperance. All honour to those who did their best to lift this burden from the peeple of England— (cheers) ; and he could not but believe that the weighty opinions and the persuasive eloquence of Cardinal Manning would have a very great effect upon Warrington from that night for h. (Cheers.) They bad all beenvery much im- pressed by what they had heard from him that night, and he had never heard the arguments in favour of Local Option so clearly and so conclusively put before an audience as they bad been that night. /(Cheers.) The proposition WAS carried with enthusiasm, and his EhIINENCE briefly replied.

The Rev. T. B. FIitENT proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and expressed his belief that Mr. McMinnies had attended with the honest conviction that he was doing good to the people of Warrington. (Cheers.) Councillor CROSFIELD, in seconding, said he had kn )wn Mr. McMinnies intimately for the past quarter of a centary and he did net know any man who bad as tender a heart, or who was more desirous to do good to his fellow men. He knew the motive that had made him take the chair that night. It was to do somethingif he could to benefit his fellow- townsmen. (Cheers.) He trusted the chairman would long be spared, and that they might have him member for War- rington for many years to coma. He thanked his Roman Catholic friends for asking him to come upon the platform that night, and considered it a great privilege and great honour to listen to his Eminence Cardinal Manning. (Cheers. ) lie had heard a good many men speak on the subject of temperance, but he must say he had never heard a speech so convincing, so sincere, so touching as the speech that he had heard that night. (Cheers.) He could assure Cardinal Manning that he knew the people of Watrington well enu to say they never could forget the acords which he uttered that night. (Cheers.) As he had said he sideredit a great privilege to be preset t, and he hope cpn- might have the pleasure of listening to Cars)inal ti"Y again at an early date. (Cheers). atanzing The rroposition was carried with cheers, and The CILIRIIAN having acknowledged the the meeting terminated. tomplinunt,

NATURAL CURIOSITIES. 1 Sir,—Your Newton correspondent (whom for the future I shall take the liberty of calling " Newtonian"), in his corn- munication of the 9th inst., says he hopes I will keep the subject of hares and rabbits before the public, in and out of season. I think I have said about all I have to say on the subject of bares, and should have concluded sooner had he not unnecessarily dragged bees, ants, phenomenal cows and greyhounds, rabbits, conies, dm., across the course or scent. In his last communication he also expresses a hope that some extracts he gives from a, Bishop Wilkins and Matzner will satisfy my curiosity, and that of others about • the identity of the cony in a scriptural sense. I will leave " others "to speak for themselves, and answer for myself. "Newtonian" says that "the cony may mean either the cuniculus or the Hyrax Syriacus,"—that is, in plain Englisis, he asserts that it may be two distinct animals at one and the same time! He then quotes from the authority who in a previous communication it is asserted has put it on record that the cony had a hutch all to itself in Noah's ark, as follows :—" These [beasts] may be distinguished into the bigger-kind; whether such as are covered with hair; living either above ground; being, of all others, the most fearful, hare leveret, underground; either that with long ears and a short tail, or that with short ears and long tail, being said to sleep all the winter, conny, rabbet, mar- motto, Mus. Alpinus." "Newtonian" then jumps to the conclusion that the "learned bishop," when speaking of the conny in a scriptural sense, meant the rabbit. "Newtonian" may have the gift of second sight, or he may possess the peculiar faculty a Bengalee would describe as that of "being able to look into another person's stomach." —(said person having died nearly two hundred years ago)— and so be able to satisfy himself that the bishop is right about Noah and the rabbit. But seeing that the rabbit is not a "Bible animal," and that it is not enumerated among the animals of Palestine, I decline to take such statement upon trust, the more especially as the bishop, in the extract given above, and relied on by my woald-be commentator, actually describes the cony, rabbit, and marmot as having "short ears and long tails!" lam afraid "Newtonian" has quoted Scripture as rashly in this instance as in the case of the bees and ants. The H. Syriacus is the cony of Scripture, and the substitution of " rabbit " for " shaphan " is simply another corruption. It has been observed that an old male hyrax is set as sentry near the holes and crevices in the rocks where he and his associates live, when the 'rest of the

, group are out feeding, and that he warns the wanderers of approaching danger by a whistle-like cry; and we may assume that this fact was known to the writer of the passage in Scripture in which this animal is pronounced as "ex- ceeding wise." See "Bible animals," D. 312; "Warren's letters," p. 12; and " Haydn's Bible Dictionary," p. 134. One is almost tempted to ask whether "Newtonian " has not made a mistake, and instead of quoting from the well- known Bishop Wilkins, borrowed from that pawkie Peter Wilkins, who, getting shipwrecked on an out-of-the-way island, married and consorted with the glums and gawreys, whose wings when folded served for dress, and when ex-- pacded were used for flight. Or 113 s the worthy man been spending his holiday in the somnolent region where goats are sent to get their beards combed and printers' devils their nails pared? Of course, due allowance must be made for "Nowtenian's " peculiar " swallow," seeing that he told tts in your issue of August 12th that "he enjoyed an emetic, if not too strong!" One could better believe the assertion of the existence of a winged female than of a abort-eared and long-tailed rabbit. Women (bless them all, widows included!) can with little trouble turn themselves into veritable angels of light—or otherwise; but I do not think rabbits, conies, or marmots can at will lengthen their tails, to say nothing of the first-named rodent being able, in addition, to shorten its ears. "Newtonian" next proceeds to attempt to administer a rebuke. He says:—"What possible good can it do him [meaning me] to ferret out who or what we are? When once we adopt the French fashion 'of signing our articles he will know all about us, perhaps. Meanwhile it is amusing to find a well-read writer so much at fault in a sporting sense, on account of a simple enallage." Fie, Mr. Corres- pondent! Do you mean to talk tr6risois against the editor? He, properly, decides whether the real name (given in con- fidence and as earnest of good faith) or the nom de plums of writers shall be used. As to French fashions, ink-splashing above one's real name often leads to blood-letting on the other side of the channel. And.a bipedal colour metamor- ..

phose hi this connection would be as startling as a quadru- pedal one of ears and tails. lam not aware of having done anything of the kind as that here imputed to me; and I shall leave readers of the Examiner to judge whether I have been at fault in a sporting or any other sense. I prefer the " snaviter in modo "to the "fortiter in re." The conditions between "Newtonian" and myself are as equal in ink-slinging ae in the snorting of a sprig of myrtle, so long as readers are interested or amused, and not offended. And I have no doubt that if either or both of us took to the wearing of skirts to save trowsar-mending, the pattern of tartan we should don would be of a green colour, checked with black, purple, yellow, and white. "Newtonian" concludes by setting me a puzzle, in the course of which he tells me his family arms are a pitchfork, and the motto "Over, fork over." Their origin was, to use his own words, as follows: "The original owner of the name took a shake fork and scattered hay over Malcolm Canmore when escaping from Macbeth." The only guess I can make in the matter is this,—That whereas the ancestor exhibited a ready and praiseworthy resource in using a hay- fork and hay to corer up and hide a person flying from his enemies, so, by one of those curious and unique phases of physical development there has been transmitted to the descendant a faculty of using pen and ink in such a way as to set down contradictory terms and veil to ordinary persons the meaning the latter would seek to convey upon certain subjects with which he deals earnestly, and with the best and kindest intention. As my critic seems proud of unearth- ing living curiosities, if he should visit London, I will have pleasure in introducing him to an establishment (and not a very large one) where there are sixteen widowers. But he must come quick, or they may have all changed their con- dition. Jam glad to hear that the "Belgian bare" has been introduced into Newton; and, if any of your young readers wish to know all about this splendid rabbit (for it is a veritable rabbit, and not a leporide), they cannot do better than consult Mr. Gill's capital manual for breeders and ex- hibitors, "The Book of the Rabbit." Thanking you again in anticipation for the space afforded me, and trusting that none of my remarks will be taken amiss, or looked at in the wrong light, I remain, yours truly, 243, Beresford-street, Newington, London, S.E.

WORK OF THE CHRISTIAN ARMY MISSION IN WARRINGTON. A tea party in connection with this mission took place in a large room behind the chapel in Orford-lane on Monday r evening. The tables, which had all been supplied out of Major Ferris's private resources, were amply supplied with creature comforts, and the room, which had been decorated for the occasion, presented a tasteful and at the same time cheerful appearance. No less a number than 350 children and 130 adults sat down to tea. The work of the mission, it may be stated, was commenced in June last, and was otta.blished by the Rev. M. Baxter, a clergyman of the Church of England, for the purpose of carrying the gospel among those of *he poorer -class who have not suitable • clothing to appear in church, and consequently never go to a plaee of worship. The mission was also established for the purpose of attending the sick and dying at their miser tble homes. Day schools are also op9ned, and here the poor children of tlie locality are collected and taught. Teas are provided at intervals to the 'poor people ; and Sunday schools and children's services form also a prominent part of the scheme of the rfission. The sympathy of the generous public is earnestly s kited in the form of donations or subscriptions, to carry A' this most requisite and desirable undertaking. Sine, work of the mission took its root in Warrington Major re is has worked assiduously and untiringly, and services lave been held each day in various parts of the town. The subscriptions which have been handed in to support the mission have long since been exhausted, and the whole of the expenses—and they are very great—are now depending altogether upon the Major. The good done by this humble charity is very great indeed. .14-fter the tables bad been cleared on Monday evening a miscellaneous entertainment was teone through, over which Mr. lintchinsen pcemided. A'eout 700 parents and children attended. Mr. Edward Bolton gave a recitation entitled "A soldier out of uniform." Miss Jones sang "When this cruel war is over" in a very praiseworthy manner, and was loudly applauded. Mrs. Waterford gave the hymn "Wash me ad I shall be whiter than snow," the children joining in the chorus. Mr. Mills delivered a short lecture, after

which Mr. London addressed the audienoe on the war in Egypt, describing the ancient country and its antiquities.— Major Frneas, in the course of an address, said that they hoped in about a fortnight to have another similar meeting to the one that evening. The object of the nfssion was for nothing but the poor—the neglected poor; to give bread to the hungry and clothing to the neglected. The bulk of the work of the mission and the expenses attending it was entirely upon himself, and on his private income. Some kind friends of the town had pitied his bleak labours and had sent him donations; but they were inadequate to meet the demands upon him. He had been obliged to cease giving clothing to poor women and children at the close of his services because he had no funds to go on with. Many families he had visited were in a destitute condition. On more than one occasion he had to send to the market to buy garments to clothe the indigent before he could be admitted to the bed- side of persons who were dying on some straw. Those cases of destitution were not known but to those who visited them. The other day he found a man, his wife and four children who had not had a morsel of bread within their lips for three days, and when they had become so destitute they at hat sent for him. When he got there he found that they had sold all their clothing and all their furniture, and the children were literally sinking from starvation. He sent for a doctor, who, after examining them, said they were simply sinking for the want of food, and be immediately sent for bread with which to feed them. Both the man and his wife assured him that they had not had a meal for 3?-5. days before. He could show them many a family like that. Might he ask them to try and spread the mission amongst themselves, and do their utmost to make it known to the public. If the rich men of the town would send him sub- scriptions he would see that everything he spent was recorded on a balance sheet, but inasmuch as the money he ' was now spending was his own, it would not be necessary to present a balance sheet.—Other songssand recitationswere given during the evening, and a vote of thanks to the chair- man brought the meeting to a close.

The 18th annual show of the Farnworth Agricultural Society was held at the Show Field, Farnworth, on Thurs- day. Acting on a general feeling which prevailed last year, the committee decided to hold the slow this year on one day only, thus returning to the original custom of the society. It is pleasing to note that the change has had, on the whole,a rather beneficial effect, the subscriptions show- ing a slight increase on those received in 1881. During the year the society has been placed under new management, which appears to have worked well. Mr. Robert Whalley, of -Bald, the originator of the show, who laboured in its be- half in the days when it had not attained a position in the county, has, we regret to say, been very much afflicted with illness during the past year, in consequence of which he has been compelled to retire from the chairmanship of the committee of management. The position is now filled by Mr. William Longton, of Eccleston Grange. A change, too, has been made in the secretaryship. Mr. John Hough, of Widnes, having vacated the post, it has been filled by Mr. R. Whiteside, of Victoria-road, Widnes. Considering the difficulties he must have had to contend with in arranging the vast amount of detail connected with the shew, he has performed the duties in a manner which reflects considerable credit upon him. The committee of management are to be congratulated upon their success in securing for the pre- sidency of the society a man so deeply interested in agricul- tural pursuits, and so popular among the farming classes, as Colonel Ireland Blackburn, M.P. At 10 o'clock, the time for the opening of the show, Farnwerth presented a scene of unusual bustle and anima- tion. Flags fluttered in the breeze on various points, and "Aunt Salleys," gingerbread stalls, and other paraphernalia occupied positions in the road. On the field during the , morning the spectators were far from numerous, explained to a great extent by the fact that the sky was dull, the wind cold, and the general atmospheric condition pointing to a storm. As the day wore on, however, the sky assumed a brighter hue, and about two o'clock people poured into the show field in crowds. The exhibits were arranged on the field in the manner usually adopted, and were easy of access to the spectators. Inducements were offered to in- tending exhibitors in the shape of 14 silver cups and £6OO in prizes; and the entries in all classes were about equal to those of last year. The following table shows the entries for four years:- 1879. 1830. 1881. 1882. Cattle Horses and donkeys ll3 ... 157 ... 153 ... 133 Pigs Butter Roots Potatoes Seed, corn, &c. Poultry Pigeons Dogs 274 267 ... 291 ... 282 Implements Extra stock

Taken as a whole, the exhibits were scarcely equal to last year in point of numbers, but the quality was very good. The unsettled weather of the past few months, and the cold ness of the season, must have deterred many farmers from exhibiting their stock, but the show of horned cattle was nevertheless a very goood one. A number of the animals were in splendid condition, Mr. Robert Whalley showing some exceptionally fine cattle, and lie was successful in winning about eleven prizes. Amongst the horses shown were some animals of sterling merit, the draught horses, although perhaps not above the average in appearance, had a "lot of work in them." In the jumping classes some fine animals competed, and the exhibition, which took place at two o'clock, was most attractive. The grand stand was well filled, and the ring was hemmed round by spectators. The " turnouts " were scarcely less pleasing, and the com- petition in the various classes was very keen. Pigs were chiefly ntoiceable for the number of local exhibits, which carried away the majority of the prizes. They were a very good show. The show of vegetables and grain was an ex- cellent one, and quite equal to that of previous years. The , quality was extremely good. In the poultry classes the buff cochins were a splendid show, as may also be remarked of the light brahma. Indeed, the quality of the birds excelled those exhibited last year, but the exhibits were not so numerous. The ducks and geese were, as usual, an uncommonly good show. Mr. Thomas Wakefield, of Golborne, exhibited some fine ducks, and he carried off the silver medal, which he has been successful in doing for a great number of years. The pigeons exhibited also included some splendid birds, and the show was a very good one. The entries, howevzr, were considerably below those of last year. Dog fanciers had a treat prepared for them. In ro show in the district could the animals exhibited have been beaten. Each class contained some really fine specimens of the canine race, but the bull dogs carried off the palm, and it was admitted that better animals could not possibly have been shown. Among the miscellaneous exhibits we may mention the picturesque rustic summer- houses of the executors of Mr. Henry Inman, of Stretford, near Manchester, a firm celebrated for these productions. The judges were :—Horned cattle and pigs: Mr. R. B. Brownlow, Liverpool; Mr. J. Roberts, Saltney, near Chester ; and Mr. S. Drinkall, West Derby. Heavy horses : Mr. C. W. them his sorrow and regret at being unable to be present, in consequence of the time being so short before his services would be required in London. (Hear, hear.) It was abso- lutely necessary that be should have some relief from the exertions that he had undergone—from sunrise to sundown he might say, for members of Parliament had seen the sun rise many a time while at their labours. (Applause). The toast he had to propose was one that would certainly be received with the utmost pleasure at all times, but at the present time they were very much inclined to be over jubi- lant at the actions which had ben performed by " the army, navy, and volunteers," which was the next toast on his list. (Hear, hear). He felt he could not do sufficient justice to it, but he wished to say that every Englishman was most proud of the gallant acts of the navy and army in Egypt. He was not there that day to enter into particular facts and particular instances that had occurred, which would delight the hearts of all loyal subjects of Her Majesty. • (Applause.) He must, however, allude to that wonderful victorv—(hear, hear)—which was gained on the 13th inst., and which would rank amongst the most biilliant examples of • skilful planning on the part of -Sir Garnet Wolseley—(hear, hear) ; it would rank antengst the most diligent and able execution of instructions by officers, and victorious dash on the part of brave men, who fought for the konour of Old Edgland. (Applause.) The battle had been described, and might be described, as an advance under the cover of the night; 20 minutes burst in the open under fire ; their complete victory owing to the bravery and deter- mination of our excellent soldiers. (Applause.) He was not there to discuss for one moment the necessity or cause of the army being sent out—that had te be done hereafter it was no part of his business there—but the troops were now under orders to return. It must not, hewever, be con- sidered that all the difficulties of the situation were at an end. There was still to be established a stable government in Egypt. It could not be forgotten our Turkish negotia- tions had to be c,enpleted before England could secure to Egypt the same tranquility anal peace that existed before. The Volunteers, who had won for themselves the admire-

tion and regard of all classes of society, and who at this moment were ready to take their part in any difficulties that Old England might have to contend with, were also deserv- ing of the warmest praise. He had the honour of asking to respond to the toast Colonel William Assheton Cross (the brother of their distinguished member), who was the hono- rary colonel of—well, it was the Royal Lancashire Militia ; what it was now he could not tell. He (the chairman) knew his own name—(laughter)—but he had not learnt that. At the time of the Crimean war Colonel Cross and his men volunteered for foreign service and went to Dalitz, where they were ready at any moment to travel on to Crimea. The toast was drunk with great enthusiasm. Colonel CROSS responded, remarking that the Army,Navy, and Reserve Forces had been well represented in the Egyp- tian war, and had performed their work in a manner which must command the admiration of everyone.

The CHAIRMAN then proposed "Success to the Farnworth I Agricultural Show," and, in doing so, congratulated the ' Chairman (Mr. Longton) and the committee upon the gloriovs show they had managed to collect that day. He believed that the show that was in the yard that day would I bear comparison with any, if not all, that had been held there. At any rate it had given pleasure to those around him, and be heartily congratulated Mr. Longton—(hear, hear) and the Committee upon the exertions they had put forth, and for the trouble they had taken in their endeavour to forward the agricultural interests of the neighbourhood (hear, hear) for be was one of those who very much desired the Society to be carried on. He was aware that he held opinions contrary to many of his valued friends, and he thought it was very desirable that they should have an opportunity of meeting on occasions of this sort. Farmers, by these meetings were enabled to meet together and discuss matters of mutual interest, and by that means gain information which would help each of them to improve his method of farming. (Hear, hear.) He could only say that so far as he was concerned, he should, whilst he resided in the neighbourhood, do all in his power to assist the Farnworth Agricultural Society in order that the show might be held so long as the farmers of the neighbourhood wished it. (Hear, hear.) He was not going to lecture, or give information to farmers, as to the cultivation of their farms. In many instances those persons who offered their opinion on the working of laud had never had any practical experience in the matter. (Hear, hear.) Farmers knew full well how to manage their own affairs,—(hear, hear)—and by their industry and abili- ties, pluck and patience, had managed to overcome the diffi- culties and troubles of late years. (Hear, hear.) What they had gone through of late years with respect to the weather and otherwise was an example to us in private life, as well as public, to those engaged in industries and in com- merce, to persevere. What did farmers require? He would tell them what he thought they required. They should hold their farms on well understood tenancies agreed upon be- tween landlord and tenant,—(hear, hear, and applause)— and with the knowledge that all real unexhausted improve- merits should be duly considered on leaving their farms. Then with improved dwellings and farm buildings of tenants, awl improved dwellings for the labouring class,— (hear, hear)—with an institution for teaching agriculture in different localities, they might fairly expect an improved cultivation of the soil ; and with fine weather for their seed and harvest time farmers would be enabled to compete with foreign countries without failure or loss. He would refrain from troubling them with any further remarks, but with the heartiest wish for the welfare of the society he proposed the toast, to which he added the name of Mr: Longton. (Applause.) Mr. LANGTON, in responding, said from the feeling which he saw expressed in the face of each person present he thought they must join with the committee in wishing the society success. (Hear, hear.) He hoped their good wishes and feelings would be realised. (Hear, hear.) Up to a year or two ago the society had been attended with success, but the depression in agriculture and trade in general for the last two years had told upon its resources. The committee were not in a position at present to say that the society was in a flourishing condition, but it was doing good, and although short of funds they trusted by the aid of farmers and neigh- bours, and the landlords of the neighbourhood, to carry the society forward. It would and had proved of great benefit to the farmers. He must say he did not agree with some gentlemen in the country that small societies, like Farn- Worth, ought to be done away with. (Hear, 'hear) There' was a certain class of farmers who would attend a small show but were afraid to go to a large one; and by seeing their neighbours' stock they -were encouraged, if they had any- thing better, to become exhibitors, when if they were very successful they mustered up sufficient courage to compete in a large show. (Hear, hear.) Tenant farmers were a. class of mete who required more encouragement from the landlords and also from the manufacturers of the district. He con- sidered the tenant farmer a very brave man to face the hard times as he had done for the last few years. (Heat hear.) As a practical farmer himeelf, he believed that there was not oae farmer within 20 miles of where he was sitting, who even it he had had his farm free of rent for the last three or four years, could make ends meet. (Hear, hear.) He was not giving his opinion merely; for he knew from practical proof; but he hoped they might have more sunshine, the want of which was really the cause of the farmers' misfor- tunes. (Hear, hear.) He knew one practical farmer who had ten acres of corn ready for the scythe. It was standing between three and four feet high, and was in splendid con- dition; hut the storm and tempest came, beat ip down to a foot high, and knocked all the corn out of the ears. Natagr enough the man was disheartened, because the weather *as against him. Let them have fine weather and fair compe- tition, and the farmers of this country would hold their own. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Longton concluded by giving "Tire President." The CHAIRMAN suitably responded. The toast of. "The Press" having been given and responded to, the company broke up.

The usual meeting was held on Wednesday at the Work- house. Present—Mr. G. Blackhurst (chairman), the Rey. G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Greening, Cooper, Woo Hall, urn. MORE UNWASHED LINEN: LIYELT DISOUSSION.

The Barracks Committee's book contained the following entry: A letter from Major Lock to the Rev. S. Wilkinson asking for boys to join the band of hie regiment was read ; and Mr. Mines was instructed to cominanicate with Major Lock informing him that we have four buys suitable and wishing te.go. The superintendent reported that the soiled sheets were sent to the Workhouse on Tuesday, the sth inst., to be washed, but were returned on Friday, 18th inst., un- washed. The blankets still remained unwashed, although they were ordered to be washed about the end of June last. —At a -meeting held on the 19th September, the committee pressed that the l'aigate schools be at once -inspected by a Government inspector if necessary, as they are elisions to remove the children at an early date. Six boys were taken to the "Orford Depot," and pissed medical inspection for Major Loch's regiment, and await orders from the War Office. Mr. BROWN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, felt it necessary to call attention to the soiled linen again. He regretted that the committee were hound to do so. He re- minded the Board that winter was fast approaching, and that the cold nights would be upon them directly, but as things now stood they had no blankets to cover the children. The blankets were removed about the end of June, and they had still not had the time or the facilities for washing them in that large establishment. They did not wish to overwork the inmates, but they would like to haVe some clean blankets for the temporary schools. As to Major Lock's application, be said the committee hoped they would be able to place six of the boys permanently in the military band. (Hear, I hear.) This was the object for which the band was estab- lished about 20 years ago, but it was the first time they had been able to accomplish their object.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE seconded.—Major CARTWRIGHT said that with regard to the washing, the members of the Schools Committee were not aware of the position the Reuse Committee were in. If they took the trouble to inspect the House they would see at once the committee were incapable of doing the work, be- cause the machinery was out of ordet.—Mr. BROWN: It is a long time out of order.—Major CearrevutGeer remarked that it was difficnit sometimes to get an order from the Board for repairs to be executed. But such an order had been given, and the work was in hand; but it was impassible without the machinery was in order to wash the blankets.—Mr. LoreaserAw said it appeared they might go to the' Local Government Board and ask their opinion, but it amounted .to nothing. The House Committee and Mr. and Mrs. Mackey were determined to manage both the Board and the Schools Committee and everything connected with the con.

div.head: LUNCHEON.
div.p: THE LUNCHEON.

At one o'clock luncheon was served in a large tent on the ground, ard the guests, who were very numerous, were excAlently cateted for by Mr. A. C. Doe, refreshment con- tractor, Liverpool. Colonel Ireland Blackburne, the presi- dent, occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Rev. G. Bond, Colonel W. A. Cross, Colonel Wyatt, Messrs. W. B. Longton, Robert Whalley, Hale, Harding, W. A. Meadows, W. Longton, Dr. Mackie, J. Farrington, LicAson, Ockle- shaw, &c. Luncheon concluded, The CHAIRMAN proposed "The health of Her Majesty the Queen," and the toast was drunk with enthusiasm. The CHAIRMAN said the next toast deserved their especial attention. (Hear, hear.) Many in that room would remem- ber the delight with which the Prince and Princess of Wales was received in Liverpool some- twelve months ago, when they did honour to that famous city--(hear, hear,)—by opening the docks, &c. The courtesy which their Royal Highnesses exhibited to all classes of the community went to the hearts of everybody there :and therefore Lancashire men would be very glad to join with him (the chairman) in doing them honour. As to the rest of the Royal family, they were too distinguished to enable him to go fully into their desserts—to lay before them dis- tinctly their multifarious labours, but lie might say this—that we-had two Royal Dukes at present high in com- mand, where dangers existed. Lately we bad had in the county a Royal Duke who came at a moment's notice and performed his duties to the admiration of all learned men, and he; therefore, felt certain, they vcCmld j.)in with him in drinking the toast, "'('he Prince and Princess of Wales, and the rest of the Royal Family. (Applause.) The toast having been honoured, The CHAIRMAN gave "The bishop and clergy of the I diocese, and ministers of all denominations." He was happy to think, he remarked, that the ministers of all denomina- tions, and the clergymen of England, vied with each other in doing their duty towards the people among whom they laboured and lived. (Hear, hear.) The Bishop of this diocese was a gentleman who had his duties thoroughly at heart; who worked morning, noon, and night in behalf of his diocese,. The toast was duly honoured, and the

Rev. GEO. BOND, Vicar Farnworth, responded. As Iregardeti the Bishop, he need add no words of commendation to what had already been said by the chairman. The work of the clergy would speak for itself; but he might say that while they valued these tokens of their sympathy, they on the other hand heartily sympathised with those persons who were engaged in business and were doing active work, and wished them all God speed. As regarded agriculture, the clergy seemed to have an especial sympathy with it. Many of them,more or less,depended upon it—he was speaking of clergy in country districts—and every Englishman was more or less bound to show sympathy with it. It was the substratum or foundation of almost all our prosperity throughout the land. The country depended on the farmer. The wholesale shop depended on the chntry shop, and the manufacturer depended on the whole- sale dealer, so that after all the countryman was at the bottom of the whole matter, but he hoped he would not he at the bottom much longer, but rise in the world. (Applause.) He believed that in these days farmers were having better harvests than they had in former times, and he hoped their prospects would improve. They ought to do all they could to encourage such institutions as these, which, more or less' conduced to the improvement of the breed of cattle and the lessening of the manual labour, and were exceedingly useful in enabling farmers to adapt the scientific improvements of the age to the wants of the agriculturist. He took the opportunity of saying this: that the clergy were always ready to give every aid in matters of this kind, and to show their sympathy with any work that was going on around them. (Hear, hear.) He should be glad on every occasion to attend the show, and exhibit as he had done that day, not that he might obtain a prize, but that he might encourage other persons also to become exhibitors.

The CHAIRMAN said he learned that Father Finegan was present,—(hear, hear)—and he was sure those present would rejoice to hear a few observations from him. (Applause.) The Rev. Father FINEGAN expressed his obligation at hearing his name mentioned from the chair. The CHAIRMAN said before he proceeded further with the toast list he had to say one word as to the absence of his distinguished colleague, Sir Richard Assbeton Cross. (Cheers). He charged him (the chairman) to express to

He objected to Mr. Brown making wholesale charges against I members of the House Committee. If he stated that Such and such work was purposely put off to avoid the washing of the elothing from the Barracks it was totally untrue.— Mr. BROWN: That is my opinion.—Major CARTWRIGHT said that some time ago the Board passed a resolution that Stephen Moss should do the work, and he had it in hand, and had instructions to complete it as soon as possible. It was totally unfair to state that the members of the Com- mittee were determined to set the Board at defiance. If the Board wished to be satisfied they should have the persons before them, and let them answer the charges. They were not determined to oppose the Board. He hoped Mr. Brown would visit the House, and then he would be qualified to judge of the matter.—The CHAIRMAN could scarcely accept the explanation of Major Cartwright as to why the washing had not been done. WRIGHT: Quite true.] It was not a question of machinery at all, and there was no excuse, for Mrs. Mackey could have done the work if she had had the disposition. There was not the slightest doubt about it. He thought Mrs. Mackey would have allowed the matter to pass over, and that they would have heard ne more about it. But it appeared to him whatever resclution the Board passed, or whatever the Local Government Board said, they would do just as they liked. He did not think they should pass a resolution, but should simply instruct the clerk to acquaint the Local Government Board of the position the Board were in.—Mr. LONGSHAW: Hear, hear. He thought it would be wise for the Board to suspend the present chairman of the House Committee and appoint another, because he believed as long as Major Cartwright was inee, that position he would put a difficulty in the way of the washing being done. He was exceedingly sorry, but he would not be responsible if anything occurred. (Laughter.)—Mr. BROWN: You must not forget the motion was not seconded.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE : Oh, I will second it. SHIRE : I am in a remarkably good temper.- —Major CART- WRIGHT : Oh, you sit down like a lamb always! I wish he would not show that feeling. MISTRR'S REPORT.

The MASTER reportea mat tnere were 49d inmates in the House, as against 483 in the corresponding week of the previous year. The Master and Matron, on behalf of the sick inmates of the institution, are desirous of thanking the Rev. B. B. Prescott for a quantity of flowers and fruits he sent then, also Mr. Edward Bolton for a number of papers.

BUILDING commrrna. A meeting of the above committee was held on the 10th September, when a report from Mr. Timmins, with respect to the well, was read and adopted. The committee directed that the report be laid before the Guardians. The architects presented the balance sheet of account with Mr. Napier, showing the amount duo to him to b 3 £240. The committee recommended the adoption of the balance sheet, and that the sum of £240 be paid to Mr. Napier. That would still leave £27 Bs. in the hands of the Guardians. The tenders for the erection of laundry, washhouses, &c, were opened and considered. The following were the amounts tendered : -1-,Messrs. Collin and Son £1,750, Mr. George Napier £1,695, Mr. Wm. Porter £1,897, Mr. IL Beckett £2,293. It was resolved that the tenders of Messrs. Collin and Napier be referred to the Guardians, with the recommendation that one of them be accepted. Mr. Pierpoint presented the statement of his account with the Guardians showing the balance due to him to be £l5l 17s. The committee recommend pay- ment of the same.—Messrs. Collin subsequently sent in an amended tender for £l99s.—The minutes were adopted, and the tenders were referred back to the committee.

APPOINTMENT OF VACCINATION orricEß. For the post of vaccination officer, rendered vacant by the death of Mr. S. McLelland, there were 25 applications. These were subsequently reduced to seven, as follow :—B. Hobson, Penketh ; G. Hol.ford, Warrington ; P. Worthing- ton, Latchford ; W. Waley, Latchford ; W. T. Wilkinson, Latchford ; Peter Taylor, Warrington ; and Basil Shearer, Warrington. Votes were again taken, and the number re- duced to two : Messrs. Holford and Worthington; and eventually Mr. Holford obtained a majority of six votes, and received the appoint:neut.

THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD AND THE " 2,.TEMO " FUND.
The Assistant Clerk read the following letter from the Local Government Board :

Whitehall, S.W., 9th Setember, 1882.--Bir,-1 ant directed by the Local Government Board to forward to the Gua, duns of the Warrington Union the accompanying extract from a report made by Mr. J. It. S. Knott, Jate assistant auditor, respecting his audit of the accounts of the Warrington Union for the half-year ended at Michaelmas, 1881, together with an extraot from a declaration made by Mr. John Dun, treasurer of the Union, before Mr. Haslehtust, dist rict auditor, at his recent audit of the accounts of the Union for the half-year ended at Lady Day, 1882. Mr. Haslehurst has also forwarded a cony of the report made to the Guardians by you on the 22nd of June, 1882, and f the resolution of the Guardians thereon. lam to state that as the money at the bank appears to be the produce of the ratepayers' money which has been entrusted to thAr predecessors, the Board will be glad to be furnished with the observations of the Guardians on the subject generally, and especially as to whether they consider that there are any grounds on which they would be justified in applying such money to pur poses not entered in their accounts as Guardians. The extract was as follows :

A member of the Board, Major Cartwright, attended the audit and informed me that the Guardians had a separate f and called the "Nemo fund," and that payments whioh the Gum- dians ot the Poor cannot legally make were made out of this fund. I enquiced of him as to how the fund arose and he stated that about 13 or li yews ago on a threatened outbreak of cholera, the Guardians erected a building at a cost of from £7OO to £l,OOO, which was paid out of the funds of the Union The building was not required for the purpose fo. which it was erected, and on the ocgasion of a railway accident it was atied by the London and North-Western. Railway Company, and also afterwards by the Government, 13,th of whom had paid the Guardians for the use of it; and from the money so paid arose the "Nemo fund," He was chairman of the Board at the time
