div.p: FRIGHTFUL DEA.TII IN A WIDNES CITEMICAL WORKS.

---IMPORTINT INQUIRY. An accident, by which one man lost his life and another had a narrow escipe, occurred at tile chemical works of Messrs. Hutchinson, on Saturday. In connection with these works a process for the recovery of sulphur from alkali waste is carried on, and is known as the sulphur making department. On Saturday morning it was in charge of a man named Thomas Hughes, who it appears had engaged a man reamed Patrick Kiernan to help him. At noon Hughes went to the pay office to receive his wages, leaving Kiernan in charge of the decomPosers—the vessels in which the de- composition of the alkali waste is effected. He did not return for a period of 20 minutes, when he found the liquor . _overflowing the top of the vessel, and noticed that sulpha- , ratted hydrogen gas, which is very poisonous, was being produced in large quantities. With admirable promptitude he stopped the engine, checked the flow of the liquor, and seeing Kiernan lying on the ground ran to his aid. Stooping to raise Kiernan and convey him into the open air, Hughes felt himself being overcome by the strong fames, sheuted for help, and, staggering to the door, remarked that he was "done for," falling to the ground in an unconscious state. Aid quickly arrived, but too late to save Kiarnan's life. Hughes, who had not- been so long under the deadly influence of the gas, "came to himself" in the apace of an hoar and a half; an on Tuesday was suffi- ciently recovered from the effects of the fumes, as to be able to give evidence at the inquest which was held on the body of Kiernan, at the George Inn. Tie coroner was Mr. Driffield and the forem 01 of the jury was Mr. Pankhnrst. Mr. A. E. Smith, the manager of the works, watched the proceedings on behalf of the firm. The evidence is ap- pended.—James Kiernan, of 53, Cromwell-etreet, Widnes, said he was employed at the works of Mr. Bolter. The de- ceased was his brother, 22 years of age, and they lived to- gether. On Saturday he (witness) got his breakfast with the deceased, who was in his usual health. At neon he heard that his brother was I dead, and went to the works to verify_the statement. He saw his brother, who was still at the works. He wle dead but had no wounds apon him. His brother used to get a great deal of gas, but he (witness) did not understand the work and could not explain where it came from, or whether or not it was the result of some de- fect in the machinery.—Thomas Hughes, of 56, Cromwell- street, said he was employed in the sulphur department of Messrs. Hutchinson's works. The deceased worked under him. A man named Pat Murphy worked on the opposite " shift" to witness. On Saturday forenoon witness was decomposing the sulphur, and deceased was also at the same employment. At twelve o'clock at noon he (witness) left the deceased alone in the place in order that he might fetch his wages from the pay office. The deceased was then charging a " melter." At the end of 20 minutes be returned, and found one of the decomposers overflowing. He stopped the engine at once, and then the flaming liquor. Afterwards he saw the deceased lying up to one of the decomposers. He jumped off the decomposer and pulled the deceased two yards away from where he was lying, when he (witness) was " catched" with the gas himself, and he screamed for help. He told a man that went in the room that he was "done for," and fell the ground insensible. He could not tell whether the deceased was dead or alive at the time he was himself overcome with the fumes. He (witness)"came to himself" in about two hours, when he was in the public- house. He had worked in the sulphur department since February. He had, however, been employed at Messrs. Hutchinson's works previous to that time.—By the Coroner: The decomposers overflowed on some days, and not on others. Sometimes they commenced to overflow so suddenly that they could not stop the stream. When the decomposers were in that state, the gas cm-, off freely, and it was im- possible for them to work in the place. Neither he nor the other men wore any cloth over their month. He knew that the gas would kill him if he stayed in it too long. —The Coroner: Can you tell what the .deceased had been doing? I think he had gone to open the pipe at the bottom of the vessel, when he saw the overflow.—Had the deceased any tool in his hand ? Zio,mir.—By Mr. Smith: He (witness) could have stopped the acid and sulphur liquor running into the yeeeel had he been there.—Mr. Smith observed that the accident had occurred in consequence of the witness leaving the process at work instead of shutting off the acid and liquor before doing so.—The Coroner: Do you mean to bring a charge against this man for leaving his work ?—Mr. Smith: The man that was killed was not employed by us, but by Hughes.—The Coroner: But you killed him, never- theless. I don't kuow that you are more entitled to kill a man you don't pay than one you do pay. There is no dif- ference in the law.—Mr. Smith: I admit that.—The Coroner: Do I understand from you that this man (witeess) ought to have altered the taps before going for his pay?— Witness : I left the decomposers in working order, as I had done before.—Mr. Smith: From my impression The Coroner: Was he right or wrong in leaving the thing work- ing ?--Mr. Smith: It is possible for the decomposers to work right for a long time without a man being there.—The Coroner asked would not toe witness be then justified in leaving the vessels. He did so, and left there a man of indiscretion.—Mr. Smith (to witness) Could not you have shut off the acid and liqwor had you been there? Yes; if I had been there in time.—A juryman: You are not expected to allow the decomposer to overflow on any day ?—The Coroner: He says it does on some days.— The juryman : I don't think he needs to do so.—The Coroner: He says it is so. Us cannot prevent the vessels overflowing; he can stop them when theydo so —ln answer to a juryman, witness said he could regulate the flow of the sulphur liquor, hut the acid came in such a way that it could not be controlled.—Mr. Smith explained that if the man wished to stop the acid from flowing into the vessel he lifted up a plugs and allowed it to run into a sewer, whereas the sulphur liquor, which did the demage, could be con- trolled by taps. If there was an excess of acid in the vessel, no sulphuretted hydrogen gas would he fumed, and there would be no danger in working. When, however, the sulphur liquor was in excess of the acid, gas was produced. The deceased, instead of turning the tap, attempted to open a plug at the bottom of the vessel, and, as the gas was very heavy, he would probably be then overcome —John Hig- gins, of 9, Field-street, who said he was employed at Messrs. Hutchinson's te feed the ashmill, was next 101 examined. He deposed that the foreman, hearing that gas was escaping, told him to go and stop the tap.--The Coroner: Why didn't he go himself Witness said he did not know, but when he himself got to aog; the place, Hughes was crying out, saying "I am done for," gear and dropped down outside the door. He (witness) and several other men pulled deceased outside and placed him near a chimney.—When questioned with regard to the work- ing of the process, witness said he was ignorant of every- thing carried on in the sulphur room.—Mr. Smith interposed and said it was not a room, but an open shed. He hal four , medical men on the decomposers half-an-hour after the accident—The Coroner: Did you turn the gas on for them! • (Laughter.)—Mr Smith: No. They could not understand • how a man could lose his life in that way in an open shed. —The Coroner: They were net Widnes men, I think.—Mr. Smith : They were Widnes doctors.—The Coroner: But I mean they had not been horn here.— Patrick Murphy, 'iv- ., lug at 22, Cromwell-street, who was in charge of the- decomposers on the opposite "shift" to Hughes, was ex- amined as to how the process was worked. He said the decomposers could be left without an attendant for a long time and not overflow. Sometimes they overflowed and they could not stop the stream for two minutes.—The Coroner in- quired if there was any getage by which they could tell when a vessel was going to overflow.—Witness replied that they could tell if they looked into it.—Mr. Pankhurst : Is the overflowing a matter of daily occurrence? No. Some- times it might not overflow for matiy a month.—The Coroner: And then it occurs three or four times a day ? It might occur twice in an hour for that matter.—Mr. Pank- hurst inquired if this was through the negligence of those who had charge of the vessels,*ut the answer was inaudible.—A Juryman: Can you resist the influence of the gas for two minutes ? Yes; and witness added that a man who understood the matter would get out of the way of the gas.—Mr. Smith observed that the process had been worked in the same manner as now for over 15 years, and no fatal accident had before resulted from it.—The Coro- ner: Tam afraid that only brings us to the same conclusion that we should have come to—that we shall have to alter it. It is quite time we should, if it has been going on for 15 years. We shall have to make it safe for the future, or re make the men safe, rather.—Mr. Smith was then sworn, and stated that Hughes had been employed at the works for many years, and at the sulphur process for three or four months. The process was the recovery of sulphur from the alkali waste. If the process was worked rightly sulpha- retted hydrogen gas was not found. It was only when there was too much sulphur liquor in the vessel—that was, when the liquor and acid were not properly mixed, that the gas was generated. Over the top of the vessel was a flue to convey away any gas that might be formed, as they said, through the carelessness of the workmen. His explanation of the accident was that while Hughes was away from his work the vessel became quite full and stopped the outlet for the- gas. There was not the least doubt the deceased had been poisoned by the sulpburetted hydrogen gas.—The Coroner: The deceased has evidently wished to stop the mischief, and he has lost his life in an ignorant attempt to do so.— Mr. Smith farther explained that the process was a continuous one, and that on the day in question the liquor had been coming too fast. —TheCoroner: I want to know, and these gentlemen will want to know, how you are going to prevent this recurring ire the future.—Mr. Smith: How !—The Coroner: Yes. gem say you have not had the possibility so vividly before your eyes before.--Mr Smith: Ne, no.—the Coroner: Now you have, how are you going to meet it?—Mr. Smith said he would arrange an overflow about six inches below the top of the vessel, so :that the gas would always have an out- let through the flue. Replying to Mr. Pankhurst. Mr. Smith said the deceased was employed to put the precipi- tated sulpikur into vessels to be melted. He had nothing to do with the decomposition of the liquor.—The Coroner then summed up, remarking that the only wonder was that there had not been a fatal occurrence with this process during 15 years. It was satisfactory to learn that there was a definite way of meeting possibilities of the same character as the uresent one and that steps would be taken to carry that out. did not that the jury could blame Hughes in the anateer, or very much at all events. It was a creation be- tween `‘im and his masters. He (Mr. Driffield) did not hnew th,e Eleghes had been turned adrift. Perhaps he would Ire aeafieeranianwasto reemtupruloed.y in the future.—A verdict • of accidentai,th

div.head: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the members of the Widnes Choral Society was held in Simms Cross Board Schools on Monday evening. It was generally known that the question of the dissolution of the society would be decided, and there was a numerous comptny—which included many ladies—present. Mr. Eustece Carey occupied the chair, and called upon Mr. J. W. Davies, the hon. secretary, to read the fourth annual report, which was as follows :—"The number of members on the "books were—ladies 45, gentlemen 35, total, 80; of these seven were half members. These numbers show a falling off to the extent of 28, viz.: 16 ladies and 12 gentle- men ; and the committee regret, as in the case of the last report, to have to complain of the poor attendance at rehearsals. During the season the society gave three con- certs, viz.: a performance of "Judas Macabeate" November 17th; "The Messiah," December 22nd, 181; and Sterdale Bennett's "May Queen," and a miscellaneoue selection, April 13th, 1882. At the first concert a trio of professionals were engaged, viz., Madame Porter, Mr. J. J. Hodgson, and Mr. Cuzner. At the second Madame Porter was again engaged, and Mr. Eaton Batty kindly gave his services; and at the third Miss Emily Stuart, Birkenhead, Miss Janet Fierpoint, of Runcorn, and Mr. Ernest Batty kindly came without remuneration at the invitation of Mr. Argent, and undertook the solo parts. The committee feel that they are greatly indebted to those ladies and gentlemen who so generously gave their services as mentioned, and they ask the society to pass a vote of thanks to the Misses Stewart, Miss Janet Pierpoint, Mr. Eaton, and Mr. Ernest Batty, and also to those gentlemen of the orchestra who so kindly helped us. In conclusion the committee regret to state that they find themselves with a balance on the wrong side. At the same time they feel that much has been done during the season to improve the musical capacity of the members, and they think that the special thanks of the society are due to Mr. Argent for his energetic and successful labours."—The financial statement which was appended showed that the society commenced the year with a balance of £2 12s. 3d. The subscriptions amounted to £l2 is. 3d., the balance from s mires was Ifs. Ll., and the receipts from the three concerts given were £53 173. 7d.; making a total of £74 73. 2d. The expenditure amounted to £B9 14s. 5d., leaving a balance or the wrong side of £l5 7s. 3d. It seemed the first concert cost £23 Os.; the second £l5 103. 61., and the •third £l7 163. 5d.; total £56 15s. 11d.—The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the report. It was the first time in the society's history, he said, that it had been lin debt, and when that report was passed he I should ask the members to consult as to how it was to be met, and whether the society was to continue its operations.—Mr. SCHOFIELD seconded the motion, which was carried—The CHAIRMAN then said the society com- menced its labours with the very good intention of paying its own way, without asking the public for any contribu- tions, and that any money that might be made from time to time should be given to any charitable object in the neigh- bourhood in which they could all feel an interest. For the first two or three years, as they knew, the society had money to spare for these objects; but last year, owing, he sup- posed, partly to the novelty of the society having worn off, and the members getting either tired of it (there were fewer members this year than last); and also to the public, he supposed, being tired of the society's performances, they had not been successful; and they had got the debt of £l5, for which of course all the Members were equally liable, and must be paid. He should like to have the opinion of the meeting as to how the money was to be raised. He had heard it suggested that the members should each pay a double subscription, but in that case it was taken for granted that the society would again start operations. If the society did not start operations again, or postponed them for a year or two, it would not be very difficult for them to put their hands in their pockets and pay a small sum each, which would soon amount to the £l5 required. Did the members thiple they could face another session with this burden of debt upon them ?—The Rev. J. BOND, vicar of Farnwortb, suggested that a guarantee committee should be formed to be answerable for the debt, and for any deficiency that might occur in the future. This method had been found practicable in other cases, and he should be glad to become a member of the committee. In another year the society might have a reaction and become very successful. It was an institution which had done much good in cultivating a taste for music, and afforded a large amount of amusement to the inhabi- tants of Widnes, who were considerably more musically inclined than he had found in other parts of England. He really thought the society should be kept on. (Hear, hear, and applause.)—Mr. HurrrEß remarked that the meetings of the society had been of great benefit to many of them during the past year, and, he believed, had given many of them a great amount of pleasure; and, apart from all phil- anthropic notions, he thought they ought to keep on the society a little longer, even for the members' own pleasure. In his opinion it was not necessary at present to rely upon any outside aid. The society had lived for three years, and could live another three by their own exertions. He begged to move that the succeeding year members pay double sub- scription; and if at any time the funds of the society were sufficiently elastic, the subscriptions should be paid back in whole or in part. . Taking Mr. Davies' figures, that would pay off the debt and give the society a new start. The claims of the society had been advocated in so many quar- ters lately that he felt sure they would have no difficulty in getting a good audience next time.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that he was strongly its favour of postponing the operations of the society until he found that there was a general feeling among the public in favour of the society continuing, and he hoped the society would be willing to put its shoulder to the wheel. If it did there was no doubt it would soon he in a goo 4 position.—ln response to a call from the Chairman, those in faeour of the society continu- ing its operations held up their hands; and the feeling seemed to be unanimous for the adoption of that course.— Mr. CROSSLEY pointed nut that the subscription, when doubled, would amount to 103, which he considered too large a sum for many of the members to pay, and suggested that it would be better to have a voluntary subscription at the -first rehearsal.—Mr. SCOTT asked the reason for the falling off in receipts of the concerts. It would perhaps be advisable to adopt some other class of music to that which had been formerly given. There were some new members present that night which showed that the interest in the society was not dying out, but gaining ground, and , from conversation which he had held with various people he gathered that it was the general opinion that the society had done a good work, and he did not think it was desirable to wind up so early in its career, unless some member of th:, committee could state very good reasons for doing so. He should like to know a little more on the subject.—The Cetainetaet observed that it was a very important question as to whether the music which had been performed was of too " dry " a character, and whether it would not be well to have more secular music.—Mr. SCOTT said he had heard from various persons that the people of Widnes would be better pleased with secular music than the performance of two or three oratorios in a season.—The CHAIRMAN said I that was suite possible, and he pointed out several reasons I why the last oratorio had not succeeded in bringing together a larger audience. He suggested that instead of the sub- scription being doubled, it showld remain as at present, and each member purchase his or her music. There was a lot of old music in the library.—Mr. WIDEN announced that he intended to become a member of the society, and re- marked that the Widnes people did not approve altogether of oratorical music, suggesting that in future the concerts of the society should be of a miscellaneous character— say oratorio in the first part and secular music in the second. He thought it would he very inadvisable to increase the subscription to 103., for many persons would then be debarred from entlrint.t. If he might be allowed to make a suggestion, it would be that Mr. Carey, who so kindly conducted the nociety for three years, .should help it by again undertaking those duties. (A opl -ruse.) Last year Mr. Argent was engaged, and of course he had to be paid for his services. Mr. Carey could materially help the society out of its difficulties by again conducting the society, if it were not asking him to perform too much.— Mr. Iluerrest approved of this course.—The Rev. J. BOND said the debt might be cleared off by soliciting donations from the proprietors of the works in the neighbourhood, whose workpeople derived great advantages from the society. —The CHAIRMAN: It is quite right to think of that sugges- tion, but I, as a member of the society, dislike going round with the hat.—Mr. DAVIES (the secrettry), referring to the suggestion thrown out with reeard to the conductor, said the committee had had that question under their consideration, and they had taken upon themselves to decide that, for this season, at any rate, they could not widertake to engage Mr. Argent, because they saw the finances were in such a state they could not guarantee his salary. If Mr. Carey could see his way clear to resume the baton for this season the society might sail on well again, and have a balance in hand to pay off the old debt. (Applause.)—Mr. HUNTER observed that it was not money that was needed to make the society suc- cessful; they wanted determination on the part of those who undertook the singing and the conducting—(hear, hear)— and if the people did not feel sufficient interest in the society to make a little effort, he did not see what hope there was of it continuing with success. He thought they might derive considerable en- couragement from the report of the last concert, by which they realised £l5, and there was no reason why they should not do the same again. To ask Mr. Carey to again under- take the duties of conductor would be throwing the burden of the society on him. The members would be glad if Mr. Carey would again conduct, but that would be putting the burden from 80 on to one. The members ought to help themselves. Surely a debt of £l5 was not going to floor them.—The CHAIRMAN said he was very much ohliged to them for the kind way in which they had received the sug- gestion, but, as l•e told them before, he did not feel musically fit for the work, nor at present had he the energy to manage it. But he ha ct pleasant intelligence for them, which, he thought, would render it unnecessary to discuss that sub- ject. Mr. Argent called at his (Mr. Carey's) house the other evening, and he wished him to undertake to let his vieweiwith regard to the society be known to the members on certain conditions. If the society really wished to pro- ceed with its operations, and there was a reasonable pros- pect of the members working with enthusiasm, Mr. Argent permitted him to say that rather than allow the society to stop for want of funds to pay his salary, he would come from then to Christmas without charge whatever. (Ap- plause). He thought this was an extremely generous offer on the part of Mr. Argent. From what had been heard that night, there was a determination and a desire on the announcementt part of the society to meet its liabilities, and he thought he was Argentfehaind making to him.e Of course if of the the society e ing the ff ei- was successful, he (the chairman) did not think it would be fair to take Mr. Argent literally at his word, but he did not think

they could do better than accept the offer—(hear, hear)— at all events for one season. (Applause.) He presumed that the society would realise enough money from a concert or two to wipe off the liability, and start clear once more, then they would all wish to give Mr. Argent his usual remuneration. (Hear, hear, and applause.)—lt was then put to the vote as to whether the members should for the next season purchase their own music; and those present were unanimously in favour of this course.—Mr. HUNTER said ke would withdraw his proposition if there was any prospect of the debt being wiped off at the first concert.— The Rev. G. BOND wished the members of the Press to make it known that the society would be glad to receive contributions from outsiders.—Mr. WOMEN remarked that the gentleman to whom the society owed the debt would be very willing to reduce it if he wereasked.—The CHAIMUN Slid it was a fair debt, and the society ought to pay it.-11r. Hunter's proposition,that a double subscription he levied was then put, when only four voted for it : while the suggestion that members pay the ordinary subscription, purchase their own music, and that voluntary subscriptions be solicited from members, was carried by a large majority.—The CHAIRMAN moved that a cordial vote of thanks be tendered to Mr. Argent for his offer, which the society gratefully accepted.—Mr. CROSSLEY had great pleasure in seconding the motion, which was carried.—lt was decided, on the motion of Mr. CALLENDER, seconded by Mr. HUNTER, to hold a soirée on the sth October, and those gentlemen were appointed a sub-committee to carry out the arrangements.— CHAIRMAN said on Saturday one of the oldest members of the society, Mr. Rydeheard, met with an accident at the works where he was employed, and he died on Sunday night. He (the chairman) thought it would meet with the wishes of the members of the society to pass a vote of con- dolence with his family, which he begged to move.—The proposition was carried, and the meeting separatel

div.head: RUNCORN MAN'S RAILWAY ADVENTURE.
div.p: A RUNCORN MAN'S RAILWAY ADVENTURE.

ALLEGED ROBBERY. At the Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. G. Pilkington, Henry Wilson and Thomas Henry Ridgway, young men, from Warrington, were brought. up in custody to answer a charge of stealing a £2O note from the person of Thomas Rostron, stonemason, Shaw-street, Runcorn.—The prosecutor stated thatle went to Manchester on Thursday for the purpose of receiving some money, and he obtained £32. On his return, on Friday morning, he stopped at Warrington, where he met the prisoners. Together they visited a number of public-houses, and then went to Bank Qnay Station. They all entered the 11-50 train for Widnes, and when about half the distance had been completed, Rostron alleged one of the prisoners put his hand in his pocket, and aostrasted a £2O note. Rostron admitted he was under the influence of liquor at the titne.—Mr. Smith, station master at the London and North-Western Railway station, Widnes, deposed that on the arrival of the 11-50 train from Warring- ton, the guard informed him that the window of a third- class carriage was broken. He went to the carriage, and found the prosecutor lying on the seat in a state of drunken- ness ; but very little information could be gathered from him. By his orders Rostron was removed to the general waiting-room. About an hour later a porter informed him that Rostron alleged he had been robbed of a £2O note ; and information was given to the police. Subsequently P.C. Thompson apprehended the prisoners in Warrington.—The prisoners were remanded until Wednesday.—On Wednesday the prisoners were brought before Mr. J. Brock. Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, defended the prisoners.—Mr. Super- intendent Barker applied for a further remand.—Mr. Percy Davies said that under the circumstances that the prisoners lived in Warrington, and were only locked up at midnight on Fri#lay, and could not therefore engage a solicitor to appear for them on Saturday morning, he thought this course rather had, and applied for bail. He was prepared to produce substantial bail.—Mr. Barker objected to the prisoners being admitted to bail.—Mr. Davies said that if his worship were in possession of all the facts of the case, be was sure he would be of opinion that it was a matter that ought never to have been brought into court. The prisoners first saw the prosecutor at Warrington at 'ten o'clock on Friday morning, when he asked them where he could buy a pair of trousers. They took him to a pawnshop in Horse- market-street, where he purchased a pair for 4s. 11d. After- wards they went to a secluded part of the market ground. Here the prosecutor, whose trousers were in an unclean state, put on the new pair, and, accompanied by the prisoners, went to the Hop Pole public-house and paid for three glasses of rum, and gave them a shilling each. He also paid for rum at Walker's Vaults, Market Place, the Wool Pack, Sankey-street (where the waiter would not serve the prosecutor), the Millstone Inn, Stankey-street, and the Patten Arms. At the Millstone Mrs. Stevenson, the landlady, changed the prosecutor's glass of rum for soda water. The prosecutor now asked the prisoners to go with him .to Run- corn and see him right home, and at Bank Quay station purchased two return tickets for Runcorn and one single. Rostron paid for the whole of the tickets. On the journey from Warrington to Runcorn, between the former place and Widnes, Wilson tumbled against the window of the com- partment, smashing it and cutting his head. The pri- soners were so alarmed for the consequences of the damage that had been done, that they left the train at Wilnss, and returned to Warrington by the 1-15 train from Widnes Cen- tral station. Whilst at home they heard that inquiries were being made for thefn at Widnes and consequently gave them- selves up at Warrington Police Station.—Mr. Brock re- manded the prisoners for a week and refused to accept bail.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, at the Workhouse, Whiston, when there were present Mr. Tyrer (in the chair), the Rev. Mr. Barnacle, and Messrs. Fisher, Agnew, Hall, Sadlzr, Gerrard, Newsome, Dobell, Hulme, G ilbody, Penketh, Buckley, Leatherbarrow. Syder, Birch, and Tuson, and Mr. Hartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE MASTER'S RETORT.

The Workhouse Master's report showed that there were 463 inmates in the Workhouse, against 452 last week, and 449 in the corresponding week of last year. Seven children had been sent to the Kirkland Schools during the fortnight; and three deaths had occurred in the Workhouse during the same period.
T/IR PAYMENT OE GUARDIANS' DINNERS.
The following communication from the Local Government Board was read :

I am directed by the Local Government Board to fsrward ts the Guardians of the Poor of the Prescot Union the enctose copy of a letter which has been addressed to the Board by Air, Thomas Dennett, butcher, of Prescot. The Board are desirous of 13,ing furnished with any observations which the Guardians may de,ire to make on the subject.—Signe LW. J. SENDALL. Mr. Dennett's letter was as follows :

I beg to call your attention to the following parti,ulars. I was contractor for supply of butcher's meat t,) the Pres,!ot Union, in the qaarter beginning March 29(h, 1878, at the eal of which quarter my account was paid by seve•ai instalments (itistesd of by one cheque as usual) the last amount due being £2, lie 10d. A cheque of £22 17s lid was seat to me, leaving a balance of £1 iSa ltd, with a note sating that the balance would be paid shorty. As I continued to suPply the Union after the quarter I added the balance time after time which was always deducted from my ace )unt whin payment wis made, although I protested against it, and when I spoke of con.ulting a lawyer the °Jerk said I coo d not recover it as it wls past the date allowed by your laws. I shall be extremely obliged if you will give me advice on the subject, as it has not been left tr• paid through any neglect of mins in presenting the balance due, and I.think it is not right that I sh mid loose such an amount. It was in consequence of the clerk's repeated promisei tit-a it should be paid that I allowed it ta stand over so long. The Guardians acknowledge it as a debt still owing. Mr. BARNACLE asked Mr. Hartley it he had promised very frequently that amount should be paid.—Mr. HARTLEY could not say that, but as a matter of fact the amount had been deducted from the account by the workhouse master as being the price of the beef consumed by the Guardians at their dinner. The amount ha s 1 been deducted before the account ever came into his (the clerk's) office. At the time he told Mr. Dennett that the sum would be paid, he was under the impression that Mr. Archer, the workhouse master at the time, would have paid it; it appeared he had not done so.—Mr. HALL said Mr. Archer collected money from the Guardians to pay for it.—Mr. HARTLEY said the Guardians used to pay- Mr. Archer for their dinners. Mr. 'BARNACLE: Mr. Archer received the money from the Guardians then and did not pay it to Mr. Dennett.—Mr. LEATHEREARROW said he know the Guardians used to pay for their dinners, and if there was any deficiency a whip went round, and they contributed so much a piece.—The CHAIRMAN said there was no doubt about the fact that it ought to be paid; it was very unfair to keep it back.—Mr. BARNACLE said it was very unfair to Mr. Dennett, but the question was bow was it to be paid.—The CHAIRMAN said the Local Government Board could not authorise them to pay it; and if they paid it they would be surcharged.—Mr. HARTLEY: What shall say to the Local Government Board; must I write and sty the Guardians have no observations to make on the letter P—This sugges- tion was agreed to, Mr. Hartley being instructed to write to the Local Government Board to state that the Guardians had no observations to make on Me. Dennett's letter. CONSUMPTION OF SPIRITS, frIC . AT THE WORICHOUSE.

The following returns of the quantities of spirits, wines, and malt liquor consumed at the Workhouse during the year ending 31st December. 131, was submitted by Mr. Hartley, viz :—Spirits, 1,227 pints, cost £3O 7s. 5d.; wine, 25 pints, cost £1 19s. 2d.; malt liquor, 441 gallons, £5 10s. The daily average of inmates in Workhouse during the year had been 528. This return, Mr. Hartley said, had been requested by the Local Government Board, and _would be forwarded to them.

div.head: Ea RESIGNATION.
div.p: Ea RESIGNATION.

A letter was read from Mr. Leyland, registrar of births and deaths for the sub-district, resigning his position owing to continued ill-health.—Notice was given of the appoint- ment of a successor at nezt meeting. 'THE ARREARS.-lIYTOIT OTERSEERS TO BE PROCBEDBD

div.head: AGAINST.
div.p: AGAINST.

The CLERK read the following letter from Mr. Henry Alison, county treasurer's office, Preston : I beg to call your attention to the amount of county rates, due on 281 h ult., by Presc it Union, nnd to request that the same be forthwith d'scharged, or that you furnish me with the names of the townsiiips in the above Union which are in arrears, together with the amount due by each, in order that I may be eqabled to take proceedings agalnst -the overseers of the same.

Mr. HARTLEY said the Guardians had entrusted him with a chcque for the full amount, but had instructed him to withhold it until all arrears were paid. All had now been paid, with the exception of those of Huyton ; Much Wool- ton also owing a little.—Mr. HALL asked what was to be done about Huyton; they could not let it remain in arrears.

—The CHAIRMAN : We cannot send the cheque unless Hay ton paid.—Mr. HARTLEY said if the county authorities got the full amount they would have no grounds of complaint against Huyton.—The CHAIRMAN: If we pay we must at once take. proceedings against Huyton. Mr. HARTLEY : Will you order me to send the cheque, and then take pro- ceedings against the Huyton overseers. Mr. HALL said the overseers had get the money in their hands; it was not as if they had not got the money. He would move that pro- ceedings be taken against them.—Mr. NEWSOME said he had pleasure in seconding that proposit;on.—lt was thee unani- mously agreed that action should be taken against the Huy- ton overseers to recover the arrears. THE RELIEF OFFICE RENTS.
Mr. HARTLEY read a letter from Mr. Wilcock, St. Helens, requesting that the rents of the relief offices should be paid to him in future, and not to Mr. Haslam.

THE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES. Mr. SADLER, in accordance with notice of motion, moved that the Board should give the clerk instructions to write to the Local Government Board applying for an increase of Guardians for the tewnship of Widnes. The ratepayers of that townsbip seemed dissatisfied with the present number of representatives, and he believed that according to the assessment and p pulation of the town they had room for at least two. If they wished he could give them figures as to the assessment and population.—Mr. NEWSOME had great pleasure in seconding this proposition, because he considered from the large extent of the parish of Widnes, its large .population and assessment, that they were jUstly entitled to some difference. If they took into consideration the other small townships, he thought Widnes would be entitled to at least a dozen representatives. There was also to be taken into consideration the distance, and the work which fell upon the Widnes representatives. For these reasons he had pleasure in seconding the motion.—The motion was then unanimously a Jeed to.—The CHAIRMAN : I hope this will only end in Widnes paying as well as the other towns. —Mr. Donna,: How are they paving now? Mr. HARTLEY : They are paying very well; I think the new officer is working remarkably well.—Mr. NADLER : We have r. Aid over £770 this week.—Mr. Gmßonr : It must be the commission.—Mr HARTLEY said the officers had not yet been" paid by commission.

div.head: APPOINTING A MEDICAL OFFICER.
div.p: APPOINTING A MEDICAL OFFICER.

There were two applicants—Dr. Chisholm and Dr. Wood— for the vacant post of medical officer to the district of 11/le and Woolton.—Nlr.Dormr, moved, and Mr.l3lncit seconded, the appointment of Dr. Chisholm; and Mr. HALL moved, and Mr. LauTitsnanannow seconded, the appointment of Dr. Wood. On a vote being taken only two voted for Dr. Chisholm, and 14 for Dr. Wood. Dr. Wood was, therefore, appointed.—This concluded the business.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Work- ' ouse on Tuesday. The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner presided, and there were also present—Messrs. J. Darbyshire, John Highfield, Thomas Andrews' J. Midvrood, John Weir, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Far- rington (nuisance inspector):

THE CLERK AND HIS ORITICS. The CLERK said he wished to make a remark with respect to a statement made by a member of the Board at the last meeting. It was alleged that he had deceived the Authority in relation to the special drainage district. He (the clerk-) thought the charge an unwarrantable one to be made in his absence. He read the following extract from the report on the scheme suggested for water supply to Frodsham, show- ing what took place with regard to the subject :—" The Frodsham Parochial Committee defined the special drainage district in November, 1877, which they proposed to supply with water according to Mr. Titnmins; scheme number four; but on being pressed by the Local Government Board to submit a scheme for approval they abandoned the special drainage district of the water scheme by resolution passed 9th July, 1878." He (the clerk) wished that gentlemen before they made I emarks of the kind he had alluded to, in the absence of the clerk, " knew what they were talkisg about."

div.head: SATISFACTORY STATEMENT.
div.p: A SATISFACTORY STATEMENT.

The estimates for the half-year ending Lady-day, 1533, were submitted by the deputy clerk. It appeared that the Authority had ample funds at their disposal on general ex- penses account to meet all requirements up to that date, and no calls would therefore be required from the overseers for this half-year.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER AND AM. CHALLONER.
div.p: THE MEDICAL OFFICER AND AM. CHALLONER.

The following letter had been receiTed from Mr. J. G. Bride, the medical officer : To the members of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority.— Gentiernen,—l shall be Wad if Mr. Chatloner will state definitely the nature and rosition of the nuisances he Cont- ia ,ined 11,d not been observed by Mr. Farrington and myself. e former invariably attends to his dut1,..8 in a praiseworthy linnet, aud the latter—myself—le unwilling to inte fere with the sanitary inypeotor's duties.
The Clerk was instructed to forward a copy of the letter to Mr. Challoner, who was not present at the meeting.
FRODSHAM LORDSHIP SIWERAGE. The following letter from the Local Government Board was; read : _

13th Ikeptember, 1882.—Sir,—I an directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge receipt of you letter of the 6th inst., informing them that the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Runc,rn Union have rescinded their former resolution to proceed with the deferred portions •f the sewerage scheme for Frodsham Lordship. The Board direct me express their regret at the decision which has been arrived at by the Rural Rotatory Authority in this matter. In their letter of th 3 let Aug., 1882, the Board ad wised the aural Sanitary Authority that the part of the township sewerage whic`a you now propose in- definitely to postpone was in need of proper sewers, and the entire responsibility of deferring such a necessary provisi.,n for the health of part of their district must Tea% up na the Authority. am, sir, your obedient se.vant, J. If. RorTos, assistant secretary. This was all the business of public interest.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The Rev.& W. N. Tanner presided at the meeting held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. There were also present—Messrs. William H indley, Thomas Norman, John Weir, J. Midwood, Thomas Andrews, J. Darbyshire, J. Highfield, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).
THE REPRESENTATION OVEST/0.-THE GUARDIANS
DIFEATED.

A letter dated the 13th inst., had been received from the Local Government Beard, acknowledging the receipt of a letter from the clerk, forwarding copy of the resolution passed by the Guardians rescinding the resolution passed by them with regard to the amalgamation of certain parishes in the Union for purposes of election of Guardians. The Local Government Board had carefully considered each of the resolutions passed on the 13th and 27th June, and it appeared to them that the townships of Appleton and Wes- ton were according to their population and rateable value not duly represented on the Board of Guardians. They were also of opinion that some of the parishes were so small both in population and rateable value that they might be united to the adjoining parishes for the purposes of the election of Guardians, under the provisions contained in the statute 31 and 32 Vic., cap. 122, section 6. The Board proposed, there- fore, to iesue an order adding the township of Daresbury to the township of Kekewick, and the township of S;.ockham to the township of Norton for the purposes named, antho icing the election of additional Guardians for each of the town- ships of Appleton and Weston, such order to take effect at the next annual election. Mr. WEIR advised that the consideration of the matter be postponed until next meeting, when, perhaps, the Guardians for Stockham and Daresbury would be present. --The CLERK pointed out that the Board could not postpone the matter at all. The Local Government Board were merely advising the Guardians of their intentions.—The Board in- structed the Clerk to intimate to the overseers the iutentions of the Local Government Board.

div.head: ALTERATIONS TO THE WORYNOUSE.
div.p: ALTERATIONS TO THE WORYNOUSE.

The DErtrrY CLERK read a letter which had been received from the assistant secretary to the Local Government Board, who stated that when certain forms, which were enclosed, were filled up, they would proceed to issue an order for the expenditure and loan to be incurred for the new engine and boiler for the house and the new entrance. Under present circumstances, added' the Local Government Board, the repayment of the loan could not be allowed to ex- tend over ten years.—On the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. NORMAN, it was decided to ask the Local Government Board to extend the period for the repayment of the loan to 20 years.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr. HANDLEY, in presenting the report of the Finance Committee, stated that the total ameunt of accounts passed was £1,709 3s. Bd. Considering that during the past year very substantial additions had been made to the Workhouse, he thought the estimate for the half-year ending Lady Day next was very satisfactory. The estim- ate had been very carefully and ably prepared by the clerk, and all particulars were given in detail. After the expenditure of the present half-year, which ended on the 29th September, there would probably be a balance of £2,057. The probable expenditure for the next half-year would be £7,409, male up as follows :—School fees for non- pauper children, £7; county rate, £1,905; Union fund charges £4,013, including hospital loan and interest of £BB ; balance and contingency fund, £2,091. From these items were to be deducted £715, the estimate amount of repay- ments by the Paymaster-General ; and the balance of £2,057 above-named ; which left the amount required, £5,352. He (Mr. Handley) was glad to say that the rateable value of the Union was still increasing. At the present time its value stood at £205,777, which was an increase on the corresponding half-year of last year of £4,702. A rate of BFI. in the £ would realise £5,358 15s. 7d. This was a decrease of d. in the £on the rite for the half-year just closing, and seeing that the expenditure which had been incurred included the cost of the enlargement and furnish- ing of the hospital, he thought they might consider the finances of the Union in a very satisfactory state. (Hear, hear.) No other business of public interest was before the Board.

div.head: .....-.--....1P.-'--..".
div.p: ALLEGED FAGGOT-VOTING IN LOCFIABEIL—Lord Abinger appeared personally at a meeting of the Valuation Commit- tee of Inverness-shire, on Tuesday, to defend himself from a charge of having created thirty-one faggot votes on his pro- perty in Lochaber. His lordship, in an impassioned speech, declared that the charge was a monstrous one. His tenants were as free to their political opinions as to the air they breathed. The further consideration of the charge was adjourned till Friday, the 29th inst.

div.head: ALLEGED CITA.RGE OF TIORSF,- STEALING.
div.p: ALLEGED CITA.RGE OF TIORSF,- STEALING.

Joseph Pilling was brought up under a warrant at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday—Messrs. P. Stubs and S. Rigby being on the bench—charged with fraudulently and by means of false pretences obtaining a horse, value £2, from James Ovens, the property of Peter Robinson, of Church-street, Warrington.—Mr. Moore defended the prisoner.—Peter Robinson said that on the morning of the sth inst., he bought a horse from Mr. Aaron Toft, a man who travels about the country with swing-boats, dec., the bargain being made in Mr. Toft's van at Cadishead. The horse was delivered to him when he paid for it, and he led it out of the stable a short distance away. He engaged a boy named James Ovens to take the animal to his pre- mises at Warrington. The lad, however, did not take the horse to Warrington, as directed. As he was proceeding home some time after he had deepatched the lad with the horse, he met the Prisoner driving in the direction of Cadis- head with two dead horses in his cart, and a live horse tied behind. As the prisoner passed him he shouted to him and told him that the horse he had tied behind his cart was his property. Prisoner replied that he did not kiiow anything about it, and drove off. The same night about ten o'clock prisoner's nephew brought the horse to his house. He, how- ever, would not receive it, and told the lad to take it to the police station. During the course of the day the prosecutor had obtained a warrant for the arrest of the prisoner. He found the horse about two days afterwards in a pin-fold. —Cross-examined by Mr. Moore, Mr. Robinson said that he did not tell Mr. Tuft that his name was Pining. When he met Pilling on the road he did not get out of his trap and examine the horse, nor did he say that the horse was not his. He shouted to Pilling "that is my horse behind your cart," and the prisoner replied "I do not know anything about it," and drove off.—James Ovens, a lad, who was tramping with his father and family from Manchester to St. Helens, said that when passing through Cadishead Mr. Robinson asked him if he was going to Warrington, and whether he would take the horse to his premises there. The lad replied in the affirmative, and en being assured that he would receive piyment if he delivered the horse safely at Mr. Robinson's residence in Church-street, he took charge of thnetnimal and went on his way. He had not got far on the road before he was met by the prisoner who asked him where he was taking the horse. Witness replied that he was taking it to Mr. Robinson's at Warrington. Pilling then said " That horse belongs to me ; I bought it last night. If you take it to Warrington you will only have the trouble to bring it back again. I have to meet Mr. Robinson at Irlain Station, for I am his 'gaffer?' The lad then said that before be gave the horse up he should require to be paid for his trouble. Pri- soner offered him 6d, but subsequently gave him 13 6d. Prisoner tied the horse behind his cart and drove off.— Cross-examined by Mr. Moore, Ovens said that it was his father who received the money from the prisoner. Mr. Moore, for the defence, contended that Oven's evidence was not to be relied upon. The prosecator and prisoner were rivals to a certain extent in the same trade. The prisoner had made arrangements to buy the horse from Mr. Tort the night previous, and, when he met the boy, he was on his way for the purpose of buying the animal. The lad had for- gotten the name of the person to whom he was taking the horse, and, en prisoner asking him if it was Pilling, the lad replied that he thought that was the name. When Robinson met Pilling with the horse he got out of his trap and examined it, and said, "this is not my horse," and that was the reason Pilling took the horse away. The prisoner, on getting to Cadishead, went to the police station and saw a constable. He told the officer that he had made arrangements to buy the horse the previous night, and that the lad he met did not know where he was taking the horse to. The officer then went with him to Mr. Tuft, and on being told that the horse had been sold to Robinson the prisoner sent his nephew with it to Robinson's house. The prisoner never stole the horse. There was no felonious intention at all, and in his (Mr. Moore's) opinion it was an action of spite on the part of the prosecutor.—P.S. Berry spoke to the man coming to his place and going with him to Cadishead to see Mr. Tort. —The Chairman said.: Pilling, you are very near being sent for trial at the quarter bessions, but there is some doubt about the case, and we have decided not to send it. It is dismissed, but be very cautious for the future.

div.head: DARING ROBBERY AT HUYTON POST OFFICE.
div.p: DARING ROBBERY AT HUYTON POST OFFICE.

On Thursday, a robbery of a singularly daring character took place at Huyton post office. About one o'clock in the afternoon Mr. Newlands, the postmaster, was engaged in the domestic portion of his premises, when his attention was attracted to the shop. On going there be saw a man lean- ing over the counter, and on attempting to get hold of him the man turned round ana struck Mr. Nevrlands a violent blow On the head with a life preserver, which rendered him insensible. The man then appears to have emptied the till of its contents, about X 25, and made his escape. Mr. Newlands was found some few minutes after still in an in- sensible condition, and on recovering consciousness the only description of the thief he could give likely to lead to his detention was that he was very tall. Information was at once given to the police, but every effort to discover the whereabouts of the thief has hitherto proved unsuccessful.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE STATE OF EGYPT.
ADVANCE ON DAMIETTA.

A Central News telegram from Alexandria, dated Friday, 10-30 a.m., says :—" The difficulty at Damietta will pro- bably end without bloodshed. One thousand of the rebels surrendered at Tantah, last night. Another train load is expected in this morning. General Wood proceeded at day- break to Damietta, with the 53r1, 38th, and half of the 35th• Regiments. The 49th remain here, and the Malta Fencibles take their place in the exppditi3n. Numerous arrests continue to be made."

Another telegram says :—All the rebel officials below the rank of colonel who have been brought to Ramleh have been liberated. The remainder, numbering over fifty, were brought to Alexandria under escort last night. The expedi- tion to Damietta started early this morning, via Tantah. The naval expedition consists of a corvette and two gun vessels, under the command of Captain Seymour, of H.M.'s despatch vessel Iris. No resistance is anticipated.

The Press Association learns that Messrs. Charles Orton and D. Smith have received an anonymous gift of £lOO for the purpose of starting at once for Australia, there to identify, if possible, the patient Creswell, in the Paramatta Lunatic Asylum, as Arthur Orton. On Wednesday week a boy, named James Coulter, aged five, of Elizabeth-street, Farnworth, was missed from home. His younger brother told his parent that James had fallen into a reservoir at Farnworth Paper Mills, and men have been engaged daily dragging the water. On Thursday night the joyful intelligence was conveyed to tha parents that the boy had been found alive at Worsley. How he came there is not known.

At Liverpool, yesterday, an assistant letter carrier, named Ashton, was remanded on a charge of stealing a post letter. Letters having been missed from the Eastern District office, a test letter was sent containing Money and stamps to the amount of 15s. .111 e prisoner did not deliver the letter, and the marked money was found on him. A member's card for a betting club and a book containing bets were also found on him. The prisoner, who said it was his first offence, was remanded.

A shocking case of female savagery was disclosed in the Livetpool Police-court, yesterday. A woman named Martin was charged with cruelty to her children. On Thursday night, while in a drunken passion, she seized her son aged seven and bit him savagely on his cheek, inflicting an ugly wound. She also struck him on the head with a poker. She then hit her daughter aged four. Neither children had given any provocation. The Stipendiary, in remanding the pri- soner, said she ought to be caged like a tiger. At Sheffield Town Hall, yesterday morning, William Grey and Cornelius Whittaker were sent to gaol for two months each for savagely assaulting two fellow workmen. The men were employed by Messrs. Andrews, steel manufacturers, and the firm wishing their employee to go on piece work, the prisoners came out on strike, and waylaid the prosecu- tors, Irwin and Thompson, kicking them seriously. Such terrorism prevailed that one hundred workmen dare not go into the shop. EXTENSIVE FRAUDS AT HANLEY.

Yesterdiy the Hanley magistrates committed for trial Samuel Cheadle, on a number of charges of obtaining money by false pretences under extraordinary circumstances. The prisoner—pretending that he had had £3,900 left him by a deceased relative, and producing documents that are alleged to be false—obtained large sums of money in advance from solicitors and others on the strength of his "expecta- tions."

div.head: SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE MINERS AND THEIR
div.p: THE SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE MINERS AND THEIR
WAGES.

At a large representative meeting of miners, held yester- day at Lower Goma!, it was resolved to give notice for an advance of 4d. a day in thick coal and 2d. in slack. The meeting condemned the course being pursued ty some miners in demanding a large increase in., wages, but con- tended- that South Staffordshire coalmasters could easily give a small increase, as the coal trade was now very brisk throughout the district. LETTER FROM MR GRAY, M.P.

Mr. Gray, M.P., the imprisoned High Sheriff of Dublin, has written a letter to the Lord Mayor Dawson, regading the development of Irish manufactures. He recommends that a second exhibition should be held next year, and the formation of an association to push the sale of Irish mann- - factures. Ho advocates the holding of an Irish exhibition in America, and that the American Government should be asked to modify the tariff in favour of Irish productions. xEcurioN OF THE LETTERFRACK MURDERER. Patrick Walsh was executed yesterday morning at Gal- way. Accompanied by Marwood, the condemned inan pro- ceeded from the hospital to the wing of the gaol. He walked firrnly, with bent head and tears in his eyes. Walsh stood pinioned and ascended the scaffold with slight evidence of feebleness. Just before the veil was nut over his head, he said, "I am n going before my God tied up as a criminal. All the witnesses swore falsely against tie." The noose being adjusted, the bolt was drawn, and the drop fell in a moment. Very few people were outside the prison. A large number of soldiers and policemen were on the ground. The con- demned man's thother was outside the prison walls crying all the morning. SAD INCIDENT AT THE TRADES UNION CON- GRESS.—DEATH OF A DELEGATE.

At the Trades Union Congress, at Manchester, yesterday, on the delegates re-assembling the p tint ul announcement was made that shortly after midnight, John Whalley, secre- tary to the Weavers' Association, Blackbarn, who on leaving the Congress on Thursday, was apparently in good he ilth, had been found dead in one of the rooms at the Falstaff Hotel, where he had been staying, apoplexy bAng the cause of death. A resolution of condolence was ordered to be forwarded to the deceased delegate's family. CENSURE BY A JURY.

An inquest was held at Oldhatn yesterday forenoon on an old man named John Marsland, who was killed in a trap accident. He was knocked down whilst standing in Do- mingo street by a trap driven towards Royton, and his skull fractured. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, but passed a censure on some person or persons unknown for their inhumanity in not attending to the deceased after knocking him down. _ THE SOCIAL SCIENCE CONGRESS.

The proceedings of the Congress commenced yesterday morning by an address in the Mechanics' Hall, by Mr. Woodhall, M.P. for Stoke, president of the Education Depart- ment. Mr. Hastings, M.P., was in the chair, and there was a large audience-. The barometer is rapidly rising, and the weather is beautifully fine but cold. The sale of tickets has not been as large as at some of the other meetings, but between six and seven hundred have been disposed of. The special questions considered were, in the International and Munici- pal Law Department, the expediency of altering the system of trial by jury • in the Repression of Crime Department, criminal law reform; in the Education Department, the en- dowment research; in the Health Department, the adminis- tration of the hospital; in the Economic Department, the reform of the licensing laws; and in the Art Department, the new Royal College of Music.— Mr. Woodall, in his opening address, reviewed the educa- tional changes which have been accomplished during the five and twenty years of the existence of the Congress, and the work which has also been carried out in other countries. With regard to the new code, he asserted that while it gives evidence here and there of compromise and concession, on the whole it contains some unnecessarily inconvenient pro- visions.—Mr. C. Lloyd and other gentlemen, in discussing the new Royal College of Music, anticipated the most satis- factory results from its operations in rendering the British public more musical, and re-establishing a national school of composition.—Mr. Yates, in the Health Department, advo- cated bread reform, condemning the exclusive use of white bread.—Mrs. King discussed national dress, and Sir J. Pope Hennessy gave an interesting account of the Chinese system of sewage.

eIOWLEY'S MIDDLE SCHOOL.—These Schools' will be IL-, OPENED for tuition on MONDAY the 9th OCTOBER NeXT. M. E. J. SIMPSON, M.A., Trinity College, Cambridge, Head- ma,ter of Hinckley Grammar School, has been appointed Head Master of the boy's school, and Miss Kate Jurgenson, L.L.A., Et And ewe, late assistant mistress at Norwich High School, Head Mistress of the girls' school. Tuition fees: boys, £8 per annum ; girls, £7 per annum ; entrance fee, XI. To enable the governors to determine the number of assistant masters and mistresses required, intending pupPs are requested ti apply for admission ti) the schools without delay. Applications for ad- mission must be made on forms to be obtained from me, the undersigned. No boy or girl under 8 years admittei. The ex- amination for admission will be held at the schools on Thurs- day, the sth day of October next, the following being the standard. Reading simple narrative, writing text hand, sums in the first rules of arithmetic with the multiplication table. THOMAS BREWIS, Clerk to the Governors. Town Hall, St. He!ens, lOtia Angust, 1882. TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- couraging amongst their consumers the use of GAS FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Sell, Let out on Hire, or Pnrchase, Lease, GAS COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be selected from the best makers for ec momy in consumption of gas, rerfection in cooking, and construoted on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee. in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, wig lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, Manager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882.

-- SEAFIELD HOUSE, LIVERPOOL. This New Hotel, which combines all the social advantages of a Hydropathic Establishment, will be open for the rc.seption of visitors on the 25th September. The hotel is situated on the etore, on the lAncashire side of the Mersey. seaward of the Lighthouse and Fort at New Brighton. Its position thus secures to visitors the first of the ozone as it CORM in its purity, fresh from the open sea. There are two asciendas, from whieh a view is obtained of the arrivals and deps,rtur,s of the qnsurpassed extent of shipping which frequents the Mersey. The Conservatories. Winter Gardens, and Recreation Grounds cove • an area of about ten acres. The Bedroom accommodation is for about 250 visitors, to- gether with requisite Sitting Rooms. Salt Water and other Baths Gymnasium. Re ding, Concert, and Recreation Rooms. Billiard Room, Five Tables. Telephone. Special Telegraph Wire to all parts of the IC ing- dom T,legraphic and Cable Address—" &afield, Liverpool." Table d'Hote at 6-30. The distance from the Exchange station. Liverpool, of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, is from 15 to 20 minutes. The service is most complete. 104 trains rnn daily to and from Waterloo A new and commodious station has lately been pro- vided there. Private conveyances from the hotel will meet every train. The drive to the hotel is about 5 minutes. The Waterloo omnibus also passes the establishment every half hour to and from the Liverpool Exchange. Special terms can be arranged for permanent residents. Add: ass— C. NAV., Manager. The hotel will be opened on Monday afternoon, 25th Septem- ber, at Three o'clock, by the Right Honcurable the Earl of Lathom, on which occasion the Countess and the Ladies Eikel- meri.dale have signified their intention to be present.

THE EXAMINER, &Ayr URDAY, SEPTEMBER 23, 1882. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. An adjourned meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held at Alforde Chambers, yesterday afternoon. Mr. Pank- burst was voted to the chair, and there were also present Messrs. Carey, Midwood, Martley, Webster, Sadler, Ker- shaw, Higginson (surveyor), Allen (clerk), and Dixon (nuisance inspector). The object of the meeting was to discuss and adopt the bye-laws of the various co:nmit tees. lIRAL'fII BYE-LAWS. Pit I Mr. CAREY proposed, and Mr. MARTLEY seconded, the adoption of the bye-laws of the Health Committee. After a little uninteresting discussion, Mr. CARIIY said it was felt by many members of the Board, and also by Mr. Dixon, that a clause with reference to chaff beds was re- quired. Mr. Drecoer suggested that a bye-law should be drawn up prohibiting the emptying of chaff beds in open places. The chaff might be placed in the ashpit. Mr. MIDWOOD remarked on the nuisance caused by the practice, and Mr. KERSHAW was of opinion that persons ought to be compelled to burn the chaff. Mr. CAREY pointed out the dangtr of this course. Mr. HANDLEY considered that the clause with reference to the depositing of dust and rubbish would meet the case. Ultimately chaff beds was classed with rubbish, and it was prohibited front being deposited on vacant land. The bye-laws were passed. MR KERSHAW ON THE MODEL BYE-LAWS. Mr. KERSHAW, as chairman of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, submitted the bye-laws relating to their depart- ment, and said he had certain alterations to suggest, but he should not-vote for them, so that in the event of an inquiry being held, he should be able to take an untrammelled course. _He bad before him a book which it would take a week to digest in reference to the model bye-laws issued by the Local Government Board, which he first saw on the previous evening. The book he referred to was a report by the Council of the Liverpool Architectural Society. It was dated 6th September, 1877, and entered into the subject fully and in a technical manner. His (Mr. Kershaw's) opinion of the model bye-laws was that they were altogether too impracticable to be carried out—they were thorough rubbish. The Board then proceeded to consider Mr. Kershaw's alterations to the Board's bye-laws. The discussion was not of general interest, the matter being of a very technical description. The Board adjourned at half-past five.
